title: From Hunt the Wumpus to EverQuest: Introduction to Quest Theory
venue: Entertainment Computing: ICEC 2005, Lecture Notes in Computer Science 3711
summary: Theory paper defining quest games by concrete, attainable goals and proposing three basic quest types (place, time, objective) and their combinations, alongside three landscape types (linear corridor, hub, open landscape). Argues that quests are the designer's main tool for directing the player's agenda, that spatial layout and quest structure constrain which stories are possible, and that the most story-like games are the most spatially constrained.
notes: ICEC 2005 refereed conference paper (IFIP, Springer LNCS 3711); Crossref types LNCS proceedings papers as book-chapter. Full text read via the IFIP digital library.

title: Bringing BioShock Infinite's Elizabeth to Life: An AI Development Postmortem
summary: Postmortem of the companion AI for Elizabeth in BioShock Infinite. The abstract frames companions as characters engaged with the player for hours and often the focus, expected to be leader and follower, dynamic and scripted, entertainer and entertained, and describes resolving those competing goals with ideas from other entertainment media and a studio design pillar, illustrated by before-and-after footage.
notes: Only the Vault abstract was read; the session is not on the official GDC YouTube channel.

title: Galak-Z: Forever: Building Space-Dungeons Organically
summary: 17-BIT's lead engineer on Galak-Z's dungeon generator, adopted after hand-built levels proved too slow. Whole-level cellular-automata caves looked right but were hard to control and populate, so CA was limited to fixed-size room templates that designers touched up and annotated in a layered editor with an in-game preview. BSP plus spanning-tree layouts failed; a Hilbert curve sampled at a random offset gave the main path, and layouts without enough dead ends for objectives were discarded and regenerated, which was cheap. Zones gave variety and orientation. Advice: one coordinate system, keep drawings, data in JSON, and a hand-made benchmark level.
notes: Alternate Vault pages for the same session (same title and conference in the Vault crawl) are listed in alt_urls.

title: I Shot You First: Networking the Gameplay of HALO: REACH
summary: Bungie's lead networking engineer on 16-player competitive Halo: Reach (host-client, no dedicated servers). The host is authoritative for nearly everything; clients have bounded authority over their own character. Replication splits droppable state, unguaranteed events and compact per-player control data, filled into packets by per-object priority. Mechanics were split into predicted and host-adjudicated parts: grenade throws hide the round trip behind the throw animation, and Armor Lock shipped only after the host shortened its startup by the measured round trip, a change made after two earlier versions failed, the second in the public beta. Advice: ask where each mechanic hides lag.
notes: Audit 08: transcript re-read. Armor Lock v1 never shipped (failed in internal take-home tests); only v2 reached the public beta, so the summary no longer says beta players rejected 'earlier versions'. Title, speaker, year unchanged. Alternate Vault pages for the same session (same title and conference in the Vault crawl) are listed in alt_urls.

title: Always Be Composing: The Flexible Music System of 'Plants vs. Zombies Heroes'
summary: PopCap's audio director on the adaptive score of a card game, built to support gameplay. The on-screen phase indicator (each side's turn, tricks, combat) became the music's structural driver. A shared tempo and a shared key per hand held different hero themes together; a shared instrument set, faction instruments and one or two unique instruments per hero gave identity; intensity built across the typical number of hands. Transitions were tuned by playing: an interruption that sounded better at a musical boundary felt unresponsive, so it was made immediate. Content was cut to fit mobile size and schedule budgets.

title: Valve's Approach to Playtesting: the Application of Empiricism
summary: Valve's experimental psychologist sets out the studio's playtest philosophy: designs are hypotheses, playtests are experiments, and sessions test for fun rather than bugs, balance or focus-group opinion, early and repeatedly, with data gathering continuing after ship. Each method gets pros and cons: observation (what players do beats what they say, but observers bias sessions and one salient event can skew reading), think-aloud, Q&A and surveys (group and question biases; people cannot always say why they acted), gameplay stats (objective trends, but averages hide extremes and patterns can be illusory), design experiments, and costly, intrusive physiological measures.
notes: The Vault entry is the slide deck (PDF, 72 slides, marked free content); no recording is available. The deck was read in full; summary and citing claims stay within the slide text.

title: The impact of tutorials on games of varying complexity
venue: Proceedings of the SIGCHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI 2012)
summary: Online multivariate experiment with over 45,000 new players of three games made by the authors' lab (Refraction, Hello Worlds, Foldit). Tutorials raised play time by up to 29% and levels completed by up to 75% only in Foldit, the most complex and unconventional game; they had no significant positive effect in the two simpler casual games. In-context instructions beat an up-front manual only in Foldit; blocking 'stencil' tutorials showed no benefit; an on-demand help button helped Foldit but reduced progress and play time in Refraction. The authors caution that the games are not commercial titles.

title: Level Design in 'HITMAN': Guiding Players in a Non-Linear Sandbox
summary: IO Interactive designers describe closed-alpha players who were lost and overwhelmed in HITMAN's Paris sandbox. Isolated test chambers teaching one mechanic each did not prepare players for the combined sandbox, so the tutorial became small but real sandboxes, iterated from paper prototypes with user research every other week. An optional guidance system for scripted assassination routes followed principles such as: information should never be a prerequisite for progression, the level must stay playable without guidance, and each guide must fail gracefully.
notes: Alternate Vault pages for the same session (same title and conference in the Vault crawl) are listed in alt_urls.

title: AI Arborist: Proper Cultivation and Care for Your Behavior Trees
summary: Three practitioners on behavior-tree practice. Vehkala: keep the blackboard compact, move conditions, cooldowns, retries and debug tags or breakpoints into reusable decorators, split trees by reference or runtime attachment (smart objects, weapons), and avoid uninterruptible nodes. Anguelov: trees are acyclic and handle cyclic state changes, transitions and context-dependent priorities badly, which pushes control-flow flags into agent knowledge; use small trees to execute a chosen behavior and a state machine or other method to choose it. Weber: patterns from a reactive-planning StarCraft bot, such as concurrent daemon goals, managers and message passing.
notes: Transcript from the official GDC YouTube upload. The Vault also lists id 1024703. Alternate Vault pages for the same session (same title and conference in the Vault crawl) are listed in alt_urls.

title: App Review Guidelines
summary: Apple's rules for App Store submissions. Guideline 2.1 (App Completeness) requires submissions to be final versions with complete metadata and working URLs, with placeholder content removed, tested on-device for bugs and stability, and with demo account details when login is required; incomplete bundles and binaries that crash are rejected. A 'Before You Submit' checklist lists common causes of rejection.
notes: Read the App Completeness guideline and the Before You Submit list on the checked date.

title: Do You Copy? Dialog System and Tools in 'Firewatch'
summary: Campo Santo programmers on Firewatch's event system, built on Valve's rule-matching approach. Events carry requirements tested against scoped blackboards (per object, per day, global) and fire responses such as lines, captions or level scripts. Sorting by requirement count picks the most specific match, but designers needed a priority override once facts implied one another. Lessons: flexible tools are fragile, so log every event and match; modal conversation state must be released at every exit; a web content system gave each line a stable ID for recording and translation. Advises pseudo-localization early and persistent string IDs rather than English text as keys.
notes: Alternate Vault pages for the same session (same title and conference in the Vault crawl) are listed in alt_urls.

title: Building Cognitive Accessibility Into Your Games
summary: Accessibility specialists from EA, Xbox and independent practice on cognitive accessibility: helping players process what they perceive before acting. Barriers: cognitive and sensory overload, unclear objectives, illegible text, over-complicated instructions. Practices: manual saves at any time; specific, well-timed content warnings written without spoilers; clear subtitles; always-available practice and tutorials; toggleable control prompts; navigation help; letting players turn off non-essential UI animation; regular testing for light and motion sensitivity (EA's free IRIS tool is mentioned); publishing accessibility details before launch. Options and accessible defaults are both needed.

title: ECS in Practice: The Case Board of 'Alan Wake 2'
summary: Session abstract: for Alan Wake 2, Remedy moved gameplay code from an object-oriented framework to a new data-oriented ECS framework, citing cache coherency and multithreading as performance gains and changes to how gameplay programmers write code. The talk walks through one feature, the Case Board, covering its components, system registration, interaction with other modules and the C++/Lua boundary.
notes: Alternate Vault pages for the same session (same title and conference in the Vault crawl) are listed in alt_urls.

title: Hitchhiker's Guide to Rapid Prototypes!
summary: Former PopCap PopLabs designer's low-budget method for someone with little coding, art or money to build a testable prototype in about a month. Aim for a 'minimum viable interaction' rather than a minimum product; find the core mechanic first; scope around listed internal and external limits, since bad scope is rarely chosen deliberately; keep mock-ups quick and disposable. Barrett's example began as a no-code interactive mock-up made with a wireframing tool and stock images and shared for feedback; a volunteer programmer then added a few weeks of code, followed by surveys and five half-hour user tests with the target audience. Offered as personal experience, not a universal process.
notes: Game Career Seminar session. Audit 08: transcript re-read (~lines 505-545). Order corrected: the five half-hour user tests came after the volunteer programmer coded the prototype, not before.

title: Open-Ended Puzzle Design at Zachtronics
summary: Zachtronics designers discuss open-ended engineering puzzle games. Walls of tutorial text and click-here walkthroughs failed; they now build spaces where players try things and are steered toward the goal. The first puzzle must work for almost everyone, and the last need not be the hardest. Their main difficulty signal is 'bounce', players who open a puzzle and never solve it; a spike flags one bad puzzle, which they replace. Opus Magnum made completion easier and put depth into optional optimisation scores; removing arbitrary constraints widened the solution space.

title: Independent Games Summit: Sparking Curiosity-Driven Exploration Through Narrative in 'Outer Wilds'
summary: Outer Wilds' writer on a game where curiosity is the only driver and knowledge the only reward, accepting that this deters some players. Big hooks are shown, not told; information is pulled rather than pushed, and the time loop lets players revisit it. Early builds gave no direction, which unsettled some players, so an optional pointer was added. Every text serves as clue, lore and theme and points backward and forward; with no gates, small self-contained story arcs pay off in any order, and text is layered from surface to hidden, with placement checked in playtests. The ship's log records only what the player certainly knows. Death costs nothing and is framed as learning.
notes: Alternate Vault pages for the same session (same title and conference in the Vault crawl) are listed in alt_urls.

title: Level Design Workshop: Singleplayer vs. Multiplayer Level Design: A Paradigm Shift
venue: Game Developers Conference 2017, Level Design Workshop
summary: A designer who moved from narrative single-player work (BioShock Infinite, Mafia III) to multiplayer (Doom, Call of Duty remaster) compares the two. Single-player spaces are sized around encounters and scenes, and key information goes where players are sure to look: leaving a door or elevator, the top of a ladder, the base of a T-junction; a large landmark orients. In multiplayer, unintended sightlines feel unfair because players must understand why they died; layouts need several routes, pickups placed with the layout, and frequent playtests.
notes: Alternate Vault pages for the same session (same title and conference in the Vault crawl) are listed in alt_urls.

title: Game VR/AR: Until You Fall: Building Satisfying VR Combat on a Budget
summary: Schell Games designers on Until You Fall, a fast VR melee game built by a small team. They used feedback from non-VR hack-and-slash games (screen flash, camera shake, hit pause) as starting points and tone targets; screen flash and camera shake worked better in VR than the team expected and needed only minor tweaks. Weapon weights were designed to mimic the animation lag of heavy hits in non-VR action games. They warn that the pull toward realistic secondary VR interactions can become a scope trap when the game's fantasy is narrow.
notes: Captions spell the second speaker 'Patrick shell bear'; the Vault lists Patrick Jalbert. The talk does not specify how its camera shake was adapted for VR. Alternate Vault pages for the same session (same title and conference in the Vault crawl) are listed in alt_urls.

title: Game Feel: Why Your Death Animation Sucks
summary: The developer of Move or Die builds a player-death effect live while audience members play, adding one layer at a time: animation, layered death sounds, quiet jump sounds with random pitch variation, persistent paint splatter and particles, then screen shake (toned down after an exaggerated first pass), chromatic aberration, a shockwave and rumble. Argues that feedback is functional as well as cosmetic because it confirms that an input registered.

title: Beyond 'Killzone': Creating New AI Systems for 'Horizon Zero Dawn'
summary: Abstract: Guerrilla's AI technology was built for one human enemy type in closed corridors, while Horizon Zero Dawn needed more than 25 very different characters in a large open world. The talk covers the changes made to navigation and animation so the machines moved believably, and how those changes affected the team's workflow.
notes: Only the Vault abstract was read.

title: Module bevy::ecs
summary: Module documentation for Bevy ECS. The built-in parallel executor runs as many systems in parallel as their data access allows; to control system ordering, define explicit dependencies between systems and system sets.

title: Fixed
summary: API reference for the fixed-timestep clock, which advances in fixed increments for logic such as physics that must behave consistently regardless of frame rate. The default timestep is 64 hertz; the page explains that 60 hertz can interact badly with a 60 Hz monitor refresh rate, alternating two and zero fixed steps per frame.

title: Virtual
summary: API reference for the virtual game clock, the default Time resource during updates. It can be paused, sped up or slowed down (set_relative_speed), and it caps how far one update can advance; pausing or changing speed does not affect the delta of the update already in progress.

title: SD-πXL: Generating Low-Resolution Quantized Imagery via Score Distillation
summary: Generates pixel art at a fixed size with a given palette by optimising a per-pixel palette choice under guidance from an image diffusion model, optionally following an input image. The paper notes that prompted or fine-tuned diffusion models cannot enforce strict palette or resolution limits, and that classic pixelization ignores what the image depicts. Stated limits: about 1.5 hours per image on an RTX 4090, reliance on text prompts, pixels sampled independently, and no frame-to-frame consistency for animation. In a 56-person study it ranked first on aesthetics but not on fidelity to the input.
notes: arXiv comments: SIGGRAPH Asia 2024 conference track; Crossref confirms the ACM DOI. Read the abstract and the first 100k characters of the arXiv HTML (introduction, comparisons, limitations); supplementary material not read.

title: Crash Course in Online Features for Programmers
summary: Sony London online consultant's introduction for generalists and indies: lean on platform services first, start real-time networking with middleware and send less data, and keep servers small because running them is a large commitment. Blackshaw warns against making every packet reliable and ordered, replicating everything, and executable code in cloud configuration; notes that letting the client judge hits, a basic technique for responsive shooters, is open to cheating; recommends checking that the core game still works when your server is down; and notes that player concurrency limits matchmaking, so keep matchmaking buckets few.

Summary adjusted. Alternate Vault pages for the same session (same title and conference in the Vault crawl) are listed in alt_urls.

title: Apply (Object > Apply)
summary: Applying location, rotation or scale resets those values (origin to world origin, rotation 0, scale 1) while keeping the object visually in place; shared data must be made single-user first. Transforms affect how modifiers, constraints and parenting behave; Corrective Flip Normals fixes inverted shading when applying negative scale. Applying does not change poses or animation, so the manual recommends applying transforms before rigging and animating.

title: Render Baking (Cycles)
summary: Cycles baking reference. Selected to Active casts rays from the low-poly toward the high-poly; Max Ray Distance or Cage Extrusion handles high-poly surfaces outside the low-poly. A cage (auto-inflated or a supplied object) avoids edge glitches of normal-direction rays, and hard-edge splits can give non-smooth results. Tangent normal space is the default and suits most cases including animated objects; the material's image setting must match. Margin pads UV islands to prevent seam artifacts from filtering and mipmapping, by extending border pixels or copying from adjacent faces.

title: Scene Properties: Units
summary: Unit System offers None, Metric or Imperial; Unit Scale converts between internal values and displayed values. The manual states Unit Scale only changes what the interface displays, not internal behaviour, and physics simulations ignore it. Length can be adaptive or fixed to metres, centimetres or feet.

title: 'God of War Ragnarok': Building the UI for a AAA Sequel
summary: Santa Monica Studio technical designer on the UI of God of War Ragnarok and the role of a UI team. Full controller remapping required re-architecting input, because designers had hard-coded specific buttons for every action; afterwards they specified the action suited to the context (such as aim, interact or evade). The speaker calls full remapping the most requested accessibility feature by far. Other lessons: playtest video showed players repeatedly opening the pause menu to find their goal, fixed by surfacing quest information in the world; consistent menu navigation; in-menu tutorials that restrict input to the step being taught.

title: SF3D: Stable Fast 3D Mesh Reconstruction with UV-unwrapping and Illumination Disentanglement
venue: 2025 IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR), pp. 16240-16250
summary: Turns one image into a UV-unwrapped mesh in about half a second, with a delit albedo texture, a normal map, and one roughness and one metallic value for the whole object. It names the faults of earlier fast methods: vertex colours force dense meshes, baked shadows prevent relighting, marching cubes leaves stair-stepped surfaces, and missing materials look dull. Stated limits: delighting removes only low-frequency lighting, albedo fails in dark parts of the input, materials are uniform across the object, and materials are learned without direct supervision.
notes: Full text read as arXiv HTML v1; venue and pages on the CVF open-access page; DOI from Crossref.

title: Emergent Storytelling Techniques in 'The Sims'
summary: Maxis' creative director on emergent story in The Sims. Sims choose randomly among top-scoring actions, so they make mistakes players want to fix; memorable events such as a first kitchen fire are made likely by tuning, not scripted. Ambiguity (Simlish, thought balloons) lets players fill in meaning, and a wrong specific detail is worse than none. A behaviour made correct but identical for everyone was replaced by randomness because it was unfunny. Autonomous behaviour follows relationships the player builds. Wants and fears in The Sims 2 decayed on a timescale tuned to player memory; off-screen Sims in The Sims 3 ran a cheap coarse simulation. Spinning want slots made wants look random.

title: Math for Game Developers: End-to-End Procedural Generation in 'Caves of Qud'
summary: Bucklew and Grinblat walk through village generation in Caves of Qud: an abstract village history is generated at world creation and made concrete over later steps (location, culture, layout, object fabrication), with defaults used where no abstract input exists. Steps are decoupled modules whose outputs combine freely. Every random call draws on the world seed, so they can rebuild a zone from a player's save to reproduce odd output. Building interiors are found with seeded Dijkstra maps.
notes: Alternate Vault pages for the same session (same title and conference in the Vault crawl) are listed in alt_urls.

title: Math for Game Developers: Tile-Based Map Generation using Wave Function Collapse in 'Caves of Qud'
summary: Bucklew explains how Caves of Qud uses WaveFunctionCollapse in its overlapping mode, trained on small hand-drawn images, to fill map regions. Problems met: output becomes homogeneous at large scale, and adding colors for detail overfits so outputs repeat one arrangement. Fixes: segment the map first and fill each segment from a different template; use WFC only for wall structure and place doors and furniture in a later pass; find disconnected spaces and path between them, punching doors where the path crosses walls, so regions connect.

title: Animation Bootcamp: High Resolution Pixel Art and Animation
venue: Game Developers Conference 2018, Animation Bootcamp (Visual Arts track)
summary: Bunk animates large sprites as Flash vectors so parts can be rotated and scaled, then cleans every exported frame: select the shape, grow the selection one pixel and delete to strip blurry anti-aliased edges, then separate colour regions. Index a small palette first so one swap recolours all frames. Keep poses readable in silhouette, vary spacing, and add smear frames for large moves. Banded shading with one or two mid bands won over dithering, which is hard to keep aligned across animated frames; in-between tones fake half-pixel motion. A drawn 360-degree turnaround is reused as a parts library. Export with transparency.
notes: Transcript is GDC YouTube captions; the colour count is from captions. Examples are personal animations of game characters rendered for video at 30 fps, not shipped game sprites. Captions garble the cleanup program name (apparently Aseprite). Audit 2026-10-15: the palette size (about 32 colours) is a single hedged spoken mention in auto captions with no slides or second source, so it is unconfirmed and was dropped from the summary.

title: 'Fallout 4's' Modular Level Design
venue: Game Developers Conference 2016, Visual Arts track
summary: Bethesda's level designer and environment artist, building on their 2013 Skyrim kit talk. Choose the footprint first: it fixes how pieces tile and the proportions of space; a cube tiles every way, while wide one-direction kits cannot loop back. Treat the footprint as a maximum extent, built out only on tiling edges with a buffer elsewhere, or walls go coplanar and z-fight and details poke into neighbours. Fix pivots early and never move them, since that breaks placed work. Local snap parents let pieces leave the world grid and rejoin it. Blank grey-box kits caused trouble later, so early kits carry the details that matter; naming follows long-standing conventions.
notes: Vault also lists the session as 1023202. Vault access tier not confirmed, so members is the cautious default; the full talk is on GDC's official YouTube channel. Access set to free because the full talk is on the official GDC YouTube channel (alt_urls).

title: Future design of accessibility in games: A design vocabulary
summary: Argues that accessibility guidelines work as evaluation checklists but not as design tools, and that splitting them by disability misses how players use options (in one AbleGamers sample 27 players reported a hearing impairment but 83 used subtitles). From 101 guidelines rewritten as 75 player outcomes and content-analysed, it proposes a vocabulary of options: access options (input, control, presentation, output) that let players into the play loop without changing the game, and challenge options (performance, training, progress, social, moderation) that change the game so players can meet its challenges. Games should be difficult but not difficult to access.
notes: Read from the accepted manuscript in the White Rose repository (CC BY-NC-ND).

title: Repopulating the Earth: Character Production on 'Horizon Zero Dawn'
venue: Game Developers Conference 2018, Visual Arts track
summary: Guerrilla's deliberately small character team (four artists, two contractors) on making a large cast. A Lego-style modular kit for layered costumes failed: each added piece multiplies fit dependencies, forcing either near-identical forms or fitting tools that cost upkeep and lose folds and bulges. On outsourcing: keep in-house the subjective, collaborative work where the studio adds value, and outsource work whose outcome is objective and easy to communicate. Once a design read well, partners did the final high-poly detailing, and partners did mechanical steps such as baking and LODs on nearly every character; by hours, partners did most of the work on most content.
notes: Team size and shares (about 90% and 99% of characters) from captions. Vault access tier not confirmed, so members is the cautious default; the full talk is on GDC's official YouTube channel. Access set to free because the full talk is on the official GDC YouTube channel (alt_urls).

title: UX Summit: Loud and Clear: Improving Accessibility for Low Vision Players in 'Cosmonious High'
summary: Owlchemy Labs on a vision accessibility update for a VR game: text-to-speech descriptions of objects and places, spatial audio, haptic pulses and high-contrast highlights. External testers unfamiliar with the layout got lost where the team had not, so more locations were marked. Automatic speech overwhelmed players, so it moved to a player-triggered assist button that can also cancel speech, with other game audio ducked meanwhile. Descriptions were reordered to give state and name first, and flavour text was cut on a tester's advice. Turning the mode on first needed sighted help; a gesture fixed that but was poorly announced. Low-vision playtesters rated the mode highly.
notes: Audit 2026-09-26: transcript describes the tester who advised cutting flavour text (James Rath) only as a tester and accessibility consultant, not as blind; summary narrowed.

title: Animation Bootcamp: Fluid and Powerful Animation within Frame Restrictions
summary: Skullgirls' lead animator (Lab Zero Games) on hand-drawn fighting-game animation under designer-set frame counts. Player moves must answer a button press almost at once, so they get little anticipation, while enemy attacks need wind-ups players can react to; a move can snap to its active key pose and let follow-through, smears and overshoot carry the motion. Moves are roughed in at standard frame counts and made playable before the art is finished; the designer sets how a move works and the animator makes it read. Hitstop, freezing both characters' poses on impact, is described as mainly a programming task that keeps impacts from looking weak.
notes: The official GDC YouTube upload is titled "Making Fluid and Powerful Animations For 'Skullgirls'"; the speaker introduces the talk by its Vault title. Alternate Vault pages for the same session (same title and conference in the Vault crawl) are listed in alt_urls.

title: As real as real? Macroeconomic behavior in a large-scale virtual world
summary: Uses transaction data from a large commercial virtual world, the first such dataset given to outside researchers, to compute production, consumption and money-supply metrics with real-world definitions. Their movements over time were consistent with common macroeconomic theories. When a new server with the same rules opened during the study, its aggregates quickly came to nearly replicate those of existing servers, which the authors read as evidence that macroeconomic outcomes in a virtual world are largely explained by its design structure.

title: Classroom to the Console: The Autobiography of flOw
summary: Chen and Santiago (thatgamecompany) on flOw's path from Chen's USC thesis to a PlayStation 3 game. Chen argues that one static difficulty, or a menu of difficulty levels, cannot keep a widening audience between frustration and boredom, and that computer-controlled dynamic difficulty adjustment can feel intimidating and break flow when players sense the game changing without their control. flOw instead lets players steer their own challenge through in-game choices, as open-world players pick harder or easier activities. Also covers founding the studio and the move from the Flash version to a console team.

Replaces Chen's 2007 Communications of the ACM article, a magazine piece that does not meet the peer-review tier. title: MeshAnything: Artist-Created Mesh Generation with Autoregressive Transformers
summary: Treats mesh extraction as generation: given a point cloud from any 3D source, a transformer produces an artist-like mesh with hundreds of times fewer faces. It argues that marching cubes and other extraction methods give dense meshes with poor topology that ignore geometric features and smooth away sharp edges and flat areas, costing storage, rendering and artist cleanup. Stated limits: a hard cap of 800 faces, so no large scenes or very complex objects; less stable than reconstruction, with failure cases; lower geometric accuracy than marching cubes; and degradation under heavy input noise.
