title: The first hour experience: how the initial play can engage (or lose) new players
venue: Proceedings of the First ACM SIGCHI Annual Symposium on Computer-Human Interaction in Play (CHI PLAY 2014)
summary: Grounded-theory analysis of 212 Amazon reviews and 35 long-form 'first hour' reviews of Xbox 360 games, plus six industry interviews. The first sustained session is an evaluation period: players bring expectations, can quit over deal-breakers or 'pitfalls' (a missed piece of information), and may persist because of 'holdouts'. Players want both clear direction and room to discover; the authors argue for direction early, with hints of depth, and discovery later. Reviewers complained less about dying than about imprecise controls and slow loading between deaths. Single coder with an external audit; self-reported data.

title: Latency and player actions in online games
summary: Synthesizes earlier testbed studies that added network latency to commercial games (Unreal Tournament 2003, a racing game, EverQuest 2, Madden NFL 2004, Warcraft III, Age of Mythology). Argues that an action's latency sensitivity depends on the precision it needs and its deadline, and at game level on interaction model and perspective. Proposed tolerance thresholds: about 100 ms for first-person avatar games (shooters, racing), 500 ms for third-person avatar games (sports, RPGs) and 1,000 ms for omnipresent games (RTS, simulation). In UT2003, high-precision weapon accuracy fell sharply, about 35%, at 100 ms; Madden running showed no significant drop until beyond 500 ms.
notes: A synthesis of prior network-latency experiments, not a new user study. Its perspective-based thresholds are contested by halbhuber2023-latency-perspective.

title: Perspectives, frame rates and resolutions: it's all in the game
venue: Proceedings of the 4th International Conference on Foundations of Digital Games (FDG 2009)
summary: Lab study of how frame rate and resolution affect two actions common to many games, shooting and navigation, across camera perspectives, using a purpose-built game with more than 25 participants. Frame rate had a much greater effect on player performance than resolution across all perspectives and actions; both affected players' opinions of playability and quality.

title: Effects of steering locomotion and teleporting on cybersickness and presence in HMD-based virtual reality
summary: Twenty-five participants explored a commercial VR nature game for 16-minute trials over two days using steering locomotion or teleporting, seated or standing. Steering was more sickening on average, but nine participants were sicker when teleporting, and they differed in postural sway measured before VR. Standing did not change sickness but increased presence. Sickness grew with time in trial for both methods; presence grew over time only with steering. The authors found no clear overall advantage for teleporting and some benefits of steering for presence. Summary limited to the published abstract.
notes: Published online 2019, issue year 2020 (Virtual Reality 24(3), 453-468).

title: Production Essentials Summit: Anti-Crunch: Patterns and Practices
summary: Pragma's CTO distinguishes crunch mandated by leadership from 'accidental' crunch adopted with good intentions. On League of Legends' Team Builder (about 15 months, no crunch) disciplined estimation produced velocity-based projections that let the team push back when told to crunch. Practices: estimates are not commitments; low-resolution estimates far out, finer ones close in; count newly discovered work, which Cobb calls the most common planning mistake; don't plan with unfilled headcount; embed QA from kickoff; share knowledge to avoid silos; keep a steady pace so any push is an opt-in exception.
notes: Vault page offers the slide deck free; the session was read from the GDC YouTube upload. Alternate Vault pages for the same session (same title and conference in the Vault crawl) are listed in alt_urls.

title: 'Dreamscaper': Killer Combat on an Indie Budget
summary: Afterburner Studios' designer-animator on combat feel in a small-team action roguelike. About 130 ms of Switch input latency from engine thread syncing was nearly halved by a low-latency frame-sync option; the Switch parry window was widened. Attacks start in their anticipation pose, movement has almost no acceleration, dodge and block interrupt almost any action, and early inputs are buffered without over-registering mashes. Hit reactions skip blending. Hitstop freezes only attacker and target for about 115 ms, eased in and out, while effects and camera continue. Shake scales with hit class and is weaker when the player is hit; players should be able to reduce or turn off shake and rumble.
notes: Captions spell the speaker 'ian caffino'; the Vault lists Ian Cofino. Alternate Vault pages for the same session (same title and conference in the Vault crawl) are listed in alt_urls.

title: Appearance-preserving simplification
venue: Proceedings of the 25th annual conference on Computer graphics and interactive techniques - SIGGRAPH '98, pp. 115-122
summary: The authors decouple surface position from colour and curvature: colours go into texture maps and normals into normal maps, so the mesh can be simplified heavily while shading detail is kept. A texture deviation metric bounds how far mapped colour and normal detail may shift on screen, in pixels, for a chosen display resolution. On several large parameterised models, a few static levels of detail switched at suitable distances showed little or no loss in rendering quality. Normal maps then needed prototype hardware (UNC PixelFlow).
notes: Peer-reviewed SIGGRAPH 1998 paper. Metadata from Crossref; abstract from the UNC GAMMA project page. Full text read 2026-10-15 from the authors' PDF at http://gamma.cs.unc.edu/APS/APS.pdf (linked from the GAMMA project page). Summary adds the switching-distance condition and the hardware note from sec. 1. Metadata matches the paper.

title: Wang Tiles for image and texture generation
venue: ACM Transactions on Graphics 22(3) (Proceedings of SIGGRAPH 2003)
summary: Wang tiles are squares whose edge colours must match their neighbours'. The authors give a simple stochastic algorithm that tiles the plane non-periodically at runtime: with at least two tiles for every pair of north and west edge colours (as few as eight tiles), each placement is a random choice. Tiles are filled with synthesised texture, Poisson point sets that keep their statistics across tile edges, or pre-lit geometry, so large non-periodic areas are produced efficiently. Small sets can still show repetition artifacts, which larger sets reduce; a corner-coded extension lets objects cross tile corners.
notes: Pages 287-294. Crossref also lists 10.1145/1201775.882265 (SIGGRAPH 2003 Papers). The abstract does not discuss game tilesets or pixel art. Access: 'free' reflects a free copy at the alt URL or venue page; the ACM DL copy was not checked. Full text read 2026-10-15 from the authors' PDF linked from the Uni Konstanz publication page (https://pub-085d059a8619439494873b401c0986ce.r2.dev/Cohen2003WangTilesImage/Cohen2003WangTilesImage.pdf). Summary now adds the two-tiles-per-edge-pair condition and the paper's note that small sets can still look repetitive. The PDF is paginated 295-302 (copyright line 0730-0301/03/0700-0295), while Crossref gives 287-294; the registry venue field carries no pages, so nothing else changed.

title: PCG Shotgun: 6 Techniques for Leveraging AI in Content Generation
summary: Six short practitioner talks. Used here: Short on making generated personalities legible to players; Adams on storing event data inside generated objects so agents and players can refer to it; Aikman on storing run-length-encoded cave output rather than regenerating rooms from seeds at runtime, and on using position along the path to ramp difficulty and treasure; Kruel on designers drawing the high-level map flow while a generator fills rooms; a closing segment on seeds that players type, derive from positions or user IDs, share, or decompose into sub-seeds for parts of a level.
notes: Alternate Vault pages for the same session (same title and conference in the Vault crawl) are listed in alt_urls.

title: Game Sound: An Introduction to the History, Theory, and Practice of Video Game Music and Sound Design
summary: Introduction to the history, theory and production of game music and sound. Its two themes are how games differ from film and other linear media, since player actions trigger dialogue, effects, ambience and music, and how technology has constrained audio production. It covers the production roles on a contemporary game, the functions of audio in gameplay, and the difficulties that nonlinearity and interactivity pose for composers. Summary limited to the publisher's description.
notes: Content checked against the publisher description (Crossref DOI 10.7551/mitpress/7909.001.0001).

title: Practical Procedural Generation for Everyone
summary: Compton (Spore planets, Tracery) surveys PCG as additive methods (tiles, grammars, distribution, parametric spaces, interpretive pipelines, simulations) and subtractive ones (keeping the seeds of good outputs, generate-and-test, search, constraint solving). Compton advises defining the artifact narrowly, interviewing experts to encode their process, ranking candidates instead of rejecting until one passes (which can hang), using an existing solver rather than writing one, designing for perceived rather than mathematical variety, letting players claim and share finds, and keeping generators in data formats that ease testing and visualization.

title: It IS Rocket Science! The Physics of 'Rocket League' Detailed
summary: Psyonix's lead gameplay engineer on Rocket League physics and netcode. Physics runs at a fixed 120 Hz in an embedded open-source engine, and car handling is deliberately simplified (hand-set mass, designer acceleration curves, faked suspension and stability forces) for consistent control rather than realism. The server is fully authoritative and buffers client inputs; clients predict every car and the ball and, on a server correction, rewind all objects and re-simulate to the present. Lag compensation was rejected because it warped the ball for low-ping players. Costs: whole-scene re-simulation is expensive and the input buffer adds latency.
notes: Alternate Vault pages for the same session (same title and conference in the Vault crawl) are listed in alt_urls.

title: 'Rocket League': Language Ban System Postmortem
summary: Psyonix's community manager on replacing manual chat moderation with an automatic system triggered only by player reports: the reported match's chat is checked against a short word list with per-word thresholds, bans escalate from 24 hours and step back down after 30 days of good behavior, and permanent bans stay with humans. Comparing three months before and after launch, reports rose by about a third; almost 100,000 bans were issued in the first 90 days (about 82% of them 24-hour bans), and 98% of banned players returned to play. Limits: word lists miss indirect abuse, it was English-only, and it needs daily human attention.
notes: Audit 2026-09-26 (transcript): the talk reports almost 100,000 bans in the first 90 days (81.6% 24-hour), not 100,000 players banned; summary reworded accordingly and de-escalation period (30 days) added. Title, speaker, year, venue match the Vault page.

title: Goal-Oriented Action Planning: Ten Years Old and No Fear!
summary: Three views of GOAP a decade after F.E.A.R. Monolith (Higley) describes the fixed-priority goal list and planner extensions used on Middle-earth: Shadow of Mordor. Crystal Dynamics (Conway) describes Tomb Raider's GOAP, a designer-editable behavior graph for choosing goals, and stresses debugging because designers fall back to scripting when they cannot see why an NPC acts. Jacopin analyzes logged plans from GOAP games (the data included an alpha build) and, finding plans short and a small share of actions accounting for most planning work, advises keeping plans short and using action costs deliberately.
notes: Transcript from the official GDC YouTube upload (titled 'Goal-Oriented Action Planning: Ten Years of AI Programming'); captions garble several names and figures, so exact counts were not used. The short-plans finding is also reported in Zubek's Game AI Pro 3 chapter. The Vault also lists ids 1022020 and 1022462. Alternate Vault pages for the same session (same title and conference in the Vault crawl) are listed in alt_urls.

title: Forgiveness Mechanics: Reading Minds for Responsive Gameplay
summary: Butterscotch Shenanigans' designer-programmer on forgiveness rules added to the platformer Levelhead after watching players mistime inputs. Late inputs: jump permission that lasts 0.1 s after leaving ground (coyote jump) and a grapple target locked at the moment of the press. Early inputs: 0.2 s input buffering, later applied to most actions. Accidental inputs: input resets (jumping cancels fall-through mode) and a 0.3 s hold on a restart button that about a third of players pressed by accident when gripping hard. Collision: pinched hitboxes so the avatar pops over ledges and gaps, tucked-in hazard hitboxes, enlarged pickup hitboxes with magnetism, and hit checks ordered to favor the player.
notes: Captions spell the speaker 'Seth Koster'; the Vault lists Seth Coster.

title: 'Weekends became something other people did': understanding and intervening in the habitus of video game crunch
venue: Convergence: The International Journal of Research into New Media Technologies
summary: Critical discourse analysis of Game Developer magazine, 2000-2010, on how developers talked about crunch. Crunch was framed as inevitable through three themes: games as an unmanageable creative industry, an anti-corporate ethos, and a developer identity built on passion and perfectionism. With project-based work and cultures of secrecy these make crunch part of the 'habitus' of game work. Because habitus can change, the authors propose interventions by employees, companies and labour organisers toward a more sustainable one.

title: Massive Crowd on Assassin's Creed Unity: AI Recycling
summary: AI level of detail for Assassin's Creed Unity crowds. Distant crowd members are cheap instanced meshes with a small animation rig, simple scripted reactions and no entity; nearer ones borrow a pooled NPC's visuals while still running the cheap logic; only a few closest ones become fully simulated NPCs, which cost far more per character. Designers place 'shepherds' that own groups; members are referenced by stable ids rather than pointers because entities are recycled. Fully simulated NPCs must be able to start a reaction mid-way when promoted, and complex reactions fall back to spawning a real NPC at a noticeable CPU cost.
notes: Transcript from the official GDC YouTube upload; exact timing and distance figures from captions were not used. Alternate Vault pages for the same session (same title and conference in the Vault crawl) are listed in alt_urls.

title: A Missing Data Imputation GAN for Character Sprite Generation
venue: Anais do XXIII Simpósio Brasileiro de Jogos e Entretenimento Digital (SBGames 2024)
summary: Generates a character sprite for a missing facing direction from the other available directions, treated as filling in missing data, on 12,074 sprites at 64x64. Reported faults: colours land in sensible places but use many near-identical shades instead of a fixed palette (the authors suggest palette quantisation), faint facial features leak into back views, quality drops sharply with fewer input views, and one variant added wrong features such as extra eyes. FID and L1 did not always agree, so the authors leaned on visual review.
notes: Full text read as arXiv HTML v1 (arXiv comment: published in SBGames 2024); venue and pages 436-455 from the SBC proceedings page and Crossref.

title: Measuring how game feel is influenced by the player avatar's acceleration and deceleration: using a 2D platformer to describe players' perception of controls in videogames
venue: Proceedings of the 19th International Academic Mindtrek Conference
summary: Players controlled a 2D platformer avatar whose acceleration and deceleration response was varied between rounds and described the feel after each round. Most used basic words such as heavy, slow, responsive and realistic. Some participants noticed small changes while others reported no difference, and although all agreed feel matters, they did not agree on how to describe particular feels.
notes: Only the abstract was read; sample size and parameter values are not cited.

title: Weaving 13 Prototypes into 1 Game: Lessons from 'Edith Finch'
summary: Giant Sparrow's creative director on finding What Remains of Edith Finch (team of three growing to about 15) through prototypes rather than documents: the story was adjusted to fit what prototypes showed, and the game became its own design document. Early prototypes were built alone in Unity although the game shipped in Unreal, to keep them light; ideas that still felt like hard work after a couple of days were dropped. In playtests, trust that players are upset more than their explanations; about five players per round gave most of the value; stories tested alone behaved differently in full playthroughs. Dallas notes the approach suited this game, not a sequel.
notes: Design track. Vault id 1025556 is the same session; 1025016 is used consistently. Alternate Vault pages for the same session (same title and conference in the Vault crawl) are listed in alt_urls.

title: 'Into the Breach' Design Postmortem
summary: Subset Games on Into the Breach. About a year of discarded prototypes (real-time countdowns, action points, timelines) produced complex but shallow rules. Showing every enemy attack in advance made dodging trivial until immobile buildings gave players something to defend; a turn limit instead of kill-all enabled non-lethal push weapons and short battles. Losing buildings could leave unwinnable turns, so a small random defense chance was added. The need to show target and attack type in the UI constrained enemy design. The strategy layer shrank from a board-game map to choosing missions, and an optional run length confused players looking for an optimal stopping point.
notes: Alternate Vault pages for the same session (same title and conference in the Vault crawl) are listed in alt_urls.

title: Playtesting 'God of War'
summary: Sony Santa Monica on external playtesting for God of War (2018) with PlayStation user research from alpha onward. Tests checked how well the set vision was realised, not the vision itself; goals had to be clear and measurable; a fixed test calendar kept credibility. Unguided playthroughs found friction and one-on-one usability sessions isolated causes (a 'combat isn't fun' complaint traced to camera sensitivity). Undirected feedback was collected before survey questions; feedback was cross-checked with video, telemetry and difficulty setting; the team learned not to react to feedback on unfinished features. Large tests had 20 players, chosen for breadth.
notes: Vault id 1026280 is the same session; 1025978 is used consistently. Alternate Vault pages for the same session (same title and conference in the Vault crawl) are listed in alt_urls.

title: Playtesting: Avoiding Evil Data
summary: Independent developer of Bounden and Hidden Folks on playtest data that distracts or misleads. The setting shapes results (Bounden was tuned on five-minute event sessions for a game meant to take about an hour); don't explain anything beyond saying the build is unfinished; testers describe symptoms well but propose fixes for problems they don't understand; the speaker dropped surveys and ratings; funnels and averages show where players stop but not why, so the why is left to guesswork; self-recorded remote sessions come closest to watching in person but cost hours of viewing. De Jongh tests throughout development, triggered by milestones.
notes: Independent Games Summit session. Vault id 1024451 is the same session; 1024132 is used consistently. Audit 2026-09-26 (transcript): Bounden comparison is 5-minute event playthroughs versus an hour-long game; the talk does not say players played far longer at home (about 1% played over 30 minutes). Vault metadata matches. Alternate Vault pages for the same session (same title and conference in the Vault crawl) are listed in alt_urls.

title: Adaptation in digital games: the effect of challenge adjustment on player performance and experience
venue: Proceedings of the 2015 Annual Symposium on Computer-Human Interaction in Play (CHI PLAY 2015)
summary: Lab study: 42 players played a 90-second top-down shooter; for 22 of them the timer secretly ran faster when they were doing well and slower when they struggled (a factor of 1.4, adjusted four times). The adaptive group reported significantly higher immersion, mainly cognitive involvement and sense of control; nobody noticed the change and perceived challenge did not differ; scores did not differ significantly. The authors note it is one game in one short session and that awareness of adaptation over repeated play is untested.
notes: Peer-reviewed short paper (a 'note') in the CHI PLAY 2015 main proceedings, not an extended abstract.

title: Player experience and deceptive expectations of difficulty adaptation in digital games
summary: Two lab experiments: 120 players of a short shooter with an adaptive or standard timer and three levels of information about it; 60 players of a level-based game whose difficulty adapted between levels, over two 10-minute sessions. Telling players that the game adapts raised reported immersion whether or not adaptation was present, and real adaptation also raised immersion; the two effects did not interfere. The authors conclude that disclosing adaptation need not harm experience and that expectations can bias playtest self-reports. Short casual games; questionnaire measures.
notes: Read the authors' accepted manuscript on White Rose Research Online.

title: Cooperation and Interdependence: How Multiplayer Games Increase Social Closeness
venue: Proceedings of the Annual Symposium on Computer-Human Interaction in Play (CHI PLAY 2017)
summary: The authors frame collaborative game mechanics as two factors, cooperation and interdependence, and test four versions of an online game with pairs of strangers. Both factors independently improved play experience and increased social closeness; the closeness gained from interdependence was explained by more conversational turns between partners.

title: Using heuristics to evaluate the playability of games
venue: CHI '04 Extended Abstracts on Human Factors in Computing Systems (Late Breaking Results)
summary: Introduces Heuristic Evaluation for Playability (HEP): 43 heuristics in four groups (game play, game story, mechanics, usability) compiled from earlier game and usability heuristics and reviewed by playability experts. An evaluator applied HEP to an early Flash mock-up of a new game (screens, no playable gameplay), and four players then took part in two-hour think-aloud sessions. HEP found more issues, while the user sessions found more game-specific problems such as terminology; the authors conclude HEP suits general issues early in development and works best combined with user studies.
notes: Four-page CHI 2004 Late Breaking Results paper, published in the juried CHI Extended Abstracts; it is cited in the text as a short early study, not as a full paper, and its evidence is one mock-up and four players. The later development of these heuristics is summarised in Desurvire and Wixon's chapter in drachen2018-gur.

title: Mastering uncertainty: A predictive processing account of enjoying uncertain success in video game play
summary: Hypothesis-and-theory article arguing that predictive processing explains why players enjoy uncertain success: positive affect comes from reducing uncertainty faster than expected, that is, doing better than expected, which tracks learning progress. The account is applied to balanced challenge, to Idle games (guaranteed success enjoyed as faster-than-expected progress) and to Soulslike games (repeated failure lowers expectations while players keep learning, so eventual success feels intense). Links the model to Koster's theory of fun and to competence and curiosity motives, and suggests uses in difficulty adjustment and automated playtesting. No new data.
notes: Read abstract, the section on Idle and Soulslike games, the discussion and the implications of the open-access PDF.

title: Improving AI Decision Modeling Through Utility Theory
summary: AI Summit session arguing that binary if/then decision logic produces equally abrupt yes/no behavior, and that techniques from utility theory, such as response curves, population distributions and weighted random selection, give agents graded preferences, broaden the space of possible decisions and handle edge cases that rule-based systems stumble over.
notes: Only the Vault abstract was read; the session is not on the official GDC YouTube channel. The Vault also lists ids 1012747 and 1012841. Speaker order follows the Vault page. Alternate Vault pages for the same session (same title and conference in the Vault crawl) are listed in alt_urls.

title: AI Summit: Where The $@*&% Are Your Tests?!
summary: Game AI veteran (Kythera AI) on why Dill's automated tests used to cost more than they returned and what changed: testing larger pieces through public interfaces instead of mocking every neighbouring system, turning the code's own errors and warnings into test failures, and adding stress tests that run many iterations. Tests catch bugs QA reaches only by chance, reproduce rare combinations and act as a safety net for later changes. Advice for starting: don't aim for full coverage, add a test with the next bug fix, and if maintenance outweighs payoff, write coarser tests.
notes: AI Summit session. The Vault page offers the slides free; the session was read from the GDC YouTube upload. Alternate Vault pages for the same session (same title and conference in the Vault crawl) are listed in alt_urls.

title: Hearthstone: 10 Bits of Design Wisdom
summary: Hearthstone's lead designer on principles from development and early live balance. Emotional design can outrank strict balance: Mind Control was widely called the strongest card though the numbers were fine, and its cost was raised to make it niche because having it played against you felt bad. Discard, counterspell and resource-denial effects were left out for the same reason, and one-turn-kill decks were targeted because opponents got no 'little victories'. Arena's random draft creates stories because runs end quickly. Renaming the matchmaking result from 'perfect' to 'worthy' opponent changed how blowouts felt.
notes: Alternate Vault pages for the same session (same title and conference in the Vault crawl) are listed in alt_urls.

title: Deterministic vs. Replicated AI: Building the Battlefield of 'For Honor'
summary: For Honor sends only timestamped inputs peer to peer; when an input arrives late, every peer rewinds and resimulates from history buffers. About 200 ambient soldiers run as deterministic AI inside the simulation, costing no bandwidth but CPU on every rewind, handled with time slicing, simplified collision and designer-drawn navigation flows. Hero bots are replicated: one peer computes their inputs. Lessons: state kept outside the history buffers causes desyncs, resimulation cost can snowball, determinism was one obstacle to cross-platform play, which they thought might be solvable, and they would not necessarily use the model for a shooter.
notes: Alternate Vault pages for the same session (same title and conference in the Vault crawl) are listed in alt_urls.

title: The Vertical Slice Challenge
summary: Volition senior producer reviews vertical slices on Saints Row 1-4 and the Red Faction games, more failures than successes by Donovan's account. Volition defines a slice as a section of the game that communicates the intended player experience with major systems working together near final quality, used as the gate into production: does the team know what it is making and how, with acceptable tech debt. Lessons: build around experience, not a feature list; a tech demo or aspirational visual target is not a slice; unquantified tech debt and unscheduled late features broke plans; on Saints Row 1 the studio chose crunch over cutting scope.
notes: Vault id 1022329 is the same session; 1022328 is used consistently. Alternate Vault pages for the same session (same title and conference in the Vault crawl) are listed in alt_urls.

title: Adventures in level design: generating missions and spaces for action adventure games
venue: Proceedings of the 2010 Workshop on Procedural Content Generation in Games (PCGames '10)
summary: Argues that action-adventure levels combine two structures that should be generated separately: a mission (a directed graph of tasks, such as obtaining a key before opening its lock) and a space (the layout). A graph grammar generates the mission; a shape grammar then builds space to accommodate it, with tightly coupled edges so keys land behind the tests that precede them. Loops added by reconnecting nearby spaces can short-circuit the mission and must be controlled. Grounded in a study of one Zelda dungeon; no player evaluation.
notes: PCGames 2010 was a peer-reviewed workshop held with FDG 2010; this is an 8-page full paper in the ACM proceedings.

title: Making of 'ASTRO BOT Rescue Mission': Reinventing Platformers for VR
summary: Sony Japan Studio's creative director on a third-person VR platformer. The player's head is the camera, so levels were built to use looking around, up and near/far, checked by watching playtesters' necks; full 360-degree moments were tiring and mostly cut. Comfort rules: levels run in one direction, the camera follows on a leash, the player never moves backwards, and respawns use a plain fade. A player health bar was cut; taking hits blurs the view. The game began as asymmetric VR-plus-TV multiplayer, whose camera forced corridor levels; cancelling it midway freed the VR level design. Prototypes are built for mechanics before art.

title: Games User Research
summary: Edited handbook of games user research written by industry researchers and academics. Chapters relevant here: Medlock on the RITE method (its philosophy, definition, benefits, practical notes and the original 2002 case study); Desurvire and Wixon on the PLAY and GAP heuristics, which they report as much more effective than informal expert reviews; Louvel on unavoidable lab biases and test validity; Nacke and Chalfoun and Dankoff on when biometrics are worth their trade-offs; Drachen and Connor on analytics alongside user research; Mirza-Babaei on reporting findings so teams act on them; and several chapters on testing with small budgets and little experience.
notes: Read: the publisher chapter abstracts (Crossref, DOIs 10.1093/oso/9780198794844.003.0001-0031). The text names the chapter and author it relies on; claims stay within those abstracts.

title: Crunch time: the reasons and effects of unpaid overtime in the games industry
venue: 2017 IEEE/ACM 39th International Conference on Software Engineering: Software Engineering in Practice Track (ICSE-SEIP)
summary: Studies postmortems and interviews with game-industry employees to characterise crunch (unpaid overtime). Proposes four types of crunch with different effects on product, schedule and staff; one type had only positive effects on product and schedule, but all types raised stress. Identifies reasons for crunch and reports that crunch was less pronounced in studios that regularly prioritise features.

title: Math for Game Programmers: Juicing Your Cameras With Math
summary: Eiserloh (SMU Guildhall) demonstrates camera math. Shake: keep a 0-to-1 trauma value that events add to and that decays linearly, and make shake proportional to trauma squared or cubed so small and large hits read differently; combine translation and rotation in 2D but use rotation only in 3D, where translation feels worse and can push the camera into walls; avoid shake in VR; add it to a clean copy of the base camera each frame; drive it with smooth noise rather than per-frame random values so it follows time scale and frame rate. Smoothing: per-frame asymptotic averaging, tuned per axis and direction, noted as frame-rate dependent. Also points of interest and Voronoi split-screen.
notes: Alternate Vault pages for the same session (same title and conference in the Vault crawl) are listed in alt_urls.

title: Developing the Art of 'Fortnite'
summary: Epic's art lead on Fortnite's stylised look. A simple guide (start from a box, taper, bulge or pinch it, remove parallel lines) let artists stylise props from photo reference. The style clashed with gameplay: crates that would not stack, and guns so exaggerated that aim direction was unclear in third person; some modular walls could not follow the shape language. An engine change forced conversion to physically based rendering. Lessons: push the style where players look and interact most, not on every asset, since a style is the sum of its parts; characters may carry their own style. In Q&A: standard sizes, such as a minimum doorway size for the largest characters, kept collision workable.
notes: Audit 2026-10-15: transcript re-checked; the doorway rule comes from the Q&A and is stated as a minimum size so big characters fit through any portal, not specifically a width, so the summary was corrected.

title: Game Analytics: Maximizing the Value of Player Data
summary: First edited volume on game analytics (30+ chapters, 50+ contributors from industry and research) covering telemetry system design, analytics in production, sampling, data mining, spatial and visual analytics and quantitative user testing. Canossa's chapter argues that behavioural telemetry has no intrinsic meaning and must be interpreted, and that the variables chosen for tracking bound which analyses and inferences are possible. Zoeller describes BioWare's developer-facing telemetry on how developers and testers use unfinished builds; Lynn (Volition) combines back-end telemetry with established user-testing protocols.
notes: Read: Springer's book description and the chapter abstracts shown on the chapter pages (chapters 1, 2, 6, 7, 9, 13, 14, 21, 22). Claims citing this entry stay within those.

title: Board Game Design Day: White, Brown, and Pink: The Flavors of Tabletop Game Randomness
summary: Tabletop designer on kinds of randomness. Input randomness randomizes the state before the player decides (Dominion hands, Into the Breach's telegraphed attacks); output randomness resolves after the decision (Risk combat). As broad generalizations, input randomness feels strategic and rewards skill, output randomness feels more tactical with a shorter planning horizon. Many rolls average out. A second axis is correlation between successive results: uncorrelated (white), random-walk (brown) and mostly-small-with-rare-large changes (pink), with board-game examples of each and tips for bounding extremes.
notes: Alternate Vault pages for the same session (same title and conference in the Vault crawl) are listed in alt_urls.

title: AActor
summary: API reference for the base actor class. Among its members: SetTickableWhenPaused sets whether the actor can tick while the game is paused, SetTickGroup sets its tick group, and CustomTimeDilation lets each actor run at a different time speed.

title: Unreal Engine Actor Lifecycle
summary: Describes how actors are created and destroyed along the load-from-disk, Play-in-Editor and spawn paths. Component initialization (PreInitializeComponents, InitializeComponent, PostInitializeComponents) completes before BeginPlay, which is called when the level starts; spawning also runs the construction script first.

title: Actor Ticking in Unreal Engine
summary: Explains tick groups (pre-physics, during physics, post-physics, post-update work): each group finishes ticking all its actors and components before the next begins. Actors and components can also declare tick dependencies so they tick only after another actor's or component's tick has finished.

title: Installed Build Reference Guide for Unreal Engine
summary: Reference on installed engine builds. The EngineAssociation field in a .uproject file identifies which editor version opens the project; launcher builds use the official version number, other builds a unique identifier, and non-foreign projects leave it blank.

title: Online Game Technology Summit: Scaling to 10 Concurrent Users: Online Infrastructure as an Indie
summary: A former Riot services engineer on building the online platform for a small team's 3v3 game with dedicated servers, with one or two part-time engineers: accounts, lobbies, chat and server management. Erridge argues time is an indie team's scarcest resource, recommends push-capable connections over polling, and sending whole lobby state rather than deltas, and is unsure whether their move from one server to microservices was worth the months of tooling and multi-step failure handling it cost.
notes: Alternate Vault pages for the same session (same title and conference in the Vault crawl) are listed in alt_urls.

title: Creating a Sequel to a Game That Doesn't Need One
summary: Valve writers on making Portal 2. Playtesting reshaped puzzles: a portal carousel that moved on its own schedule was slow to learn until players could open the portal with a button; lasers replaced the energy ball because the ball's long wait after failure and unexplained deaths hindered learning, while lasers give instant feedback; players rarely looked up, which forced changes to one room. Every playtest checked pacing and comprehension, and the team kept a lesson from Portal that the final puzzle should not be the hardest, because long careful solving is not a climax.
notes: YouTube upload is titled 'Portal 2: Creating a Sequel to a Game That Doesn't Need One'. Alternate Vault pages for the same session (same title and conference in the Vault crawl) are listed in alt_urls.

title: How I Got My Mom to Play Through Plants vs. Zombies
summary: The designer of Plants vs. Zombies (PopCap) gives ten techniques for teaching mechanics to non-gamers without alienating experienced players: blend the tutorial into play, have players do rather than read, spread teaching across the game (the shovel at level 1-5, a store with a limited selection about 25 levels in), get the player to act once, use few words (a self-imposed cap of eight on screen, which Fan admits breaking), use unobtrusive messages, show adaptive hints only to struggling players, cut noise, teach through visuals, and use everyday knowledge. Includes repricing the sunflower so the first affordable plant is the economy.
notes: Same session is also listed at Vault ids 1015541 and 1015959; 1015327 is used consistently. Audit 2026-09-26: re-read the official GDC YouTube captions. The store opened at 3-4 (25 levels in) with a limited selection, not the full store; tip six is unobtrusive messaging (the old wording 'avoid flow-breaking popups' paraphrased it). Alternate Vault pages for the same session (same title and conference in the Vault crawl) are listed in alt_urls.

title: Achieving the Illusion of Agency
venue: Interactive Storytelling: ICIDS 2012, Lecture Notes in Computer Science 7648
summary: Online study with a short text choose-your-own-adventure story of six binary choices in three versions: branching; linear with immediate text acknowledging each choice; linear with minimal feedback. About 150 participants recruited by snowball sampling were analysed. Branching and acknowledged-linear versions were rated similarly on most agency items, but branching scored higher on believing the story would have differed with other choices. The minimal-feedback version scored below branching on every item. Authors note priming from the choose-your-own-adventure framing and sample limits.
notes: ICIDS 2012 peer-reviewed full paper (best paper). Crossref types LNCS proceedings papers as book-chapter; the venue is a refereed conference. Full text read in an author-hosted PDF.

title: 8 Bit & '8 Bitish' Graphics-Outside the Box
summary: Ferrari, who started at Lucasfilm Games in the EGA era, on limited-palette art. Turn off every anti-aliasing and interpolation option; use the pencil and nearest-neighbour scaling. Fill a selection and slide HSV or colour balance instead of hunting the palette. Keep each object to three to seven colours and the sky to 16-32, where long subtle ramps hide dither, and reserve about half of a 256-colour palette for colour-cycling ramps. Order ramps highlight, turning edge, shadow so gradient fills pre-shade forms; keep greyscale dither templates to reuse. Every scene needs value, saturation and warm-cool contrast. On the game in progress, banded colour replaced hand-placed dither to keep pace.
notes: Numbers from captions. Vault access tier not confirmed, so members is the cautious default; the full talk is on GDC's official YouTube channel. Access set to free because the full talk is on the official GDC YouTube channel (alt_urls). Audit 2026-10-15: the three-to-seven colours per object figure is confirmed by repetition in the transcript (stated three ways, and matching the speaker's later 1-3 highlight + 1 turning edge + 1-3 shadow rule).

title: Physics for Programmers: Networking for Physics Programmers
summary: Fiedler's segment of the GDC 2010 physics tutorial on synchronizing rigid-body simulation over the internet. Fiedler argues real-time games should use UDP, since TCP's in-order delivery stalls on lost packets, names jitter and late packets as the core problem, and shows a priority accumulator for fitting many objects into small packets and a jitter buffer that trades latency for smoothness. For a peer-to-peer co-op game the segment gives an authority scheme (players own their avatar, lowest id breaks ties, interacting players take authority), warns it is open to cheating, and recommends lockstep or client-server for competitive games.
notes: Fiedler's part of the multi-speaker GDC 2010 "Physics for Programmers" tutorial session. Content read: Fiedler's slide deck with speaker notes on GDC Vault media (alt_urls). The 2010 bandwidth survey figures in the deck are not used. Alternate Vault pages for the same session (same title and conference in the Vault crawl) are listed in alt_urls.

title: Better Development Through Science: How Aliens, Odysseus, and Toyota Can Help Improve Production
summary: Former Wideload producer applies operations science and lean manufacturing ideas to game production: the critical path sets how long one item takes and the bottleneck sets throughput; add staff one at a time; keeping everyone fully busy is counterproductive; limit work in progress and tighten limits gradually; write acceptance criteria so features don't churn; fix defects as soon as they appear instead of batching QA at the end; start change with the biggest pain point. Examples are illustrative, and Fischer cautions that studios are not factories and discovery cannot be removed.
notes: Vault id 1024460 is the same session; 1024005 is used consistently. Alternate Vault pages for the same session (same title and conference in the Vault crawl) are listed in alt_urls.

title: Photic- and Pattern-induced Seizures: A Review for the Epilepsy Foundation of America Working Group
summary: Literature review prepared for an Epilepsy Foundation of America consensus conference on visually provoked seizures. Photosensitivity occurs in roughly 0.3 to 3% of people; seizures from light affect about 1 in 10,000 (1 in 4,000 aged 5 to 24). In a Japanese broadcast incident only about a quarter of the children who had a seizure had had one before. Flashes at 15 to 25 Hz are most provocative, within a range of 1 to 65 Hz; light-dark patterns and red also contribute; video games are among known triggers. Agencies in the UK and Japan and the ITU have issued risk-reduction recommendations.

title: Honoring the Blade: Lethality and Combat Balance in 'Ghost of Tsushima'
summary: Sucker Punch's lead combat designer on keeping swords lethal while providing 30 hours of gear progression. RPG level scaling and armor shields made enemies feel like 'sword sponges' and broke the samurai fantasy. The team kept hits-to-kill in short bands, raised enemy damage, aggression and move sets on harder difficulties without raising health or stagger, used stagger and stances for variety, gated regions to cap worst-case encounters, and checked bands against linear, average and wide player progression models. Players accepted a few more hits when less UI was shown.
notes: Alternate Vault pages for the same session (same title and conference in the Vault crawl) are listed in alt_urls.

title: Making it Matter: Lessons from Real Sports
summary: A designer and philosopher argues that sports matter despite arbitrary rules because of hard execution, audiences and integrity. Suggests ways for games to raise stakes: attempts that cannot be repeated freely, spectators whose reactions players hear, physically demanding controls, and national teams; criticises quicksave for erasing drama. Treats pay-to-win and grinding as integrity problems, like doping or match-fixing, and argues leaderboards and records should survive updates. Foddy deliberately left an exploit in QWOP unpatched, holding that enforcing rules too hard undermines integrity. Observations of public play show some games suit being played in front of people. No data.
notes: Alternate Vault pages for the same session (same title and conference in the Vault crawl) are listed in alt_urls.

title: 'Overwatch' Gameplay Architecture and Netcode
summary: Blizzard's lead gameplay programmer on Overwatch's ECS and netcode. Components hold state without behavior, systems hold behavior without state, singleton components replace system-owned state, shared utilities should have few side effects, and complex side effects are queued and resolved at one point in the frame. The rules took about 1.5 years to settle; older code outside them stayed a main source of bugs. The netcode uses fixed 16 ms command frames, a client running ahead of the server, prediction with rollback and input replay, input redundancy, client time dilation to refill the server's input buffer, and server-side rewind for hit registration, clamped at high ping.

title: Evolving Worlds from the Crumbling Chaos: The Art-Led Approach of 'Darkest Dungeon 2's' Procedural Generation System
summary: Artist Fox and programmer Towle describe the art-led world generator of Darkest Dungeon 2, built on a minimal set of road tiles whose art variants come from rotation, mirroring and mutators. With a two-person QA team, they made every internal test run generate a new random biome and deliberately crash when a needed tile was missing, leaving enough information to reproduce the case; they report this surfaced missing-tile cases over years of team testing and that early access launched without generation bugs.

title: Dealing with Scope Change in 'Heat Signature' and 'Gunpoint'
summary: Solo developer compares Gunpoint (three years of weekends, estimated at six months) with Heat Signature (three and a half years full time). On Gunpoint one prototyped mechanic clearly worked and the game grew around it; Heat Signature's idea could not be tested without building most of the game, and the developer spent long on a meta-layer before finding the core in the ship interiors. Francis's filter for ideas: how much must be built before knowing if it works. Scope creep helped when it deepened the core and hurt elsewhere; games needing many parts to be good are risky for a solo developer. Presented as a personal process, not a rule.
notes: Independent Games Summit session. Vault id 1028693 is a later re-showing.

title: Building the World of 'The Ascent'
venue: Game Developers Conference 2022, Visual Arts track
summary: Neon Giant (11 people, peaking at four artists) built a dense world with no concept art and no per-asset high-to-low bakes. High/low baking, pure tiling materials and pure trim sheets each failed on iteration speed, detail or draw calls, so almost every hard-surface object shares one trim texture with a reserved area of pre-baked mechanical parts, plus mid-poly geometry, weighted normals and mesh decals to hide the reuse. Because assets share one texture and shader setup, materials swap freely via Unreal material-instance inheritance, good shapes go into a reusable kitbash library, and polygon density and material cost stay uniform, which made later features and optimisation simple.
notes: Team numbers from captions. Vault access tier not confirmed, so members is the cautious default; the full talk is on GDC's official YouTube channel. Access set to free because the full talk is on the official GDC YouTube channel (alt_urls).

title: Change and Constant: Breaking Conventions with 'The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild'
summary: Nintendo's director, technical and art directors: to let players choose where to go and what to do, they dropped conventions such as impassable walls (climbing, then gliding) and replaced puzzles built from single-purpose objects ('development by addition') with 'multiplicative' play in which objects react to player actions and to each other, first tried in a prototype drawn in 2D. Physics (Havok) and a 'chemistry engine', a rule-based state calculator where elements change materials and each other but materials do not change each other, give consistent rules inviting experiment; players' own solutions count as correct. The art aimed to be easy to 'lie' with while suggesting real physics.
notes: The talk was given in Japanese with English interpretation; the official GDC YouTube upload has no captions, so its English audio track was machine-transcribed locally (whisper.cpp, small.en) and read in full. Names and terms were checked against the Vault page; wording is approximate.

title: Heuristics for AI-Driven Graphical Asset Generation Tools in Game Design and Development Pipelines: A User-Centered Approach
summary: User study with 16 game designers and developers, convenience-sampled and mostly early-career, who explored three non-functional mockups of AI graphical-asset generator interfaces (stand-alone, and two integrated in Unity) and then answered questionnaires and optional short interviews. All preferred early-design uses such as inspiration, exploring ideas and placeholders; most favoured many variations over initial quality, to refine by hand; they preferred tools integrated into their existing environments, with configurable output in common formats. The authors turn these findings into heuristics for designing such tools.
notes: Abstract read on arXiv (v2, 27 Jun 2025); journal version confirmed through Crossref (published online March 2026, pages 1-22). Access marked free for the arXiv version. Full text not read. Full text read 2026-10-15: the published IJHCI version (CC BY, published online 04 Mar 2026, pp. 1-22) from Brunel's repository (bura.brunel.ac.uk/bitstream/2438/28017/9/FullText.pdf); arXiv v2 also downloaded. Metadata matches; the journal version is itself open access, so the DOI copy is free.

title: Game Design Workshop: A Playcentric Approach to Creating Innovative Games
summary: Textbook built around a playcentric process: set player experience goals (descriptions of the situations and feelings players should have, not features), build a rough physical prototype of the core mechanics right after brainstorming and digital prototypes after that, playtest them against those goals, then evaluate, prioritise and either revise, restart or move on, repeating the loop through development. Fullerton advises against starting production before the experience goals and core mechanics are understood, because changes get costlier later, and treats design documentation as a living collaboration tool rather than a static specification.
notes: Read: the publisher's preview (front matter, table of contents and most of Chapter 1, including the playcentric process and iterative design sections). Claims citing this entry stay within that excerpt. Audit 2026-09-26 (same publisher preview, Chapter 1): the prototype built immediately after brainstorming is a physical one; software prototypes are step 4 of Fullerton's process. Copyright page reads 2019 but Open Library and Crossref give 2018; year kept.

title: Character Balance: More than the Numbers
summary: Vicarious Visions on balancing 80+ Skylanders characters for players aged about 6 to 10. Balance priorities follow the audience (PvE and character choice over PvP). Kid testing showed perceived power differs from actual power: large damage numbers read as stronger, a +20% bonus that does not cut hits-to-kill does not feel stronger, and a child still judged one character more powerful even though it took longer to clear an encounter with it. Enemy health varied only about 200% across the game; difficulty came from enemy damage; chance-based blocks confused children. A hidden PvP handicap was seen as cheating and became a toggle. Encounter counts were matched to character archetypes.
notes: Alternate Vault pages for the same session (same title and conference in the Vault crawl) are listed in alt_urls.

title: Breaking the Ankh: Deterministic Propagation Netcode in 'Spelunky 2'
summary: BlitWorks' netcode programmer on why Spelunky 2, which simulates its whole world every frame, used deterministic netcode, and why plain rollback's state copying cost too much (25-65% of frame time went to memory copies). The shipped model runs a lockstep ground-truth simulation plus a predicting fork that replaces the displayed simulation once it catches up. Launch problems included rollback degrading to about 10 frames per second on one console, a third-party service outage and a denial-of-service attack. Replays reproduced desyncs from one file. García Romero says online multiplayer is not a good default for every game.
notes: Vault lists the speaker as "Guillermo NWDD Garca Romero"; NWDD is the speaker's handle. Alternate Vault pages for the same session (same title and conference in the Vault crawl) are listed in alt_urls.

title: Multithreading the Entire Destiny Engine
summary: Bungie's platform technical lead on restructuring Destiny's engine so all work runs as jobs linked by explicit dependencies instead of locks, grouped into non-overlapping sequences for simulation, networking and rendering, with simulation and rendering pipelined. A debug-only system checked every data access against each job's declared access policy and flagged any two jobs that could run concurrently with conflicting access, even when no race had occurred. Conflicts were fixed by adding dependencies, double-buffering, queuing writes or restructuring. Retrofitting took months; Genova credits it with fewer threading bugs than earlier single-platform titles.

title: Pixelated Image Abstraction
venue: NPAR 2012: Proceedings of the 10th International Symposium on Non-Photorealistic Animation and Rendering (Eurographics)
summary: Converts a photo into a tiny, small-palette image in the style of pixel art by solving jointly for a superpixel mapping to output pixels and for the palette. Nearest or cubic downsampling followed by median-cut quantisation loses detail, blurs, and becomes unrecognisable at very small sizes and palettes. A 100-person online study and interviews with pixel artists favoured the method over that naive pipeline. Stated limits: artists wanted more control, and the method lacks edge highlighting and selective dithering, which artists use for blends and texture.

title: AI for Testing: The Development of Bots that Play 'Battlefield V'
summary: EA engineer describes 'AutoPlayers': scripted, non-learning bots that drive Battlefield V through its input layer so QA can soak-test map, mode and platform combinations that human playtests could no longer cover. The aim was test coverage, not human-like play; bots may cheat, repeat the same paths and camp objectives. In a two-month comparison, bots had found 49% of crashes seen in human playtests and another 15% were judged findable; the rest came from UI (bots skip the UI) and hardware or OS configurations the farm lacked. Bots were later reused for performance runs and for finding spots where players get stuck.
notes: AI Summit session. Vault id 1026308 is the same session; 1025905 is used consistently. Alternate Vault pages for the same session (same title and conference in the Vault crawl) are listed in alt_urls.

title: Advanced Prototyping
summary: Drawing on Spore and the Indie Game Jam, argues that prototypes validate ideas rather than generate them: each should answer a clearly stated, falsifiable question, small enough to be tractable but relevant to the real game, and be cheap, fast, tested with people and generalisable. Break big problems into prototypable pieces and state what is assumed outside the prototype. Spend on the few qualities the question needs, write code only where understanding is needed and fake the rest, avoid committing to abstractions, and when testing stay quiet and record observations, not suggestions.
notes: Read: the full slide deck with speaker notes (PowerPoint hosted on Hecker's site with the session audio); the audio was not transcribed. The Vault page is marked free content.

title: 'Slay the Spire': Metrics Driven Design and Balance
summary: Mega Crit co-founder on balancing a two-designer single-player deckbuilder. Goal: every card has a place, not equal power; warping combos are acceptable if rare and hard to assemble because no opponent suffers. Tools: a playtester Slack feedback bot, top card-game players, and a server logging every run. Cautions: the Madness card looked strong only because it was usually acquired just before the Act 3 boss, and two heavy testers dominated aggregate averages. Ascension levels let data be split by skill. Weekly Early Access patches plus a daily beta branch set expectations for constant change. Slow, grindy optimal strategies were cut; random enemy movesets felt too random.
notes: Alternate Vault pages for the same session (same title and conference in the Vault crawl) are listed in alt_urls.

title: Available 3D formats
summary: Lists glTF 2.0 as the recommended scene format: text .gltf suits version control, binary .glb is smaller. Importing .blend runs Blender's glTF exporter in the background and then the normal glTF importer; it needs Blender 3.0 or later (3.5+ recommended), a Blender path in Editor Settings if not auto-detected, and Blender on every team member's machine. OBJ lacks skinning, animation, UV2 and PBR materials; FBX uses the ufbx importer from 4.3. Blender exports backface culling disabled by default, so imported materials cull nothing until culling is enabled in Blender; models with shape keys should export deformation bones only.
notes: 4.7 URL verified (page header shows Godot Engine 4.7 documentation).

title: Advanced Import Settings
summary: Per-object import overrides. Meshes can be saved to external files and can override LOD generation (with a Normal Merge Angle that keeps edges during simplification), shadow meshes and lightmap UV generation. Materials can use an external file; the Extract Materials action writes .tres files that survive reimport, but renaming a material in the source breaks the link until it is reassigned. Nodes can generate physics bodies and collision shapes (trimesh for static bodies, convex decomposition for dynamic ones), occluders with a simplification distance, and navigation meshes.
notes: 4.7 URL verified (page header shows Godot Engine 4.7 documentation).

title: CanvasItem
summary: Class reference. Every CanvasItem has a texture_filter property; the default, Parent Node, inherits the parent's filter, so one override on a parent covers its subtree. Nearest reads only the nearest texel: pixelated up close and grainy at a distance because mipmaps are not sampled. The mipmap filter variants are described as being for non-pixel-art textures viewed at a low scale.
notes: The 4.7 URL exists and was used; the page header reads Godot Engine (4.7) documentation. Only the texture_filter property and TextureFilter enum entries were read. Re-checked 2026-10-15. Caution for users of this entry: CanvasItem.TextureFilter numbers values differently from the project setting rendering/textures/canvas_textures/default_texture_filter (here 0 = Parent Node, 1 = Nearest, 2 = Linear; the project setting and Viewport enum use 0 = Nearest, 1 = Linear), so this page must not be used to decode that setting's default.

title: Using CharacterBody2D/3D
summary: Tutorial comparing the two movement methods. move_and_collide() takes the relative movement for this step, typically the velocity multiplied by the frame timestep (delta), stops at a collision and returns collision data; move_and_slide() instead uses the body's velocity and slides along surfaces.

title: CharacterBody2D
summary: Class reference. move_and_slide() moves the body based on its velocity property, which is in pixels per second, and should be called from _physics_process(). The velocity property notes that setting it to a desired velocity multiplied by delta is a common mistake because that yields a motion vector in pixels.

title: Command line tutorial
summary: Reference for editor and engine command-line options, including --headless (dummy display and audio drivers), --check-only (parse a script for errors and quit, used with --script), --import (start the editor, wait for resources to import, then quit) and --quit / --quit-after for ending after a number of iterations.

title: Engine
summary: Class reference. Engine.time_scale sets how fast the in-game clock runs relative to real time and affects Timer, SceneTreeTimer and everything that uses delta, including _process() and _physics_process(). It does not change audio playback speed and does not adjust physics_ticks_per_second, so physics becomes less precise at large scales.

title: High-level multiplayer
summary: Tutorial for Godot's high-level multiplayer API. The default ENet implementation uses UDP only, so hosting for players outside the LAN usually requires forwarding the server port as UDP. A server is created with create_server(port, max_clients) and a client with create_client(address, port). Remote procedure calls are declared with @rpc, whose options choose who may call (authority or any_peer), whether the call also runs locally, the transfer mode (reliable, unreliable, unreliable_ordered) and the channel. The server is peer 1 and the default authority, changeable per node with set_multiplayer_authority. The page advises treating client input as untrusted and validating RPC arguments.

title: Idle and Physics Processing
summary: Tutorial. Idle processing (_process()) updates a node every frame, as often as possible, while physics processing (_physics_process()) runs at a fixed rate, 60 times per second by default, independent of the frame rate; physics-engine work belongs in physics processing.

title: Import configuration
summary: Scene import options. The root should be a Node3D-derived type; Apply Root Scale bakes scale into meshes and animations. Ensure Tangents generates missing tangents with MikkTSpace (needed for normal and height maps), though exporting tangents from the modelling tool is preferred. Per-scene switches cover LOD generation, welded shadow meshes, and Static Lightmaps light baking, which generates UV2 with a lightmap texel size. Animation bake rates above about 30 FPS rarely help. Reimport overwrites edits to the imported scene, so changes go in an inherited scene or, preferably, in the source file.
notes: 4.7 URL verified (page header shows Godot Engine 4.7 documentation).

title: Importing images
summary: Texture import settings. Lossless is the 2D default and the mode recommended for pixel art; VRAM Compressed shows artifacts in 2D and should stay off for pixel art even on 3D textures. Since 4.0 the filter and repeat modes are set on CanvasItem nodes, not at import. Detect 3D switches textures used in 3D to VRAM compression with mipmaps; VRAM compression cuts memory roughly 4-6x and mipmaps add about 33%. Detected normal maps use RG compression; Normal Map Invert Y converts DirectX-style maps; roughness can be filtered from a normal map to reduce specular aliasing; Size Limit helps mobile and web.
notes: 4.7 URL verified (page header shows Godot Engine 4.7 documentation). Merged from two research passes (2D and 3D settings).

title: Fixing jitter, stutter and input lag
summary: Jitter shows most when the world scrolls at constant speed, as in runners and platformers, and comes mainly from a mismatch between physics tick rate and monitor refresh rate, or from updating objects in different callbacks (physics versus idle). Remedies: physics interpolation (adds some input lag to physics-driven movement), tick rates that are multiples of the refresh rate, V-Sync choices, and Exclusive Fullscreen on Windows.
notes: The 4.7 URL exists and was used; the page header reads Godot Engine (4.7) documentation. The page does not mention pixel art, pixel snapping or Camera2D smoothing.

title: Mesh level of detail (LOD)
summary: Godot generates LOD meshes on import for glTF, .blend, Collada and FBX scenes using the meshoptimizer library and picks a level at render time from a screen-space metric, so field of view and resolution are accounted for. The Threshold Pixels project setting defaults to 1 px, described as near-lossless; per-node LOD Bias shifts quality. Generation can produce visual errors, especially on skinned meshes, so it can be disabled per mesh. MultiMesh and particle nodes share one LOD for all instances. Hand-authored LODs belong in visibility ranges; a debug draw mode helps measure the gain.
notes: 4.7 URL verified (page header shows Godot Engine 4.7 documentation).

title: Model export considerations
summary: Godot is right-handed and Y-up with the camera looking down -Z, so oriented assets such as characters should have their front at +Z; in Blender the front is -Y. Meshes should be triangulated before export because import-time triangulation of n-gons can be unpredictable; object transforms should be applied; skeletons should be exported in rest pose; lighting should be designed in Godot rather than imported.
notes: 4.7 URL verified (page header shows Godot Engine 4.7 documentation).

title: Multiple resolutions
summary: Stretch mode viewport renders at the base size and scales the result; the page recommends it for pixel art, with aspect keep or expand. Scale mode integer (Godot 4.2+) floors the scale factor so each game pixel becomes an even block; fractional factors (640x360 in 1366x768, about 2.13x) give uneven pixels. Typical pixel-art bases run 256x224 to 640x480; 640x360 scales by whole numbers to 720p, 1080p, 1440p and 4K. Use Exclusive Fullscreen, since Fullscreen's 1-pixel strip can make integer scaling pick a smaller factor. Viewport mode cannot show sub-pixel sprite motion; canvas_items is suggested then.
notes: The 4.7 URL exists and was used; the page header reads Godot Engine (4.7) documentation. Does not cover texture filters, pixel snapping or camera smoothing.

title: Node
summary: Class reference. When nodes enter the scene tree, a parent's _enter_tree() runs before its children's, while _ready() runs children first and the parent last. _ready() is called only once per node; removing and re-adding a node does not call it again unless request_ready() was called.

title: Node type customization using name suffixes
summary: Object names exported from the modelling tool act as import hints. -noimp drops a node; -col and -convcol add concave or convex static collision beside the mesh; -colonly and -convcolonly replace the mesh with collision; -occ and -occonly add or convert to an occluder; -navmesh converts to a navigation mesh; -rigid, -vehicle and -wheel create physics bodies; -loop or -cycle mark looping animations; -alpha and -vcol set material flags. Suffixes accept -, $ or _ and are case-insensitive; import options can disable them.
notes: 4.7 URL verified (page header shows Godot Engine 4.7 documentation).

title: Pausing games and process mode
summary: Tutorial. Setting the scene tree's paused flag stops 2D and 3D physics for all nodes and stops or continues each node according to its process mode (Inherit, Pausable, When Paused, Always, Disabled). Nodes that stop no longer receive process, physics-process or input callbacks; physics servers can be reactivated while paused with their set_active methods.

title: ProjectSettings
summary: rendering/2d/snap/snap_2d_transforms_to_pixel and snap_2d_vertices_to_pixel (default false) suit low-resolution pixel art: crisper, but movement is less smooth, especially with Camera2D smoothing; both are read only at startup and enabling both is discouraged (prefer transforms). stretch/mode viewport is recommended for pixel art; canvas_items drops the 1:1 sprite-to-screen pixel mapping and is the default for projects created in 4.7+. scale_mode integer keeps the screen a whole multiple of the base size; set Window.min_size to the base size to avoid clipping. canvas_textures/default_texture_filter defaults to 1.
notes: The 4.7 URL exists and was used; the page header reads Godot Engine (4.7) documentation. The page is about 740k characters; only the named properties were extracted and read. The description does not label enum value 1; a non-admissible Godot tutorial (GDQuest) says the default filter is linear. Re-checked 2026-10-15 (4.7 page, named properties only). Value 1 of default_texture_filter is Linear: the 4.7 Viewport class reference gives canvas_item_default_texture_filter = 1 = DEFAULT_CANVAS_ITEM_TEXTURE_FILTER_LINEAR, and core/config/project_settings.cpp declares the setting with hint 'Nearest,Linear,Linear Mipmap,Nearest Mipmap', default 1. The ProjectSettings page itself does not label the value. The listed default for display/window/stretch/mode is "disabled"; canvas_items is the default only for projects created in 4.7 or later.

title: Resource
summary: Class reference. With resource_local_to_scene enabled, the resource is duplicated for each instance of the scenes using it so it can be modified in one instance without affecting others; changing the flag at run time does not affect existing duplicates. duplicate() returns a shallow copy by default. duplicate(true) also copies nested resources that are local to the file, but resources saved as separate files stay shared; duplicate_deep() with DEEP_DUPLICATE_ALL copies those too.

title: Resources
summary: Tutorial on Godot resources. A resource loaded from disk is loaded only once; loading it again returns the same in-memory copy, and images, meshes and similar resources are shared between the scene instances that use them.

title: Standard Material 3D and ORM Material 3D
summary: Reference for the PBR material. Albedo is the base colour multiplied with its texture; metallic and roughness combine to cover most material types, roughness 0 being a mirror and 1 fully blurred; minimum internal reflectivity is 0.04. ORMMaterial3D packs occlusion, roughness and metallic in one texture. Normal maps use only red and green and follow the OpenGL convention (Y+), so DirectX-style maps need the Y axis flipped. A baked AO map affects ambient light and, by default, not direct light; the page says a well-baked AO map beats screen-space AO. Vertex colours exported as sRGB need the Is sRGB flag.
notes: 4.7 URL verified (page header shows Godot Engine 4.7 documentation). Re-read 2026-10-15 from the 4.7 page: the AO section says the map does not affect direct light 'by default'; summary now keeps that qualifier.

title: TileData
summary: Class reference. TileData.probability (default 1.0) is the relative chance that a tile is chosen when painting a pattern of random tiles, which is how variation tiles are weighted; terrain and terrain_set hold the tile's terrain IDs.
notes: The 4.7 URL exists and was used; the page header reads Godot Engine (4.7) documentation. Only the probability, terrain and terrain_set entries were read.

title: Using TileSets
summary: Terrain sets use one of three modes (Match Corners and Sides, Match Corners, Match Sides), said to correspond to the Godot 3 autotile bitmask modes (2x2, 3x3, 3x3 minimal); each tile's peering bits name the terrain expected at each neighbour, -1 meaning empty. Alternative tiles can be flipped, transposed, modulated or offset but do not inherit the base tile's properties. Use Texture Padding adds a 1-pixel transparent border per tile to stop texture bleeding when filtering is on, and is recommended unless it causes problems.
notes: The 4.7 URL exists and was used; the page header reads Godot Engine (4.7) documentation. The page does not say which 3.x mode matches which 4.x mode, or how many tiles each mode needs.

title: Vector math
summary: Godot's introductory vector math page. It notes that in Godot's 2D coordinate system the positive y axis points downwards, as in most computer graphics applications, rather than upwards as in school mathematics.
notes: Cited only for the 2D axis convention (API fact). Year is the year the stable documentation was checked.

title: Viewport
summary: Class reference. A viewport's canvas_item_default_texture_filter sets the default filter mode for the CanvasItem nodes it contains. Its default is 1, which the DefaultCanvasItemTextureFilter enum defines as Linear; Nearest is 0.
notes: The 4.7 URL exists; the page header reads Godot Engine (4.7) documentation. Only the canvas_item_default_texture_filter property and the DefaultCanvasItemTextureFilter enum were read. Added in the 2026-10-15 claim audit because the ProjectSettings page gives default_texture_filter = 1 without naming the value.

title: Visibility ranges (HLOD)
summary: Visibility ranges hide a GeometryInstance3D outside a begin/end camera distance, with margins for hysteresis or fades. They serve hand-authored LOD and hierarchical LOD, where one merged mesh replaces a group of children at a distance via Visibility Parent, cutting draw calls. Fade modes trade cost: Disabled switches instantly and is cheapest; Self and Dependencies alpha-blend. Dithered transitions avoid transparency sorting but look noisy. Distant LODs should use simpler materials (no normal maps, clearcoat, subsurface or refraction). Works alongside automatic mesh LOD.
notes: 4.7 URL verified (page header shows Godot Engine 4.7 documentation).

title: UX Summit: Step Into Your Player's Shoes: Making the Most of Team Playtests on 'skate'
summary: A UX designer on the remote skate. team (Full Circle, EA) on internal team playtests: fast and cheap, but the team is not the target audience and knows too much. Goncalves's 'focus team playtests' give testers scenarios based on player goals and split feedback by relevant traits (familiarity, motivation, shared pain points); feedback is collected in writing before discussion to limit groupthink and let quieter people contribute. Internal tests did not replace external ones: some findings needed outside confirmation, and first-time experience cannot be tested with a team that already knows the game.
notes: Vault id 1029410 is the same session; 1028859 is used consistently. Alternate Vault pages for the same session (same title and conference in the Vault crawl) are listed in alt_urls.

title: Meet Google Play's target API level requirement
summary: States Google Play's target API level rules. From 31 August 2026, new apps and app updates must target Android 16 (API level 36) or higher to be submitted, with lower minimums for Wear OS, Android Automotive, Android TV and Android XR; existing apps must target at least API level 35 to stay available to new users on newer Android versions.
notes: Platform requirement as read on the checked date; Google raises the level yearly, so recheck.

title: The identification of deviance and its impact on retention in a multiplayer game
venue: Proceedings of the 17th ACM Conference on Computer Supported Cooperative Work and Social Computing (CSCW 2014)
summary: Using League of Legends game records and player feedback, the authors build a toxicity index to identify deviant players and study the effects of playing with them. Toxic players more often played competitive modes and played with friends. Exposure to toxic players drove new players away, while experienced players were more resilient. The authors suggest ways to identify deviance and counter its effects.

title: Tools Summit: Writing Tools Faster: Design Decisions to Accelerate Tool Development
summary: An engine developer contrasts an earlier engine, where the tooling for a feature took weeks, with an editor built around one shared data model that gives every feature undo, copy and paste, serialization, prefabs and collaboration without extra code, plus immediate-mode UI and property panels generated from data. Gray argues that a small, owned technology stack is easier to debug and profile. Costs named: the central data model is complex, risky to change because it can break saved projects, and poor for large blobs; a custom UI framework took months. The evidence is the team's experience, not measurement.
notes: Alternate Vault pages for the same session (same title and conference in the Vault crawl) are listed in alt_urls.

title: Don't Call Them Whales: F2P Spenders and Virtual Value
summary: Kongregate's CEO on free-to-play spending, from platform data and one game. Spending is highly concentrated: a small share of players provides most revenue, as in other retail. In the data, large spenders were mostly older professionals, active from day one and focused on one game. Greer argues free-to-play earns more because invested players' spending is uncapped, rejects the term 'whales', calls pinch points unpleasant and ineffective, and grants a minority may spend unhealthily. In some A/B tests, making incentivized ad offers more prominent raised offer revenue but lowered total revenue, which Greer did not treat as inevitable. The data are the company's own, not independently verified.
notes: Audit 2026-09-26 (transcript): the A/B-test remark (Q&A, end of talk) is about incentivized advertising offers competing with in-app purchases, not IAP offers; summary now says so. Title, speaker, year, venue match the Vault page.

title: Data-Driven or Data-Blinded? Uses and Abuses of Analytics in Games
summary: Kongregate's CEO catalogues analytics and A/B-testing mistakes from a web game portal and a mobile publishing business. KPI shifts often reflect a changed audience mix rather than the game; averages hide small broken segments; sliced cohorts get too small to trust, so show sample sizes; revenue and play time follow power laws, so use medians and rank tests; nearly everything correlates with engagement; short tests over-represent the most engaged players; most tests show no significant change. Data describes the known world and cannot tell a team what new thing to make.
notes: Vault id 1025378 is the same session; 1025095 is used consistently. Alternate Vault pages for the same session (same title and conference in the Vault crawl) are listed in alt_urls.

title: Game Engine Architecture, Third Edition
