summary: Textbook on the runtime architecture of commercial game engines by a Naughty Dog programmer, covering the game loop and time, gameplay foundation systems and tools. Its section on updating game objects in real time explains why a naive per-object update loop breaks down and describes batched updates, updates phased around engine subsystems such as animation and physics, dependency-ordered update buckets, and the inconsistency when some objects already hold the new frame's state while others still hold the previous one, with state caching and time-stamping as remedies.
notes: Content read: the publisher-sanctioned excerpt of the section "Updating Game Objects in Real Time" published by Game Developer (https://www.gamedeveloper.com/programming/book-excerpt-game-engine-architecture), which reproduces the first-edition text; the author's table of contents (gameenginebook.com) shows the section carried into the third edition as 16.6. Claims citing this entry stay within that section.

title: Design in Detail: Changing the Time Between Shots for the Sniper Rifle from 0.5 to 0.7 Seconds for Halo 3
summary: Bungie's gameplay design lead on weapon balance across the Halo series, told through one Halo 3 change. Balance is framed as longevity: give every weapon a unique role on paper, identify the knobs that set its rhythm and its strength, and rein in an overpowered weapon by limiting its strengths rather than adding weaknesses. Process advice: balance in ordered passes, do not tell playtesters what changed, prefer 'I don't like this because' feedback to proposed fixes. The sniper rifle had become a close-range weapon with no counter; several fixes were rejected before the time between shots went from 0.5 to 0.7 seconds, a change checked by both reasoning and feel in play.
notes: Alternate Vault pages for the same session (same title and conference in the Vault crawl) are listed in alt_urls.

title: Design in Detail: Tuning the Muzzle Velocity of the Plasma Rifle Bolt on Legendary Difficulty Across the HALO Franchise
summary: A Bungie designer follows one value, enemy plasma-bolt speed, through the Halo campaigns. In Halo 1 on Legendary a global damage multiplier stacked with the shield multiplier, so dodging was no harder but hits killed fast: more punishing rather than more demanding. Halo 3 cut the damage scale and made higher difficulty faster (projectiles, AI timing). Griesemer describes 'reciprocal difficulty': an encounter pushes back harder the more the player pushes, yet forgives retreat as shields recover and enemies do not chase. Also shows a bracketing method for tuning values in test spaces.
notes: Also listed at Vault id 1014705. The caption at the Legendary passage drops a negation; context confirms the point. Alternate Vault pages for the same session (same title and conference in the Vault crawl) are listed in alt_urls.

title: Human-like playtesting with deep learning
venue: 2018 IEEE Conference on Computational Intelligence and Games (CIG)
summary: Trains a convolutional network on player data from Candy Crush Saga and Candy Crush Soda Saga to predict the most human-like move in a position, then use it to predict key metrics of new levels, chiefly difficulty. Compared with Monte Carlo tree search, the learned agent correlated better with average level difficulty and needed a fraction of the computation. The approach depends on large logs of real player moves and was shown on sequential match-3 content.
notes: Audit 2026-09-26: read the full paper from an open copy at https://gwern.net/doc/reinforcement-learning/imitation-learning/2018-gudmundsson.pdf (8 pp.). Training data: ~5,500 state-action pairs per level for levels 1-2,150 (~1.2e7 samples) tracked from ~1% of players over ~2 weeks; predictions evaluated on 200 held-out levels. Metadata (title, authors, year, venue) match Crossref.

title: The Effects of Latency and In-Game Perspective on Player Performance and Game Experience
venue: Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction 7 (CHI PLAY)
summary: 36 participants, mostly students, played a purpose-built shooting game in first-person, third-person and bird's-eye perspectives at a measured baseline latency of about 48 ms and with 150 ms added. High latency reduced hits, lengthened time to hit targets, and lowered ease of control, mastery, immersion, autonomy and enjoyment in every perspective. Bayesian analysis favored a model with no interaction between latency and perspective, which the authors read as evidence against classifying latency sensitivity by perspective or genre. Latency was measured by filming mouse and screen with a 240 fps camera.

title: Player Types: A Meta-synthesis
venue: Transactions of the Digital Games Research Association 1(2)
summary: Meta-synthesis of player typologies in earlier research. Finds the literature fairly uniform: typologies reduce to five motivation or orientation dimensions (achievement, exploration, sociability, domination, immersion) plus play intensity (casual to hardcore), mostly descending from Bartle's 1996 types. Warns that the word 'type' suggests players belong to one category, argues the dimensions are better measured as traits, and calls for validated scales and links to behavioral data. Notes that motives such as sensory or aesthetic enjoyment were absent from the typologies reviewed. Literature synthesis without new data.
notes: Read introduction and discussion of the ToDiGRA PDF.

title: Subtitles Are Changing, Don't Be Left Behind
summary: An accessibility specialist on subtitles. Players use them for many reasons (Hamilton cites Ubisoft data showing just over 60% of Assassin's Creed Origins players with subtitles on). The basics are size, contrast and amount of text: large text (the figure cited is 46 px at 1080p), a background box with adjustable opacity, at most two lines of about 38 characters. Good practice adds accuracy, full coverage including the opening cinematic, bottom-centre placement, speaker names, direction indicators, time to read, captions for important sounds, a live preview and presets. Valve added captions after deaf players wrote in and then included players with hearing loss in user research.

title: Independent Games Summit: Accessibility on a Shoestring
venue: Game Developers Conference 2021, Independent Games Summit
summary: An accessibility specialist on small studios. Disability arises from mismatches between people and designed barriers; some barriers are the intended challenge, and the work is removing the unnecessary ones, cheapest early (Hamilton cites a text-size patch that took The Outer Worlds three months). Most-complained-about issues: text size (not below 28 px at 1080p), remapping, colour-blindness (do not rely on colour alone; filters cause problems), subtitles, and intensity (let players turn off shake, blur and weapon bob; keep flashing within the published risk standard, since a warning is not enough). Debug options can become assists; involve disabled players; tell players the options exist.
notes: Alternate Vault pages for the same session (same title and conference in the Vault crawl) are listed in alt_urls.

title: Exploration in Ghost of Tsushima: Letting the Island Guide You
summary: Sucker Punch's lead systems designer on Ghost of Tsushima's exploration. Landmarks must pass a squint test, and players should see something that draws them at least every 30 seconds while travelling, a limit the team learned from players' patience; foliage and terrain were thinned to open sight lines. Quest ends were placed away from other quest starts, and each landmark type led consistently to one reward type. The compass drew players' eyes, spoiled objectives and pulled attention from story rides, so it was replaced by a wind that points the way, which needed stronger visuals, terrain-following particles and one objective at a time. One collectible type was too numerous and alike.

title: Thinking In 3D: The Development of Super Mario 3D Land
summary: Super Mario 3D Land's director on the 3DS stereoscopic display and on sayings from Miyamoto. Stereoscopy made floating objects easier to locate; to avoid blur and stereo-window violations the team kept objects away from the camera, did not let players rotate the camera freely (which also kept players from getting lost) and reduced depth range, and built stages around situations where 3D looked best. Following 'let people play the way they want', the game offers assist blocks, places the normal ending earlier and adds harder special worlds for advanced players. Watching the first session of Hayashida's son showed a player enjoying goals other than the intended ones.
notes: Most of the talk is in Japanese. Read a local machine transcription (whisper.cpp) of the English interpretation audio on Vault entry 1016364. The talk does not mention kishotenketsu; that attribution to Hayashida comes from a press interview, which is not admissible. Alternate Vault pages for the same session (same title and conference in the Vault crawl) are listed in alt_urls.

title: TrueSkill™: A Bayesian Skill Rating System
venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 19 (NIPS 2006)
summary: Microsoft Research paper introducing TrueSkill, a Bayesian rating system that generalizes Elo by tracking uncertainty about each player's skill, modeling draws, and inferring individual skills from team and multi-player results. On Halo 2 beta data it predicted the outcomes of tightly matched games better than Elo, and identified close games better in Free for All and Head to Head but not in Small Teams, which the authors suggest may be because capture-the-flag breaks the additive team model; it also converged in fewer games. On Xbox Live it matches players by predicted draw probability and displays a conservative skill estimate (mean minus three standard deviations).
notes: NIPS 2006 conference paper (peer reviewed) published in the 2007 proceedings volume; Crossref types the MIT Press record as book-chapter. Audit 2026-09-26: re-read sec 4.1; the Small Teams failure is in the match-quality (draw) test only and the paper hedges its cause ('possibly due to'); summary narrowed accordingly. Metadata ok.

title: Plot and Parcel: Procedural Level Design in 'XCom 2'
summary: Firaxis's lead level designer on replacing XCOM: Enemy Unknown's hand-built maps with plots into which building parcels and road/cover pieces stream. Goals were removing the environment-art bottleneck and map repetition. Believability rules (facings, driveways, zones) cut variety per slot and over-specified parcels rarely appeared; a quick-launch tool loaded chosen parcels for testing; tying plot types to missions restored place identity; story missions used a generated lead-up to one static parcel; they built more content than needed. Costs: artists lost control, cinematics and environmental storytelling got harder. Hess frames a scale from replayability to character.
notes: Alternate Vault pages for the same session (same title and conference in the Vault crawl) are listed in alt_urls.

title: Juicy Game Design: Understanding the Impact of Visual Embellishments on Player Experience
venue: Proceedings of the Annual Symposium on Computer-Human Interaction in Play (CHI PLAY '19)
summary: Treats juiciness as visual embellishment: redundant feedback where one player action triggers several non-functional reactions. Study 1 (40 participants) compared embellished and plain versions of two research games, a Frogger-style game and a first-person shooter; study 2 (32 participants) used Quake 3 Arena. Embellishments improved rated visual appeal in all games but affected aspects such as competence only under specific circumstances.
notes: Only the abstract was read; the specific circumstances are not stated there. A green open-access copy is listed by OpenAlex (Lincoln eprints 37129) but could not be retrieved.

title: Level Design Summit: Designing the Museum Flashback: 'The Last of Us Part II'
venue: Game Developers Conference 2022, Level Design Summit
summary: Hill's companion talk on building the same level: moments sequenced as setup, development, twist and payoff, which the talk names kishotenketsu; playable 3D blockouts built quickly in Maya and tested in engine for scale, camera and reveals, made with the expectation of being thrown away (4 to 12 weeks of blockout iteration); a 'first playable' defined as a level someone can play with no explanation; and outside playtests every 2 to 3 weeks. Hill's rule for feedback: players are usually right that something is wrong but usually wrong about what causes it.
notes: Alternate Vault pages for the same session (same title and conference in the Vault crawl) are listed in alt_urls.

title: Game Narrative Summit: Interactive Pacing from the Museum Flashback Level in 'The Last of Us Part II'
venue: Game Developers Conference 2022, Game Narrative Summit
summary: Evan Hill on pacing the optional content of The Last of Us Part II's museum flashback. Hill treats interesting moments as a four-part introduce, develop, twist, conclude anatomy from Asian literary tradition and sorts content into unmissable focal points, visible optional prospects of similar size, threads that extend a prospect when the player engages, and secrets that break expectation. Two early exhibits show that optional content can be skipped before a larger cluster, and a one-way 'hard valve' signals moving on. For one optional moment the team was content if 10-20% of players found it, and added cues when playtests fell short.
notes: Vault lists the company as 'Obisidan' (sic); the work described was at Naughty Dog. Hill attributes Mario's use of the structure to a YouTube video, which is not relied on. Alternate Vault pages for the same session (same title and conference in the Vault crawl) are listed in alt_urls.

title: The Gamer's Brain: How Neuroscience and UX Can Impact Design
summary: A psychologist then at Epic Games on limits of perception, memory and attention. Perception depends on prior knowledge, so audiences read the same image differently; Gestalt proximity and similarity group HUD elements without separators; icons should show their function, tested by asking players who have not seen them to describe form and function at in-game size. Attention works like a spotlight, so tips shown during combat are missed. Red was overused in Unreal Tournament 3 and early Fortnite; Fortnite reserved red for critical damage feedback near the reticle and made enemy bars orange, and fewer deaths went unnoticed. Players' explanations of a problem may not name its cause.
notes: Alternate Vault pages for the same session (same title and conference in the Vault crawl) are listed in alt_urls.

title: The Gamer's Brain, Part 2: UX of Onboarding and Player Engagement
summary: A cognitive psychologist then at Epic Games applies research on perception, attention and memory to onboarding, with examples from Fortnite and Paragon user tests. Eye tracking showed a player ignoring an important prompt during combat. Fortnite alpha analytics showed that players who died or struggled during onboarding were more likely to leave, so Hodent advises against punishing players while they are still learning. Further recommendations: asking testers to state the objective rather than asking whether it was clear, and spacing and varying repetition.
notes: Alternate Vault pages for the same session (same title and conference in the Vault crawl) are listed in alt_urls.

title: Controller to Display Latency in 'Call of Duty'
summary: Activision session on input latency in an engine with several parallel timelines. According to the session description, it traces data from the input sample to display scan-out, measures the segments of that path, uses a dynamic throttle to take the input sample as late in the frame as possible without dropping frames, and examines how the interaction between GPU work and scan-out adds latency when vsync is enabled.
notes: No official GDC YouTube upload was found; only the Vault session description was read. Cite for the existence of pipeline-stage latency and late input sampling, not for numbers. Alternate Vault pages for the same session (same title and conference in the Vault crawl) are listed in alt_urls.

title: Automated playtesting with procedural personas through MCTS with evolved heuristics
summary: Builds 'procedural personas': Monte Carlo tree search agents whose selection criteria are evolved towards designer-written utility functions (for example a runner, a monster killer, a treasure collector) and uses them as synthetic playtesters on MiniDungeons 2 levels. Personas behaved differently from one another and were sensitive to different level patterns, and evaluations ran quickly enough for iterative design. No human players were involved: whether personas match real playtraces is left to future work, usefulness depends on designers defining the right utilities, and scaling to complex games is open.
notes: Read the arXiv version (1802.06881v1), the authors' preprint of the journal article.

title: User Research on Destiny
summary: Bungie's user research lead on adapting methods from five Halo games to Destiny. A recruited pool of fans was handled with comparative questions and weighting; free-form and controlled tests ran in parallel because one session cannot do both; content was retested because unrelated changes shift difficulty; concept art and mockups were tested before anything was built; results were shown inside the designers' own tools and sessions streamed to the studio. Hopson treats player failure as the game's failure and notes lab findings that live players contradicted, because lab characters were disposable.
notes: Vault id 1022355 is the same session; 1022354 is used consistently. Alternate Vault pages for the same session (same title and conference in the Vault crawl) are listed in alt_urls.

title: Design patterns in FPS levels
venue: Proceedings of the Fifth International Conference on the Foundations of Digital Games (FDG 2010)
summary: Proposes a vocabulary of level design patterns for single-player first-person shooters, derived from analysing levels in commercial games (Half-Life 2, Halo 3, Gears of War, Killzone 2, Crysis, BioShock). Ten patterns in four groups (positional advantage: sniper location, gallery, choke point; large-scale combat: arena, stronghold; alternate gameplay: turret, vehicle section; alternate routes: split level, hidden area, flanking route) are each described by the parameters a designer can vary and their effect on pace, tension and challenge. A BioShock walkthrough shows a rhythm set up, broken and restored. Analytical framework; no player study.

title: Designing Text UX for Effortless Reading
summary: inkle's co-founder and UX designer (80 Days, Sorcery!, Heaven's Vault) on making large amounts of game text easy to read through focus (nothing competing with the text) and pacing (how text is revealed over time). Readability rests on familiarity, so over-stylised fonts add friction; margins, paragraph spacing and indents help; console text is often too small because developers sit close to the screen; Humfrey suggests about 5 to 15 words per line and placing text near the action. Text is broken into chunks and animated, but animation must never slow fast readers, and pacing is tuned by playing and testing with readers of different speeds.

title: MDA: A Formal Approach to Game Design and Game Research
venue: AAAI-04 Workshop on Challenges in Game Artificial Intelligence (AAAI Technical Report WS-04-04)
summary: Short workshop paper presenting the Mechanics-Dynamics-Aesthetics framework taught at the GDC Game Design and Tuning Workshop (2001-2004). Mechanics are rules and algorithms, dynamics the run-time behavior of mechanics acting on player input, aesthetics the emotional responses sought; designers work from mechanics outward while players meet aesthetics first. Offers an eight-term aesthetic vocabulary (sensation, fantasy, narrative, challenge, fellowship, discovery, expression, submission), treats Monopoly's runaway leader as a dynamics problem fixed through mechanics, and uses a tag game to argue that AI cannot be designed apart from the target aesthetic. Conceptual, untested.
notes: Published in the AAAI-04 workshop technical report WS-04-04; no DOI. AAAI library page and the authors' PDF checked by hand. The workshop's review process could not be confirmed beyond inclusion in the AAAI report; treat it as a short conceptual position paper.

title: The case for dynamic difficulty adjustment in games
venue: Proceedings of the 2005 ACM SIGCHI International Conference on Advances in Computer Entertainment Technology (ACE 2005)
summary: Short conference paper. Starts from the conventional worry that players feel cheated when a game adjusts itself during or across sessions, sets out basic design requirements for dynamic difficulty adjustment that does not disrupt or degrade the core experience, presents an interactive adjustment system (Hamlet), and reports preliminary evaluation results that the author says challenge common assumptions about player enjoyment and adjustment. Only the abstract was read; the study's details are not relied on.
notes: Full text not reachable (ACM DL returned 403; no open copy found). Cite only for what the abstract states.

title: Removing the HUD: The Impact of Non-Diegetic Game Elements and Expertise on Player Involvement
venue: Proceedings of the 2015 Annual Symposium on Computer-Human Interaction in Play (CHI PLAY 2015)
summary: Two lab studies with novice and expert players of one Battlefield 3 level, played with or without the HUD. Removing the HUD did not hurt initial engagement or enjoyment, but expert players reported more immersion without it, through greater cognitive involvement and sense of control; emotional involvement and challenge ratings did not differ by condition. The authors suggest the HUD distracts experts once they no longer need it. They caution that the level was chosen to be completable without HUD information, that the work covers one level of one shooter, and that samples were small.

title: Crafting Destruction: The Evolution of the Dead Space User Interface
summary: Dead Space's UI lead on its diegetic interface: health on the character's spine, a holographic inventory and a locator line in the world, and loading hidden inside in-fiction devices. Rules: the character keeps to one side of the screen so UI has a predictable home; important UI sits about 1.5 m above the floor because playtests showed players did not look higher or lower; menus that belong to the player rather than the character appear behind him; a strict colour code marks interactive, locked and decorative elements. A deliberately broken-looking font had to be made readable to pass certification, and an elaborate map went unused and was replaced late by the locator.
notes: Transcript read through the Dead Space 2 section; claims stay within that part. Alternate Vault pages for the same session (same title and conference in the Vault crawl) are listed in alt_urls.

title: Pixelating Vector Line Art
venue: NPAR 2012, International Symposium on Non-Photorealistic Animation and Rendering (Eurographics Association)
summary: Image editors' vector-to-raster conversion falls short of pixel-art standards, producing jaggies and broken lines. The authors describe Pixelator, which rasterizes vector line art into single-pixel paths following pixel artists' line conventions: straight lines from identical pixel spans and curves from spans that change monotonically, without jaggies or blips. In an online study, 148 participants hand-drew eight references and 200 rated pairs; Pixelator's output was preferred over Illustrator and Photoshop and, on average, over each group of human drawers, though symmetry, sharp corners and anti-aliasing remained open problems.
notes: Venue: NPAR 2012 (Eurographics), pages 21-28. Its DOI 10.2312/PE/NPAR/NPAR12/021-028 is a DataCite DOI, not in Crossref, so it is left out of the doi field. Abstract read from the Eurographics Digital Library metadata record; the item page returns 403 to the fetcher. Full text read 2026-10-15 from the Eurographics Digital Library PDF (bitstream afb44862-6cb2-4be4-9ddb-36fe58209d30, served via diglib.eg.org/server/api/core/bitstreams/<id>/content). Summary extended with the method's conventions and the study's sizes and results. Title, authors, year, venue and pages 21-28 match the PDF.

title: Rasterizing and antialiasing vector line art in the pixel art style
venue: Proceedings of the Symposium on Non-Photorealistic Animation and Rendering (NPAR 2013), ACM
summary: Pixel artists rasterize shapes by hand to avoid low-resolution artifacts and show pixels deliberately. Superpixelator extends the authors' earlier Pixelator for vector line art: it removes most artifacts that Illustrator, CorelDRAW and Java 2D produce (blips, gaps, extra pixels, jaggies), smooths curves, preserves symmetry, aspect ratio and sharp angles by optimization, and mimics manual antialiasing with a limited palette. Two professional pixel artists (Sven Ruthner and the group eBoy) compared 24 rotated shapes; they judged its aliased output as good as or better than hand rasterization and found some antialiased shapes too dark.
notes: Crossref gives pages 25-32. Abstract read from the Eurographics Digital Library metadata record. Access not verified: no free copy was confirmed, so marked paywalled. Full text read 2026-10-15 from the Eurographics Digital Library copy of the ACM NPAR 2013 paper (alt URL item d3a51944-...; PDF bitstream 0ea0d73f-4ead-4b54-8d5c-eddc05a757d3, freely downloadable), so access changed to free. Summary now states the evaluation was by two professional artists on 24 shapes. Metadata matches the PDF.

title: Narrative Sorcery: Coherent Storytelling in an Open World
summary: inkle's narrative director on the open-world parts of the text-based Sorcery! series. Replaces quest chains with self-contained encounters written defensively: preconditions guard nearly every line and option so a scene copes with any game state, with competent but dull fallbacks. Plot and player knowledge are tracked apart from encounters in small state machines whose states imply all earlier ones, so scenes can test ranges and new states can be inserted without breaking queries. Gains: plots start from many sources; emergent solutions. Costs: uncertainty about what players know, content most players never see, and more logic bugs, mostly missing preconditions.

title: 'Heaven's Vault': Creating a Dynamic Detective Story
summary: inkle's narrative director on Heaven's Vault. Actions and dialogue are atomic blocks gated by preconditions and written into nested scopes (moment, room, episode, game) that shadow one another, so authors rarely write structural logic. Episodes unlock through leads; clue objects are generated on demand from what suits the location, what the story needs and what the player lacks, giving one control point for how many destinations are open. Goals: every choice changes state, players never get stuck, no dead air. A script-driven random player run repeatedly found dead ends and stuck loops but could not detect continuity errors or anything in the 3D layer.
notes: Alternate Vault pages for the same session (same title and conference in the Vault crawl) are listed in alt_urls.

title: ink documentation: Writing with ink; Running your ink
summary: Official documentation for inkle's ink scripting language. Writing with ink covers knots and stitches, once-only versus sticky choices, automatic read counts on knots and stitches usable in conditions, tunnels, threads and lists for state tracking. Running your ink covers the runtime API: saving and restoring story state as JSON, reading and setting ink variables from game code, binding external functions and observing variable changes.
notes: Living documentation; year is the access year. Only the sections named in the summary were read.

title: Managing Complexity in the Halo 2 AI System
summary: Halo 2's combat AI as a behavior DAG (hierarchical state machine or behavior tree) with binary relevancy tests. Most parents run a prioritized list whose higher-priority children can interrupt; impulses change priorities situationally; state tags cheaply prune the tree; event-driven stimulus behaviors are inserted into the tree so higher priorities still apply. Per-actor 'props' store perceived rather than true world state. Designers direct squads through orders, firing positions and a small library of approved behavior styles, and character parameter files inherit from parents to curb parameter creep. Costs of complexity: coherence (dithering), transparency, run time, comprehension.
notes: The Vault entry is audio-only with no overview. Content was confirmed from Isla's written GDC 2005 proceedings paper of this talk, 'Handling Complexity in the Halo 2 AI' (reprinted by Gamasutra, March 2005); checked.content refers to that paper, which is not itself cited. Numbers in the paper (e.g. 30 Hz update, memory figures) were not used.

title: Choosing to Help Monsters: A Mixed-Method Examination of Meaningful Choices in Narrative-Rich Games and Interactive Narratives
venue: Proceedings of the 2018 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems
summary: Mixed-method study of what makes choices in narrative-rich games feel meaningful. A qualitative study collected players' views; a follow-up experiment tested the effect of meaningful choices on appreciation, enjoyment and narrative engagement. Moral, social and consequential characteristics were central to meaningfulness, and meaningful choices positively affected appreciation. Summary limited to the published abstract.

title: Math for Game Programmers: Ranking Systems: Elo, TrueSkill and Your Own
summary: Introductory comparison of Elo and TrueSkill. Elo moves points by the difference between expected and actual results, handles two sides only and converges slowly for new players; TrueSkill tracks skill and uncertainty, displays a conservative estimate and supports teams, but uses only wins and losses, and its complexity can make players distrust it. For a custom system Izquierdo stresses credibility and simplicity, placement games, decay, and a displayed score separate from the internal one, and notes that rating algorithms do not address cheating.
notes: Alternate Vault pages for the same session (same title and conference in the Vault crawl) are listed in alt_urls.

title: Metagame Balance
summary: From PlayStation All-Stars data: characters players called overpowered had middling win rates but the highest play rates, and play rates swung week to week while win rates stayed stable. Proposes treating a matchup chart as a 'selection game' and using linear programming to compute the range of play frequencies each character can have in a stable expert metagame. The bounds flag characters that are always excluded, sometimes dominant or always dominant (Meta Knight in Brawl data; one PlayStation character whose observed play rose from 18% to over 40% in three weeks with flat win rates).
notes: Alternate Vault pages for the same session (same title and conference in the Vault crawl) are listed in alt_urls.

title: Instant Field-Aligned Meshes
summary: Automatic remeshing of triangle meshes, point clouds or range scans into isotropic triangle or quad-dominant meshes, using one local smoothing operator that optimises edge orientations and vertex positions; an extrinsic energy snaps edges to sharp features. Avoiding global optimisation, it runs in under a second on meshes with hundreds of thousands of faces and handled 372 million triangles in under ten minutes. Quad-dominant output becomes all-quad after one Catmull-Clark subdivision step. The stated main limitation is more singularities than global parametrization methods, which brushes can collapse interactively.
notes: Abstract read on the EPFL RGL publication page, which links a free PDF; the full PDF and its limitations were not read. Full text read 2026-10-15 from the authors' PDF at https://igl.ethz.ch/projects/instant-meshes/instant-meshes-SA-2015-jakob-et-al.pdf. Summary now gives the subdivision route to pure quads and the singularity limitation; the previous 'not guaranteed all quads' wording dropped the paper's own all-quad post-process.

title: Developing 'Hi-Fi RUSH' Backwards and Finding Our Positive Gameplay Loop
summary: Hi-Fi RUSH's director (Tango Gameworks) on designing a rhythm-action game backwards from the desired result: actions landing on the music's beat. An early prototype with no art proved it. The rhythm system stretches or speeds animations so attacks land on the beat whatever the input timing; because impacts land on the beat, players drift back into rhythm without UI prompts, which the team called a positive gameplay loop. On-beat play earns extra audio, UI, rumble and hidden damage while mistimed input is downplayed; explicit timing UI appears only where timing changes outcomes. Adding music to a finished feature felt tacked on, so features were designed from their musical moment.
notes: Read the first half of the official GDC YouTube captions in full (pitch, prototype, loop, feedback and workflow sections).

title: Behavior is Brittle: Testing Game AI
summary: Panel on testing and debugging game AI. Advice: agree what 'broken' means for each character and whether behavior is scripted or systemic; test iteratively and try to break features rather than confirm them; separate sensors, knowledge, decisions and actions so inputs can be mocked and units tested; keep code simple and ownership clear; embed QA with the AI team. Tools discussed: debug drawing for every feature, marking scripted agents, per-agent breakpoints, state captures, overriding values at runtime, spawn and cheat commands, rolling session recordings triggered by testers, and fast headless AI-versus-AI runs to find crashes.
notes: Transcript from the official GDC YouTube upload. Mike Lewis (ArenaNet) also speaks on the panel but is not listed on the Vault page.

title: Scaffolding Player Location Awareness through Audio Cues in First-Person Shooters
venue: Proceedings of the 2016 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems
summary: Study of helping novices in multiplayer first-person shooters learn a skill experts use. The authors first established that understanding and using audio cues is critical to how experts locate opponents, then built and evaluated two ways to introduce that skill: a training system and a modified game interface. Both improved novices' accuracy and confidence in locating opponents; the training system led players to recognise more audio cues.

title: Juice It or Lose It
summary: Two independent developers demonstrate, live on stage, small feedback techniques that can be layered onto an existing plain game to make it more satisfying to play, including particles and sound, and share the demo's source code. Only the session description was checked.
notes: No official GDC YouTube upload was found. Cite only as the origin of the live 'juice' demonstration, not for specific techniques or numbers. Alternate Vault pages for the same session (same title and conference in the Vault crawl) are listed in alt_urls.

title: How responsiveness affects players' perception in digital games
venue: Proceedings of the ACM Symposium on Applied Perception (SAP '12)
summary: Players who were not told about the manipulation steered a motion-captured character through a simple path level and a harder platforming level, with or without a controller delay of about 150 ms (10 frames at just under 70 fps, varying slightly over time). The delay made the character feel harder to control, raised frustration even when players could not say why, and reduced performance on some tasks. The authors conclude that quick response matters most for challenging tasks that need precise control.
notes: The follow-up normoyle2014-latency-jitter attributes part of these effects to jitter in this study's delay.

title: Steps for Effective Localization
summary: Sony Interactive Entertainment Europe's localization project manager on efficient localization: meet localization staff early and choose a waterfall or iterative pipeline to match development; give every discipline access to one shared asset tool; let translators ask context questions in the tool, with images; communicate and enforce text-length and audio specifications before translation; support line variants such as gendered forms; and link strings to captured gameplay video for localization testing.
notes: Alternate Vault pages for the same session (same title and conference in the Vault crawl) are listed in alt_urls.

title: The Open and the Closed: Games of Emergence and Games of Progression
venue: Computer Games and Digital Cultures Conference Proceedings (Tampere)
summary: Distinguishes two ways games present challenge. Emergence: a few rules combine into many variations that players meet with strategies (board, card, action and strategy games; replayable, served by strategy guides). Progression: challenges presented in sequence with predefined solutions (adventure games; strong designer control, walkthroughs, low replayability). Separates simple rule interaction and combination from genuinely emergent strategies, notes that players pursue good strategies so a dull optimal strategy makes a dull game, and reads EverQuest as a game of emergence with embedded quest progression. Conceptual paper.
notes: CGDC 2002 (Tampere), proceedings edited by Frans Mayra for Tampere University Press with an editorial board; the editor's introduction describes selection from submitted paper proposals. Now in the DiGRA Digital Library with a Crossref DOI. Read the author's online copy.

title: The Art of Failure: An Essay on the Pain of Playing Video Games
summary: Book-length essay on the 'paradox of failure': people avoid failure yet seek out games in which they will fail. From chapter 1 (the excerpt read): failing in a game reveals a real inadequacy that the game promises the player can repair by playing on; failure makes players reconsider their strategy; good games give players a fair chance; and a failure costs either a permanent loss or the time invested, with the sense of loss growing with the time at stake. Humanities argument, not a measured study.
notes: Excerpt: chapter 1 as published by Salon, linked from the author's companion site jesperjuul.net/artoffailure.

title: Art Direction of 'Street Fighter V': The Role of Art in Fighting Games
summary: Capcom's art director for Street Fighter IV and V argues that in a fighting game art is the fastest feedback on the match state, so characters and animation are judged from the battle camera. Silhouettes are exaggerated so poses read when characters are small on screen; a realistic-proportion model was rejected early because attacks were hard to read. Height is set by impression in the fighting stance, not measured size; poses are turned slightly toward the battle camera; special moves are designed to be describable in a short phrase. Stage backgrounds use a narrower colour and value range than characters, without pure black or white; shadows are never pure black.
notes: Talk given in Japanese with interpretation; captions mix languages and garble numbers, so no figures are taken from it. Alternate Vault pages for the same session (same title and conference in the Vault crawl) are listed in alt_urls.

title: A Narrative Multiverse: The Branching Structure of 'As Dusk Falls'
summary: Interior Night's narrative lead on branching an interactive drama. Principles: keep classical structure by placing choices at its inflection points; start characters mid-arc so choices can resolve a theme either way; give each scene at least one consequential 'crossroads' choice with immediate, delayed and long-term effects; stop subdividing at roughly eight to ten outcomes per junction, beyond which players stop feeling the difference; allow no game overs or weak branches; and plan which variables a nonlinear timeline may change. Writers used screenplay format rather than flowchart tools; user research led to a late added branch.

title: The effects of juiciness in an action RPG
summary: A study (N = 3,018) compared four otherwise identical versions of an action RPG with no, medium, high or extreme juiciness, meaning visual and audio feedback. Both the no-juice and extreme-juice versions produced significantly less play time, lower player experience, lower intrinsic motivation and lower performance than the medium and high versions. The author describes it as the largest study of juiciness to date.
notes: Open access (CC BY) at ScienceDirect, but the publisher blocked automated retrieval; only the abstract was read.

title: WaveFunctionCollapse is constraint solving in the wild
venue: Proceedings of the 12th International Conference on the Foundations of Digital Games (FDG '17)
summary: Explains Gumin's WaveFunctionCollapse as constraint solving: local patterns from an example image, a minimum-remaining-values choice of the next cell, arc-consistency propagation, and a global restart instead of backtracking when a contradiction occurs. Experiments with an answer-set-programming surrogate suggest propagation, not the entropy heuristic, does most of the work. Adding a global constraint (use every pattern) caused many conflicts in one scenario, where restart-only search timed out but backtracking succeeded; the authors expect global constraints such as reachability to need backtracking.

title: Breathing Life into Greek Myth: The Dialogue of 'Hades'
summary: Supergiant's creative director and audio director on Hades' fully voiced dialogue. The roguelike was designed so each death advances a continuous story. Character story events carry eligibility requirements and are ordered from specific to generic, with new requirement types added as systems such as fishing appeared; repeatable barks play from a table that empties before it refills. Covers casting in a small studio, a line spreadsheet with context and subtext columns, recording sessions every few weeks through early access, and how voice-over and localization scope grew beyond early expectations.
notes: Alternate Vault pages for the same session (same title and conference in the Vault crawl) are listed in alt_urls.

title: Don't Juice It or Lose It
summary: An indie artist argues, per the session description, that polish added without regard to context, such as dust clouds where there is no dust or bouncy tweens on hard rocks, can cost immersion, and that visual embellishment should serve a function in the game's world rather than be applied everywhere.
notes: Only the Vault session description was read. Alternate Vault pages for the same session (same title and conference in the Vault crawl) are listed in alt_urls.

title: Scroll Back: The Theory and Practice of Cameras in Side-Scrollers
venue: Game Developers Conference 2015, Independent Games Summit
summary: Keren (Untame, Mushroom 11) surveys 2D scrolling cameras from 1980s arcades to recent indies and names techniques: position locking, camera windows, platform snapping, lerp and physics smoothing, speed-up push zones, dual forward focus with a backtracking threshold, projected focus (poorly suited to vertical platformer motion because a jump changes vertical speed abruptly), target focus from aim or stick, cue attractors, region anchors, zoom-to-fit and multi-player averaging. Goals: keeping needed elements in frame, keeping camera motion predictable and tied to the controls, and comfort, since conflicting visual and vestibular signals can cause nausea. Keren combines techniques per game.
notes: The official GDC YouTube upload is titled 'How Cameras in Side-Scrollers Work'. Alternate Vault pages for the same session (same title and conference in the Vault crawl) are listed in alt_urls.

title: Boss Up: Boss Battle Design Fundamentals and Retrospective
summary: The Mushroom 11 developer treats a boss as a gate that tests one named skill. Advice: test logic or skill but not both at the same instant, telegraph attacks, and make progress legible (Cuphead shows how far you got when you die). Asking whether a boss must block progress at all, Keren suggests easy modes, alternative challenges or skipping, noting that fewer than 10% of Mushroom 11 players reached its ending, partly because of hard bosses, and that easy-mode labels carry stigma.
notes: Alternate Vault pages for the same session (same title and conference in the Vault crawl) are listed in alt_urls.

title: Text2Video-Zero: Text-to-Image Diffusion Models are Zero-Shot Video Generators
venue: 2023 IEEE/CVF International Conference on Computer Vision (ICCV)
summary: Method paper that turns a pretrained text-to-image diffusion model into a video generator without training. Two changes keep frames consistent: motion dynamics added to the frames' latent codes keep the scene and background stable over time, and each frame's self-attention is replaced by cross-frame attention on the first frame, to preserve the context, appearance and identity of the foreground object. Reports low overhead and consistent video, and applies the approach to conditional and instruction-guided video generation.
notes: ICCV 2023 main conference paper. Abstract read via arXiv. Full text read 2026-10-15 from the ICCV 2023 CVF open-access PDF (openaccess.thecvf.com/content/ICCV2023/papers/Khachatryan_Text2Video-Zero_Text-to-Image_Diffusion_Models_are_Zero-Shot_Video_Generators_ICCV_2023_paper.pdf); arXiv v1 also downloaded. Summary, title and authors match. Summary unchanged.

title: glTF 2.0 (Blender import-export add-on documentation)
venue: glTF-Blender-IO documentation (source of the Blender Manual glTF 2.0 page)
summary: Blender's glTF exporter builds materials only from node setups it recognises around the Principled BSDF: an image on Base Color; metallic in B and roughness in G, read through a Separate RGB node; an image through a Normal Map node left in Tangent Space; emission; and occlusion (R channel) through a custom glTF Material Output group. AO and normal maps are best baked with the Cycles Bake panel. Export options include +Y Up, Apply Modifiers (exports the evaluated mesh) and vertex tangents; quads and n-gons are triangulated on export; custom properties become glTF extras; animations take the action name.
notes: This file is the upstream source of the Blender Manual page docs.blender.org/manual/en/latest/addons/import_export/scene_gltf2.html, which returned HTTP 403 to WebFetch. Repository maintained under KhronosGroup; no add-on version stated (text references Blender 4.4 behaviour). The page does not discuss unit scale.

title: glTF 2.0 Specification
summary: glTF is right-handed with +Y up, +Z forward and -X right; linear distances are metres and angles radians. The metallic-roughness model blends a dielectric and a metal BRDF by metalness, 0 for non-metal and 1 for metal. Base colour and emissive textures are sRGB-encoded; the metallic-roughness texture is linear with roughness in G and metalness in B; occlusion is linear in R and affects indirect light only. Normal textures are tangent-space, linear, with +X right and +Y up. When a mesh has no tangents, clients should compute them with MikkTSpace.
notes: Revision 2.0.1 (dated 2021-10-11); year 2026 follows the registry's doc convention. Read via WebFetch (sections 3.4-3.7) and a text grep of the downloaded HTML for the material property definitions (5.19, 5.22).

title: Tracking real-time user experience (TRUE): a comprehensive instrumentation solution for complex systems
venue: Proceedings of the SIGCHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI 2008)
summary: Argues that instrumented behaviour collected on its own cannot answer the 'why' behind the 'what', because it lacks attitudinal, demographic and contextual data. The TRUE system combines behavioural instrumentation with those data and with other HCI methods; two video-game case studies show how the authors used it to improve game designs. Presented as a method and experience report rather than a controlled comparison.

title: Predatory monetization schemes in video games (e.g. 'loot boxes') and internet gaming disorder
summary: Short commentary in the journal Addiction that defines predatory monetization schemes as in-game purchasing systems that disguise or withhold the long-term cost of the activity until players are already financially and psychologically committed. The authors argue such schemes make gaming more similar to gambling and create a risk of financial harm for people with internet gaming disorder. Commentary and argument rather than new data.
notes: Editorial/commentary article in a peer-reviewed journal; only the abstract was read (publisher PDF blocked automated access). OpenAlex lists a free-to-read publisher copy.

title: Unfair play? Video games as exploitative monetized services: An examination of game patents from a consumer protection perspective
summary: Review of 13 patents for in-game purchasing systems found on Google Patents, read against the assignees' terms of use. Described systems include matchmaking novices against players using purchasable items, prices and offers tuned to each player's behavioral and spending data, mystery-box drop rates adjusted by past spending, undisclosed wait-time reductions, and expiring event currencies. The authors characterize some as potentially unfair or exploitative given limited refund protections. Limits they state: a selective sample, and patents describe intended designs that may never be implemented or may differ in practice.
notes: Read the accepted manuscript in the UNIL repository.

title: Art Directing VFX for Stylized Games
summary: Four VFX artists (Double Fine, Motiga, Epic, Volition) on turning a game's art direction into stylised effects. On Gigantic, many heroes' unique effects risked effects noise that interfered with gameplay. On Agents of Mayhem, the art director set three visual pillars; fluid-sim blood looked off-style and did not read at a distance, so it was replaced with hand-painted textures and distance-dependent alpha erosion that keeps shapes bold far away; ability effects were kept at high saturation and emissive levels to stand out from the environment; a timing pass using animation principles such as anticipation made layered effects more readable and more impactful.
notes: Alternate Vault pages for the same session (same title and conference in the Vault crawl) are listed in alt_urls.

title: Companion Traversal in 'God of War Ragnarok'
summary: Abstract: how Santa Monica Studio let the player and several companions traverse independently within the same systems in God of War Ragnarok, using navmesh support for character-specific traversal and pathing, AI behaviors and components that give level designers a simple, flexible setup for companion traversal, and animation techniques for smooth visuals and dynamic positioning.
notes: Only the Vault abstract was read.

title: Depixelizing pixel art
venue: ACM Transactions on Graphics 30(4) (Proceedings of SIGGRAPH 2011)
summary: Extracts a resolution-independent vector representation from hand-crafted pixel art, with smoothly shaded regions separated by piecewise-smooth spline contours, so it can be magnified without degradation. The motivating problem: on the square pixel grid diagonal neighbours touch at a single point, so pixel-wide 8-connected lines that look connected at native size come apart under conventional magnification, and it is ambiguous which diagonal pixels belong together. Heuristics that resolve that ambiguity are the core of the method. Limitations: heavily anti-aliased sprites downsampled from high-resolution art, over-smoothed corners, and untested on strong dithering.
notes: Crossref also lists 10.1145/1964921.1964994 as the ACM SIGGRAPH 2011 papers record of the same paper. Access: 'free' reflects a free copy at the alt URL or venue page; the ACM DL copy was not checked. Full text read 2026-10-15 from the authors' PDF at johanneskopf.de/publications/pixelart/paper/pixel.pdf. Summary now keeps the magnification condition for diagonal features and adds the stated limitations. Title and authors match.

title: A Theory of Fun 10 Years Later
summary: Koster revisits A Theory of Fun a decade on. Restates fun as the emotional response to learning patterns and separates it from flow, which Koster calls a near-meditative optimal state that need not produce that joy. Describes games as deliberate-practice machines (repetition, feedback, difficulty, goals), shows the author's game-grammar notation built on a loop of input, mechanic, feedback and an updated mental model, argues that a game's art, sound and story work as feedback on an invisible system, and would replace typologies such as Myers-Briggs with research on the Big Five. Also covers games as art, ethics and gamification.
notes: Read the author's slide PDF in full and a local machine transcription (whisper.cpp) of the Vault video's audio. Conference code gdc-online-12. Not the GDC Next 2013 date given in earlier drafts. Alternate Vault pages for the same session (same title and conference in the Vault crawl) are listed in alt_urls.

title: A Theory of Fun for Game Design
summary: Informal, illustrated book arguing that fun is the feedback the brain gives while absorbing patterns, so games are pattern-learning systems and play is learning without real pressure. Opens with players abandoning games once their pattern is seen (tic-tac-toe) and with boredom at both extremes, too easy and too hard. Argues that a game's fictional dressing sits over an abstract system players learn to see through, that games teach by experience where stories teach vicariously, and that aesthetic, visceral and social pleasures are valuable but distinct from this narrow sense of fun.
notes: Read the author's official excerpt (foreword, prologue, chapter 1) on theoryoffun.com and the chapter excerpt 'What Games Aren't' published by Game Developer from the first edition. Claims citing this entry stay within those excerpts and the author's GDC 2012 and 2024 restatements.

title: Revisiting Fun: 20 Years of "A Theory of Fun"
summary: Koster on twenty years of the book. Fun is the reward for building pattern libraries, social and physical as well as mathematical; since players bring different libraries and motives, fun differs by person. Separates play from fun (people also play to practise or relax), says flow is often not fun and that games often create fun through frustration then breakthrough, and cites predictive processing. Contrasts Set, a bounded problem that teaches its machinery, with Connections, whose limited guesses stop players learning to search. Offers a checklist for missing fun (preparation, topology, varied verbs, skill in timing, analog outcomes, feedback, social roles) to run on every feature.
notes: Read the full English subtitle track served with the Vault video. Captions garble some terms (for example 'richly interpretable').

title: Monetization Design: The Dark Side of Gacha
summary: Pixonic's account of War Robots monetization. Event gacha chests were iterated and then made permanent; the speaker describes gacha as a way to sell content indirectly and hide its real price, and says revenue rose two to three times. Standard metrics stayed healthy, but the iOS rating fell, players attacked developers on social media, and team morale and production speed dropped. The studio moved toward long-term 'value growth' features such as randomized discount offers and reported steadier revenue and better ratings. Also says most revenue came from players spending over $1,000.
notes: Alternate Vault pages for the same session (same title and conference in the Vault crawl) are listed in alt_urls.

title: Sketching a Map of the Storylets Design Space
venue: Interactive Storytelling: ICIDS 2018, Lecture Notes in Computer Science 11318
summary: Maps storylet-based narrative systems, in which a story is assembled from discrete, reorderable chunks gated by preconditions on game state. Classifies systems by precondition type (quality checks, location, dynamic queries), repeatability, internal structure (static text, templates, grammars, branching) and selection method: player choice, random or weighted random selection as in Reigns, salience-based matching with generic fallbacks as in The King of Chicago, search, and drama management as in Facade. A descriptive taxonomy with no evaluation.
notes: ICIDS 2018 peer-reviewed short paper (LNCS 11318, pp. 160-164); Crossref types LNCS proceedings papers as book-chapter. Used only for definitions.

title: The Role of Uncertainty in Moment-to-Moment Player Motivation: A Grounded Theory
venue: CHI PLAY '19: Proceedings of the Annual Symposium on Computer-Human Interaction in Play
summary: Qualitative interview study tracing links between players' experiences of uncertainty, specific game features and motives during moment-to-moment play. Its grounded theory proposes seven types of engaging gameplay uncertainty arising from three sources (the game, the player and the outcome), tied mainly to curiosity and competence, and compares this taxonomy with earlier ones, finding partial fits and some types earlier models missed. Summary limited to the abstract; the individual types are not relied on.
notes: OpenAlex lists the paper as gold open access at the ACM DOI, but the ACM page blocked automated download; only the abstract was read.

title: Feature‐Aware Pixel Art Animation
summary: Pixel art abstracts images into low-resolution output with concise outlines and reduced palettes; animating it is harder because the constraints extend across frames. Existing tools make artists edit pixels frame by frame, which the authors call tedious and error-prone, and key-frame editors with rigid motion give broken outlines and jitter from nearest-neighbour sampling. The authors build key frames and in-betweens by as-rigid-as-possible warping, then jointly optimize each frame's feature lines against shape-similarity, line-aesthetics and temporal-coherence measures, producing animations that warping alone would ruin with artifacts.
notes: Pages 411-420. Abstract read from Crossref. Author names copied from Crossref, including the U+2010 hyphens. Full text read 2026-10-15 from the authors' PDF linked as 'Paper' on the NTHU project page (cgv.cs.nthu.edu.tw/projects/Recreational_Graphics/PixelLineAnim); the University of Bath portal also lists an accepted-manuscript PDF (researchportal.bath.ac.uk/files/148567276/paper1228_CRC_nocopyright.pdf, 403 to the fetcher). Access changed to free. Summary adds the key-frame editors' artifacts and the kinds of quality measures. Metadata matches the PDF (Pacific Graphics 2016, CGF 35(7)).

title: Exploring Cyberbullying and Other Toxic Behavior in Team Competition Online Games
venue: Proceedings of the 33rd Annual ACM Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI 2015)
summary: Analysis of over 10 million League of Legends player reports on 1.46 million accused players, with crowdsourced Tribunal verdicts. Players reported toxic behavior relatively rarely, but an explicit request to report raised reporting significantly; a sizeable share of reported players were pardoned by reviewers, showing that victims and third parties judge toxicity differently; reporting was biased by team membership; perceptions differed across regions; and match outcome was linked to toxic behavior. The authors caution that the data come from one game and are anonymized.
notes: Full text read in the authors' version on arXiv, which asks readers to cite the CHI 2015 paper.

title: Learning Blind Video Temporal Consistency
venue: Computer Vision: ECCV 2018, Lecture Notes in Computer Science
summary: Method paper on video processing. Starts from the observation that applying an image-processing algorithm independently to each frame of a video often gives results that are inconsistent over time. Proposes a recurrent network that takes the original video and the per-frame processed video and outputs a temporally consistent version, trained with short- and long-term temporal losses plus a perceptual loss, independent of the per-frame algorithm used.
notes: ECCV 2018 paper, published in Springer LNCS; Crossref types it as book-chapter. Abstract read via arXiv. Full text read 2026-10-15 from arXiv 1808.00449v1; the ECCV 2018 CVF open-access PDF (openaccess.thecvf.com/content_ECCV_2018/papers/Wei-Sheng_Lai_Real-Time_Blind_Video_ECCV_2018_paper.pdf) was also downloaded and its title, authors and abstract match. Summary unchanged.

title: Overwatch - The Elusive Goal: Play by Sound
summary: Blizzard's audio team on the director's goal that Overwatch be playable by sound. A standard HDR mix, where the loudest sound wins, buried the footsteps of enemies approaching from behind. It was replaced with a threat-based importance system: each enemy is scored on factors such as distance, aim and damage dealt; one goes in a high bucket, a couple in a medium one, the rest lower, and the bucket drives gain and filtering per sound category, with ultimates kept prominent. Path-length occlusion tells players when a threat is behind geometry; each hero has distinct footsteps; friendly and enemy versions of a sound are processed differently; key abilities have clear start and end sounds.
notes: No upload on the official GDC channel was found; content was read from captions of the session recording published by Blizzard's own YouTube channel (video 60P0hzTTJ4Q). The Vault lists the talk as free. Alternate Vault pages for the same session (same title and conference in the Vault crawl) are listed in alt_urls.

title: Modify Everything! Data-Driven Dynamic Gameplay Effects on 'For Honor'
summary: Ubisoft gameplay programmer on For Honor's modifier system, shared by feats, gear, status effects and campaign bosses. A per-entity handler holds modifiers that pair programmer-written effects (stat changes, disabled capabilities, tags, removing modifiers, spawning effects) with a duration and designer-combinable conditions, so designers built new effects in data without programmer requests. Lessons: duplicated data and missing naming standards as use spread; stacking needed per-stat limits and an order separating intrinsic sources (gear, difficulty) from dynamic ones; damage over time used snapshots; always-on and detailed debug displays were essential; unit tests were missing.
notes: The official GDC YouTube upload is titled 'Data-Driven Dynamic Gameplay Effects on For Honor'; same session. Auto-captions garble the speaker's name; the Vault name is used. Alternate Vault pages for the same session (same title and conference in the Vault crawl) are listed in alt_urls.

title: Level Design Workshop: An Approach to Holistic Level Design
venue: Game Developers Conference 2017, Level Design Workshop
summary: An Arkane designer (Dishonored 2, earlier BioShock Infinite) argues that level quality comes from gameplay, visuals and story working together. Players act with intention when they have a choice, a motivation, information from clear and consistent affordances, and time to take it in; Lee frames play as an observe, plan, execute, react loop that vertical layouts and safe vantage points support. Examples include blocking non-interactive doors so they do not read as usable and running a visible cable to every powered barrier. Immersive-sim perspective.

title: Economic Balancing and Improved Monetization Through Clever Sink Design
summary: Lecture by an Oxford Internet Institute economist on sinks, the mechanisms that remove currency and items from a game economy so the game stays balanced and purchases stay compelling. Per the session abstract, it surveys six currency sinks and eleven item sinks from classic online and recent mobile games, uses elementary behavioral economics to explain why players accept some sinks more readily than others, and introduces a spreadsheet approach to simulating sink impact for design and live operations.
notes: No transcript found on the official GDC channel; only the Vault abstract was read, so cite for the abstract's claims only. Alternate Vault pages for the same session (same title and conference in the Vault crawl) are listed in alt_urls.

title: Attention, Not Immersion: Making Your Games Better with Psychology and Playtesting, the Uncharted Way
summary: Naughty Dog designer proposes attention, rather than immersion, as a design lens, and describes formal playtesting on Uncharted 3: players new to the game play once, are not helped and do not talk to each other; each session combines logged metrics, a questionnaire and a group exit interview; a deaths-per-section table flags spikes; watching where players look and what they ignore is treated as cheap attention tracking; fixes are made between tests and checked in the next. A custom 'bad jumps' telemetry view, built in a few hours, showed where players jumped at things that looked climbable but were not. Warns against trusting metrics beyond judgement.
notes: The local caption file (GDC YouTube upload titled "Making Your Games Better with Psychology and Playtesting, the Uncharted Way") matches this session. Vault ids 1015745 and 1016154 are duplicates. Alternate Vault pages for the same session (same title and conference in the Vault crawl) are listed in alt_urls.

title: Fear and loathing in VR: the emotional and physiological effects of immersive games
summary: Two lab experiments with 128 young adults compared playing on a TV or in VR: a survival horror game (N = 59) and, with men only, a first-person shooter (N = 69). VR produced a stronger sense of presence in both. In the horror game VR lowered heart-rate variability at scare moments; self-reported fear was not significantly higher in VR overall, but presence carried a significant indirect effect of VR on fear. Hostility rose after play regardless of display, with no VR difference; VR was not more enjoyable overall, though men enjoyed the horror game more in VR in a post hoc test. The abstract's claim of stronger fear in VR rests on the indirect effect.
notes: Published online 2021, issue year 2022 (Virtual Reality 26). Audit 2026-09-26: read the full text (UvA-DARE PDF, pure.uva.nl/ws/files/100935860). Experiment 1 t tests found no significant VR-TV difference in self-reported fear and no total or direct effect, only an indirect effect through presence; fear was measured only in the horror experiment; Experiment 2 was men only. Summary corrected.

title: Least squares conformal maps for automatic texture atlas generation
summary: The authors note that earlier atlas methods needed many small charts with simple borders, and that the discontinuities between charts cause artifacts and make large regular patterns hard to paint. Their least-squares conformal parametrization minimises angle distortion, has a unique minimum independent of mesh resolution, cannot flip triangles, and handles large charts with complex borders; segmentation and packing methods complete the atlas.
notes: Peer-reviewed SIGGRAPH 2002 paper published in ACM TOG. Crossref also lists the proceedings DOI 10.1145/566570.566590. Abstract from the SIGGRAPH history archive. Blender's Conformal unwrap method is LSCM (see blender2026-uv-unwrap). Full text read 2026-10-15 from a copy of the published paper on a Johns Hopkins course page (https://www.cs.jhu.edu/~misha/Fall09/Levy02.pdf). The open HAL deposit (https://inria.hal.science/inria-00100754/document) exists but was blocked by a bot check. Summary and metadata confirmed; no other change.

title: Throwing Out the Dopamine Shots: Reward Psychology Without the Neurotrash
summary: Epic Games UX researcher replaces 'dopamine shot' talk with established reward principles. Rewards are feedback: players must know that, why and how much they were rewarded. Covers fixed and variable ratio and interval schedules and their typical response patterns, immediate versus long-term rewards with progress feedback, control, loss aversion, and effort-reward expectations (a hard room followed by nothing feels wrong). Examples: Destiny's streak bonus raising loot odds, engrams recolored to show the minimum outcome, and games that silently raise odds after a purchase, which Lewis-Evans calls perhaps a dark pattern. Warns that optimizers will compute base rates.
notes: Alternate Vault pages for the same session (same title and conference in the Vault crawl) are listed in alt_urls.

title: The Science Behind Shaping Player Behavior in Online Games
summary: Session abstract: Riot Games' player behavior team applies research from behavioral, social and cognitive psychology to toxic behavior in League of Legends, with the player-driven Tribunal and the Honor initiative as examples of reforming toxic players and reinforcing positive behavior.
notes: Alternate Vault pages for the same session (same title and conference in the Vault crawl) are listed in alt_urls.

title: What Features Influence Impact Feel? A Study of Impact Feedback in Action Games
summary: Proposes 'impact feel' for the satisfaction players get from hit feedback. An NLP model trained on about 5,000 annotated Chinese-language Steam comments ranked 44 popular action games; the authors then compared the eight highest- and eight lowest-ranked against a 19-feature framework of impact feedback. Hit stop, sound coherence and camera control separated the groups, and games lacking careful design on any of the three tended to rank poorly. An observational comparison of commercial games from review text, not a controlled experiment; the authors name the single-language corpus and small game sample as limits.
notes: Full text read from the arXiv version (v3), which matches the GEM paper's title and authors. Audit 2026-09-26: re-read arXiv v3 full text; summary now states that only Chinese-language comments were used and the 44-game pool, both limits the authors list in Section V. Metadata matches Crossref.

title: How to Restrain Inflation in Game? Monitoring and Alerting of Economic System.
summary: NetEase data team on monitoring economies in large Chinese MMORPGs with paid and earned currencies. Names five common causes of inflation: issuing too much currency, too little production of key items, a declining player base (including the players who farm), market manipulation by organized traders, and 'sleeping money' released when lapsed players return. Tools: a per-currency dashboard of daily issuance, collection and stock with breakdowns by source and sink, an exchange-rate chart between paid and earned currency, price tracking for key items, and a player-transaction network graph used to find exploits.
notes: GDC YouTube upload is titled 'How to Reduce In-Game Inflation by Monitoring Your Economic Systems'.

title: Lower is Better? The Effects of Local Latencies on Competitive First-Person Shooter Game Players
venue: Proceedings of the 2021 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems
summary: 43 experienced Counter-Strike: Global Offensive players played on identical laptops at home with total local latency of 25, 50, 75, 100 or 125 ms (added input delay over a measured 25 ms base). Accuracy, score and rated quality of experience improved roughly linearly as latency fell across the whole range: scores at 25 ms averaged about 20% above those at 125 ms, and each 10 ms reduction added about 0.8 percentage points of accuracy. Sniper accuracy was slightly more sensitive than automatic-rifle accuracy. Limits: a nearly all-male sample, uncontrolled home settings, and individual rather than team play.

title: Do Players Prefer Integrated User Interfaces? A Qualitative Study of Game UI Design Issues
venue: Proceedings of DiGRA 2011 Conference: Think Design Play
summary: Qualitative study in which players played Assassin's Creed with its HUD switched off, with observation and interviews. Removing the overlay did not by itself increase involvement for any respondent. Players accepted overlay elements that break the fiction when they gave relevant, sufficient information, and were annoyed when given more than they needed; some system-minded players preferred the clean screen because reading the world became part of the challenge. The authors conclude integrated UI is often seen as elegant but is not the best way to show critical information or values that must be gauged continuously. Preliminary results from a small sample.
notes: DiGRA 2011 full paper in the DiGRA Digital Library (peer-reviewed conference); preliminary qualitative results.

title: Characterizing and Modeling the Effects of Local Latency on Game Performance and Experience
venue: Proceedings of the 2018 Annual Symposium on Computer-Human Interaction in Play (CHI PLAY '18)
summary: Two studies of simple game interaction 'atoms' measure performance and experience under increasing local latency, the delay between an input and the resulting display change. The authors note that earlier studies report problem thresholds anywhere from 50 to 500 ms. Data from the first study yield a simple predictive model of performance from the amount of lag and the speed of the game; it predicted the second study's results accurately, especially for faster games and higher lag. They argue sensitivity follows a game's temporal demands, so some playability loss can be predicted without extensive playtesting.
notes: Only the abstract was available; do not cite specific thresholds or effect sizes from this entry.

title: It's About Time: System Design for Mobile Free-to-Play
summary: A Scopely lead designer on balancing mobile free-to-play economies around time: how fast players acquire content. Suggests a working order from player level and time per level through power, cost, actions per day, payouts and drop rates to variance, with readable starting numbers. Constraints: players must not earn content faster than the team can make it, live events must be finishable in their window, and an upgrade must never pay out less. Monetization sells time, so tell players plainly what they get. Perfect balance is dull: deliberate shortages give new modes a purpose. Combat units are balanced by effective time to defeat each other. Figures are illustrative.

title: Embracing Push Forward Combat in 'DOOM'
summary: id Software designer and AI programmer on DOOM (2016) combat. Wave fights felt contrived, so arenas used steady reinforcements ended by a 'last heavy standing' rule, reinforcements triggered by a heavy's remaining health, one 'captain' per wave, and some enemy-role pairings banned; warning signs were players retreating, holding doorways, sniping or kiting. Implementation: hit reactions as a threat-management tool; tactical-position visibility refreshed by a small budget of ray traces per frame rather than precomputed; an attack-token pool capping simultaneous attackers, with token cooldowns, difficulty-scaled counts and token stealing by enemies directly in front of the player.

title: 'Owlboy': The Evolving Art of a 10 Year Project
venue: Game Developers Conference 2017, Independent Games Summit
summary: D-Pad Studio on keeping a pixel-art game current over nearly a decade. Moving from the original resolution to widescreen meant resizing rooms by hand. After a demo felt static, the team added drifting cloud and parallax layers, kept all dialogue acting in the sprites instead of portraits, added turn and flight-flip animations, and built animated, wind-reactive textures inspired by NES palette shifting. A custom upscaling filter smooths jagged edges while staying on the pixel grid. The hero's large set of animations meant the artist could not redraw the character in an improved style, so some newer art was simplified to sit with older sprites.
notes: Numbers from captions. Transcript is GDC YouTube captions. Audit 2026-10-15: the 800x600 starting resolution and the count of about 800 hero animations each appear once, only in auto captions; no slides or second source found, so both numbers are unconfirmed.

title: Can You See Me Now? Building Robust AI Sensory Systems
summary: Practical construction of NPC vision from Assassin's Creed and Thief work at Ubisoft: filter candidates, test sensor shapes, then raycast as the expensive last step. Recommends a designer-editable shape library, a dedicated sensor bone the animator controls so sensors do not whip around with idle animations, several target points to survive small occluders, unifying line of sight and line of fire, and stacked perception modifiers that only reduce perception so learned rules still hold. Suggests deferring and prioritizing vision requests, caching results, debug drawing for QA and unit testing sensors.
notes: Transcript from the official GDC YouTube upload.

title: Automated Testing of Gameplay Features in 'Sea of Thieves'
summary: Rare engineer on automated testing for a live-service Unreal game. The team used unit tests, "actor" tests that tick a minimal world (about 70% of tests), map-based integration tests including networked client-server tests (about 5%), and a few screenshot, performance and boot tests: roughly 23,000 in all. Engineers wrote tests after a feature worked, not while prototyping; tests polled for conditions instead of fixed waits; a failing test was rerun once before the build went red; repeat failures were quarantined. Reported against Rare's earlier projects: build verification fell from about two weeks to about a day and a half, and peak open bugs stayed near 214.
notes: Alternate Vault pages for the same session (same title and conference in the Vault crawl) are listed in alt_urls.

title: Quad Mesh Simplification in Frostbite
summary: Frostbite's LOD tool for BioWare's quad-topology characters. At equal budgets, quad-preserving LODs deform better under skinning than triangulated ones, because they keep the edge rings artists place where meshes flex, and they are a better base when artists touch up generated LODs. BioWare required preserved edge flow, artist-painted priority areas that keep more detail, and symmetry, each weighted by sliders. Against hand-made LODs the results are close, but artists also simplify silhouettes, merge fingers into mittens and keep detail where parts flex, such as a tail. The tool spread across EA, including to triangle meshes, props and vehicles.
notes: The cost-savings figure in the Vault description is not repeated in the talk and is not claimed here.

title: Board Game Design Day: Balancing Mechanics for Your Card Game's Unique "Power Curve"
summary: Card game designer (The Spoils, Magic, Pokemon) on cost-versus-power curves. Power grows faster than cost because expensive cards may never be cast and are less flexible. A card's strength depends on its proportional distance above the curve, so the same bonus matters far more on a cheap card. Resource systems shape the curve: Hearthstone's automatic mana favours strong cheap cards, Magic's land drops reward expensive ones; Pokemon's deferred prize costs give a chunky curve. Small integers are coarse to tune. Discusses power creep and rotation, and argues a team that never has to pull a card back is probably not pushing hard enough.
notes: Alternate Vault pages for the same session (same title and conference in the Vault crawl) are listed in alt_urls.

title: 'DEATHLOOP': Designing Trinkets for Freedom, Choice, and Emergence
summary: Arkane Lyon designer on Deathloop's trinkets (socketable modifiers) and weapon perks.
