Principles: horizontal over vertical progression, effects strong enough to notice, no stacking, loadout limits for opportunity cost, at least one trinket per game element, and consistent systemic rules so players can plan. The combination space was far too large to test, so effects were grouped by category and only interacting categories were tuned together. Lessons: players hated effects that fired without feedback, added late; an undiscussed split between drops and placed rewards nearly ran out of items; excitement fell off in the final third. Players found builds and solutions nobody planned.
notes: Read the full English subtitle track served with the Vault video.

title: 'Knockout City's' Parallel, Deterministic, and Rewindable Entity System
summary: Session abstract: Velan Studios presents a general-purpose entity system that supports deterministic, parallel computation and rewinding world state within a time window, used for client-side prediction in the online game Knockout City, for scrubbing world state during development, and for using multi-core hardware; working with the studio's scripting language, it was used for everything from core gameplay to UI and progression.
notes: Alternate Vault pages for the same session (same title and conference in the Vault crawl) are listed in alt_urls.

title: Continuous World Generation in 'No Man's Sky'
summary: A Hello Games programmer describes No Man's Sky's real-time planet pipeline: positional seeds feed chained generators (solar system, planet, voxel terrain from layered noise, then placement), with problems from mapping flat generation onto spheres and floating-point precision. Because generated planets vary widely in cost, the team ran a smoke-test tool on each build that captured performance on the same planets over time, and McKendrick stresses investing in such tooling for generation work.

title: The Psychology of Game Design (Everything You Know Is Wrong)
summary: Keynote on player psychology from Firaxis games. In Civilization Revolution's combat, players shown 3:1 odds felt cheated by losses; around 3:1 to 4:1 they expected to win every time, treated 20 vs 10 differently from 2:1, and objected to losing two 2:1 battles in a row, so the team factored prior results into later rolls. Significant random events provoke paranoid explanations; a randomized tech tree was rejected once players knew the goal. The random seed was saved with the game to curb reload-until-win behavior, and AI that looks too clever is read as cheating.

title: Interesting Decisions
summary: Meier (Firaxis) examines games as a series of interesting decisions. Uninteresting: players always pick the same option (the game could pick it) or pick at random. Interesting decisions involve trade-offs, depend on the situation, can express play style, and have a persistence that sets how much information players need. Useful kinds: risk versus reward, short versus long term, customization that invests players, and goals at several time scales. Levers: rebalance cost, tie the choice to the fantasy, change information, offer fewer options (Civilization players were comfortable with about three to five tech choices), adjust decision time, add flavor, or cut it. Acknowledge every choice.
notes: Read the full official GDC YouTube captions. Vault also lists the session as 1016165; this entry uses 1015756. Alternate Vault pages for the same session (same title and conference in the Vault crawl) are listed in alt_urls.

title: Classic Game Postmortem: 'Sid Meier's Civilization'
summary: Sid Meier and Bruce Shelley on the original Civilization (1991). The first playable was a real-time zoning game; switching to turns made it work. Starting with one settler eased players into a large subject. Zones of control borrowed from wargames were a mistake that encouraged unit stacks, and a spearman defeating a battleship caused lasting controversy. Randomly withholding an eligible technology frustrated planners. A rise-and-fall design failed because players reloaded to avoid setbacks, reinforcing that the player, not the computer, must have the fun. With only a handful of testers they missed exploits such as spamming small cities.

title: Game AI Summit: Growing an AI Director into a Full Adventure Director
summary: Session description only. The speaker recounts growing a spawn director, building on Left 4 Dead's AI systems, into an adventure director that oversaw the whole combat experience of a co-op action game: procedural NPC encounters that follow the players, pacing, and harder opposition as they progress. Level designers were given tools to override map sections with authored gameplay and to control the flow of spawned NPCs while the director stayed consistent about what emerged.
notes: No official GDC YouTube upload found; claims are limited to the Vault session description.

title: Skill, Matchmaking, and Ranking Systems Design
summary: Separates three systems: a hidden skill rating that should converge quickly and be calibrated, matchmaking that trades match quality against wait time, and a visible ranking designed for the audience. Showing ranks not used for matching makes players question matches; progression-style ranks do not measure skill. Recommends separate skill for parties, placement matches, global matchmaking rather than server lists, widening tolerance while players wait, few playlists so populations stay large, and smurf detection. Presented as the speaker's opinions from work on several studios' shooters.
notes: Alternate Vault pages for the same session (same title and conference in the Vault crawl) are listed in alt_urls.

title: Matchmaking for Engagement: Lessons from 'Halo 5'
summary: Observational analysis of Halo 5 competitive matches (matchmaking interferes with A/B tests) to find what made players quit a match or stop for the night. Quitting rose with the skill gap between a player and the opposing team, and more steeply with the gap between team averages; stacked premade parties drove opponents away. Losing streaks, search time and latency (within existing limits) showed no clear effect. A skill model that ignored what players reacted to missed these effects. Menke cautions the results are specific to Halo 5 and proposes alternating matchmaking rules over time instead of splitting players for tests.
notes: Alternate Vault pages for the same session (same title and conference in the Vault crawl) are listed in alt_urls.

title: Level Design Workshop: Solving Puzzle Design
venue: Game Developers Conference 2016, Level Design Workshop
summary: A level designer (Ubisoft, formerly Telltale) defines a puzzle as a challenge with one best solution and gives three difficulty dials: the steps and time before feedback, new mechanics or information, and new uses of known mechanics. Menzel maps Portal's early chambers to show reuse and easier breather puzzles after hard ones, cites a Telltale rule of never more than about five puzzle-relevant things on screen, calls too many steps a very common cause of 'too hard', and contrasts Wind Waker's full-level replay after a fall with Portal's respawn near the failure.
notes: Audit 2026-09-26: re-read the official GDC YouTube captions. Menzel calls too many steps 'very very common' among too-hard puzzles, not the most common cause; summary corrected. The uncited sentence in levels.md after the dial list ('[Menzel] names too many steps as the most common reason') has the same overstatement. Alternate Vault pages for the same session (same title and conference in the Vault crawl) are listed in alt_urls.

title: Out of Sight, Out of Mind: Improving Visualization of AI Info
summary: Abstract: as AI grew more complex, debugging shifted from confirming what a character did to explaining why it did or did not act, across large amounts of agent, environment, player and game-state data. Three studios show how they exposed that information to programmers and designers: a timeline view (Turtle Rock, Evolve), an HTTP-based game-state inspector (The Sims 4) and the ReView debugging tool.
notes: Only the Vault abstract was read; the abstract also names Charles Gast as a presenter. The Vault also lists ids 1020590 and 1021106. Alternate Vault pages for the same session (same title and conference in the Vault crawl) are listed in alt_urls.

title: Xbox Accessibility Guideline 118: Photosensitivity
summary: Xbox platform guidance on photosensitivity. Every game should be tested for seizure triggers, and removing risky content is preferred over warnings because many people learn they are susceptible only from a first seizure. It defines failures for general flashes, saturated red flashes and high-contrast spatial patterns, broadly when flashes exceed about three per second or flashing or patterns cover about 20% or more of the screen, and suggests reducing contrast, frequency or area. It lists the Harding flash and pattern analyser as a test tool.
notes: Page date 2022-05-09 within XAG version 3.2; cited only as Xbox platform guidance. Audit 2026-09-26: the page title is 'Xbox Accessibility Guideline 118: Photosensitivity' (registry title omits the subtitle), and the page now shows 'Last updated on 2026-03-04'; the cited criteria are unchanged.

title: Xbox Accessibility Guideline 101
summary: Xbox platform guidance on text display. Minimum default sizes, measured as body height from descender to ascender: 26 px at 1080p (52 px at 4K) on console, 18 px at 1080p on PC and VR, scaled by pixel density on mobile. Players should be able to scale text to 200% of the minimum without losing content, and icon glyphs should scale with it; include a sans-serif option and a plain alternative to stylised fonts; platform magnification is not a substitute for adequate size. Suggested defaults cover line width, spacing and sentence case.
notes: Page date 2022-05-09 within XAG version 3.2; cited only as Xbox platform guidance.

title: Xbox Accessibility Guidelines
venue: Microsoft Learn, Microsoft Game Development Kit documentation (version 3.2)
summary: Microsoft's platform guidelines for accessible games (version 3.2, June 2023), developed with industry experts and disabled players. They are intended as a source of ideas for designers, guardrails for developers and a checklist for test teams, and explicitly not as a compliance or legal standard. Each guideline gives a goal, scoping questions, key areas to target, implementation guidance, examples and the players likely to be affected.

title: Random Class (System)
summary: API documentation. Separate Random objects given the same seed produce the same sequence, which the page suggests for test suites and replaying games; the implementation is not guaranteed to stay the same across major .NET versions, so the same seed may give a different sequence on another version; Random instances are not thread safe.
notes: Living documentation; year is the access year.

title: Social Systems Design, Implementation, and Impacts in 'Overwatch'
summary: Session abstract: why Blizzard prioritized social systems in Overwatch (endorsements and looking-for-group), the design decisions behind them, and their effect on the community, particularly in mitigating disruptive behavior.

title: AI for Games
summary: Broad technical reference on game AI, third edition. From the publisher's description and table of contents: chapters on movement, pathfinding, decision making, tactical and strategic AI, learning, board games, execution management, world interfacing, tools and content creation, designing game AI, and AI-based game genres.
notes: Only the publisher's description and table of contents were read; cite for scope and as further reading only.

title: Performance and Memory Postmortem for 'Middle-earth: Shadow of War'
summary: Monolith's technical director on how content growth (from 8 to 200 unique AI characters, heavier effects, larger maps) left the console frame near 90 ms against a 33 ms target about a year before ship. Recovery used coarse jobs on fixed cores with per-system CPU budgets, pipelining with frame pacing, renderer state work, large memory pages, link-time and profile-guided optimization, runtime fallbacks (dynamic resolution, pushing out character LODs, pausing texture streaming) and texture mip streaming to fit memory. Mintus does not advocate the fixed-core design and wanted this work to start earlier.
notes: Alternate Vault pages for the same session (same title and conference in the Vault crawl) are listed in alt_urls.

title: How does it play better? Exploring user testing and biometric storyboards in games user research
venue: Proceedings of the SIGCHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI 2013)
summary: Proposes Biometric Storyboards (BioSt), a games user research method, and studies how a classic user test and a BioSt user test help designers improve gameplay. Games revised with BioSt feedback scored significantly better on visuals, fun and gameplay quality than games designed without user tests; the classic user test did not give that significant advantage. Designer interviews suggested BioSt supported more nuanced design changes. The evidence comes from a single study reported in one CHI paper.
notes: Audit 2026-09-26 (abstract only; full text closed per Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex): the previous summary's 'small number of designers and prototypes' is not stated in the abstract, so it was replaced with what the abstract supports.

title: Illustrative Rendering in Team Fortress 2
venue: Proceedings of the 5th International Symposium on Non-Photorealistic Animation and Rendering (NPAR 2007)
summary: Valve on Team Fortress 2's look, drawn from early 20th-century commercial illustration (Leyendecker, Cornwell, Rockwell). The nine classes got distinct silhouettes through proportions, weapons, hats and footwear, and readability in pure silhouette was used to validate designs at the concept stage. Clothing folds echo the silhouette; high-frequency detail and repetitive geometry are kept low to limit visual noise; colours are near-real with raised saturation and value contrast, muted colours dominate and saturation stays in small areas; the two teams' bases contrast in colour, material and form. Shaders (warped half-Lambert diffuse, rim light) keep shape and identity readable across lighting.

title: What is the Game Loop
summary: Article on MonoGame's Game class loop. A game is fixed-step or variable-step and defaults to fixed step, calling Update at the interval in TargetElapsedTime. If Update runs too long, the game sets IsRunningSlowly and calls Update again without calling Draw in between, dropping frames to catch up.

title: AI Summit: Advanced Real-Time Hierarchical Task Networks: A New Approach
summary: Abstract: HTN planners suit long-term behavior but have no built-in way to handle accidental changes or hostile agents; games compensate by re-planning often, which tends to destroy the AI's long-term intent. Square Enix presents ART-HTN, an extension meant for real-time games, and how it deals with these problems.
notes: Only the Vault abstract was read.

title: GuiltyGearXrd's Art Style : The X Factor Between 2D and 3D
venue: Game Developers Conference 2015, Visual Arts track
summary: Arc System Works models (about 40,000 triangles) put detail in geometry and store shading data in vertex attributes, not normal maps, because vertex data stays clean in close-ups. The cel shader is a plain lit/unlit step, so artists control its inputs: a vertex-colour channel offsets the threshold to mark areas that shade easily, each character has its own light vector, and normals are hand-edited on every major feature, faces above all. Outlines use an inverted hull with per-vertex width; inner lines are drawn on axis-aligned UV strips. Animation drops interpolation: every frame is a posed key on a dense rig (about 500 bones), with per-frame distortion and scale cheats.
notes: Numbers from captions. The transcript confirms the hand-edited normals and vertex-colour shading controls that the earlier entry attributed only to secondary write-ups.

title: Cowboys, ankle sprains, and keepers of quality: how is video game development different from software development?
venue: Proceedings of the 36th International Conference on Software Engineering (ICSE 2014)
summary: Interviews with 14 developers who had worked on both games and other software, plus a survey of 364 Microsoft engineers. Game requirements were less clear (the goal is that the game is fun, which is subjective, and a planned feature may not be fun once built); game teams more often called their process Agile, valued creativity and the ability to communicate with non-engineers more, and were more diverse. Interviewees used less test automation because designs change so often that tests go stale, correct behaviour is hard to assert and state spaces are large. Survey limited to one company.
notes: Read the author-hosted PDF. Also cited by architecture.md. Audit 2026-09-26 (full text): the paper says fun is subjective and may not appear once a vision is implemented; it does not say fun is judged only by playing. Summary adjusted. Metadata matches the ICSE 2014 paper.

title: More than a feeling: Measurement of sonic user experience and psychophysiology in a first-person shooter game
summary: Lab experiment in which participants played a fast-paced first-person shooter modification with sound effects and music each switched on or off, while facial EMG and electrodermal activity were recorded alongside the Game Experience Questionnaire. Sound had a significant main effect on every questionnaire dimension (immersion, tension, competence, flow, positive and negative affect, challenge), and sound and music interacted on tension and flow; the psychophysiological measures showed no significant effects. Findings come from one game modification in a lab.

title: The Experience, Dynamics and Artifacts Framework: Towards a Holistic Model for Designing Serious and Entertainment Games
summary: Reviews design frameworks with industry backgrounds (MDA, the Elemental Tetrad, DPE, APE, DDE) and proposes a combined framework for entertainment and serious games. Summarizes criticisms of MDA: 'mechanics' lumps code, technology and game rules together; 'aesthetics' covers only player emotions, leaving art style and UI under mechanics; and saying players meet aesthetics first sits oddly with controls and UI being their first contact. Describes how DDE splits design into blueprint, mechanics and interface and treats dynamics as designer-controlled only indirectly. Conceptual comparison without empirical validation.
notes: CoG 2021 proceedings paper (pp. 1-8); read the conference PDF sections on MDA, DPE, APE and DDE.

title: The Art of Journey
summary: Journey's art director traces how its look was found by iteration. The playable character was repeatedly simplified, removing what gameplay did not need, and a detailed version with animated fingers was dropped because programmers could not make it work. Landscapes followed a colour guide mapping the game from start to end; clearer views and farther fog marked calmer areas, and blue sky was withheld until the final area as a reward. Buildings followed a self-made canon of proportions. Screenshots were painted over and the game changed to match; players wanted control to the end, so a closing cutscene was cut.
notes: Alternate Vault pages for the same session (same title and conference in the Vault crawl) are listed in alt_urls.

title: 50 Camera Mistakes
summary: Journey's dynamic camera designer (thatgamecompany) lists third-person camera failures and the fixes used on that game: orbit the avatar, avoid obstacles early with whisker raycasts, group competing constraints by degree of freedom and give player input priority, delay scripted hints after the player turns the camera, limit how far the avatar drifts from centre, keep the camera still during jumps, and treat cuts as remapping the stick. Flags small or rapidly changing field of view, screen shake and walk-cycle bobbing as simulation-sickness triggers and asks for options to reduce them; testers may not admit sickness. Warns that a general constraint solver makes behavior hard to predict.
notes: The official GDC YouTube upload is titled '50 Game Camera Mistakes'. Alternate Vault pages for the same session (same title and conference in the Vault crawl) are listed in alt_urls.

title: A mathematical model of the finding of usability problems
venue: Proceedings of the INTERACT and CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (INTERCHI 1993)
summary: Across 11 usability studies, the number of distinct problems found as test users or heuristic evaluators are added is well modelled as a Poisson process with diminishing returns. Early results can estimate how many problems remain and how many more evaluations are needed; with cost and value figures the model gives an optimal number of evaluations. For their 'medium' example the authors estimate 16 evaluations would be worth their cost, with the best benefit-to-cost ratio at four. Applies to finding usability problems, not to estimating how common a preference is.

title: Player perception of delays and jitter in character responsiveness
venue: Proceedings of the ACM Symposium on Applied Perception (SAP '14)
summary: 89 students and researchers each played a third-person 3D platformer under one condition (0 to 500 ms of constant added delay, or a 200 ms mean with 50 to 150 ms of jitter). Constant delay had little effect on enjoyment, frustration or ease of control until very high values, and fewer than half the players noticed a constant 300 ms, though path-following accuracy and completion time worsened at 500 ms. Jitter was noticed more often than constant delay, increased failures and hindered improvement with practice. The authors suggest hiding variation even at the cost of a larger constant delay, pending further work, and attribute some effects in their earlier 150 ms study to uncontrolled jitter.
notes: Audit 2026-09-26: re-read full text. Participants are described as 'students and researchers from a diversity of disciplines' with no proportions, so 'mostly students' was removed; noted the 500 ms-only path and time effects and the authors' hedge on the constant-over-variable recommendation. Metadata ok.

title: Game Programming Patterns
summary: Practitioner book on software patterns applied to games: game loop and update method, command, observer, state machines, components, event queues, type objects, object pools, spatial partitions, data locality and singletons. Each chapter states when a pattern helps and what it costs. It argues that abstraction is a bet on future change that adds code, indirection and often runtime cost; recommends a fixed simulation step with decoupled rendering; warns about update-order effects, lapsed listeners, stale queued events and global state; and says to profile before reorganizing data for cache locality.
notes: Read in the author's free online edition: Architecture, Performance, and Games; Game Loop; Update Method; State; Command; Observer; Event Queue; Component; Type Object; Object Pool; Spatial Partition; Data Locality; Singleton; Double Buffer.

title: Breaking Barriers: Combat Accessibility in 'God of War Ragnarok'
summary: A Santa Monica Studio combat designer explains opt-in combat assists in God of War Ragnarok for players with motor disabilities, each weighed on player value, cost and conflict with design intent and checked with consultants. Checkpoints between boss phases let each phase be longer and harder. A mini-boss checkpoint option first shown in the main settings was switched on and forgotten, and one player who chose a higher difficulty found a mini-boss trivial without knowing why; it moved to the accessibility menu, was locked out of the two highest difficulties, and now reminds the player on each death.
notes: Alternate Vault pages for the same session (same title and conference in the Vault crawl) are listed in alt_urls.

title: The Ultimate Trim: Texturing Techniques of Sunset Overdrive
summary: Insomniac's environment art team (8-12 artists, per the slides) had to cover an open-world city of roughly 1.4 by 2.4 km, so early in development it standardised a texturing method built on a fixed trim-sheet layout and 45-degree normal-map bevels along all edges, chosen for production speed, memory use and runtime performance. The bevels give low-poly edges a high-poly look, and with a standardised UV layout any material can be swapped while edges stay in place; each material type has a trim and a plain tileable version. A UV-mapping script made fast, precise layouts and a custom shader added procedural brushstrokes and variation.
notes: Visual Arts track, tagged free content. The Vault session description was read first. Audit 2026-10-15: free slide PDF read (https://media.gdcvault.com/gdc2015/presentations/Olsen_Morten_TheUltimateTrim.pdf, linked from CG Channel; slides are mostly images with little text). No transcript: no official GDC YouTube upload was found. Team size and city size come from slide 7; the video was not reviewed.

title: fsync — synchronize changes to a file
venue: The Open Group Base Specifications Issue 8 (IEEE Std 1003.1-2024)
summary: POSIX specification of fsync(). It requests that all data for an open file be transferred to the associated storage device, the nature of the transfer being implementation-defined. The rationale says its purpose is to ensure data written before the call is recorded on disk after a crash or other failure, while acknowledging that without synchronized I/O support implementations range from null to real physical writes.

title: rename, renameat — rename file
venue: The Open Group Base Specifications Issue 8 (IEEE Std 1003.1-2024)
summary: POSIX specification of rename(). When the new name already exists it is replaced, and a directory entry with that name stays visible throughout, referring either to the old or the new file; the rationale states the action must be atomic. rename() fails with EXDEV when the source and destination are on different file systems and the implementation does not support links between them. The page states no durability requirement after a system crash.

title: Three States and a Plan: The AI of F.E.A.R.
summary: F.E.A.R. drove a three-state FSM (go to, animate, use smart object) with a STRIPS-style goal-oriented action planner that searches action sequences with A*. Goals compete by priority and each character type has its own action set, so shared goals yield different behavior and a new enemy type was assembled late from existing goals and actions. Adds per-action costs, a fixed-size world-state array and procedural preconditions and effects that defer expensive checks. Re-planning after failure gives adaptive tactics. Squad behaviors are simple and separate; much apparent coordination emerges, and dialogue chosen after decisions tells the player what the AI is doing or why it cannot act.
notes: Content confirmed from Orkin's GDC 2006 proceedings paper of the same title (the talk's written version). The former author-hosted copy (alumni.media.mit.edu/~jorkin) no longer resolves; the proceedings PDF was read from a mirror. The Vault also lists ids 1013394 and 1013459 for this session. Alternate Vault pages for the same session (same title and conference in the Vault crawl) are listed in alt_urls.

title: Stop Getting Lost: Make Cognitive Maps, Not Levels
summary: A thatgamecompany designer trained in architecture applies cognitive-map research and Kevin Lynch's paths, landmarks, districts, edges and nodes to wayfinding. Getting lost is framed as a mismatch between the player's mental map and the space. A route walked one way is not necessarily learned in reverse; landmarks help only if they stay in place, and work better when they look different from different sides. Recommends auditing each element for legibility and playtesting without a HUD or minimap.

title: "I'm a Solo Developer but AI is My New Ill-Informed Co-Worker": Envisioning and Designing Generative AI to Support Indie Game Development
venue: Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction 8 (CHI PLAY)
summary: Qualitative analysis of 3,091 posts and comments (Aug 2022-Jan 2024) from indie-developer subreddits and Facebook groups. Developers used image generators for character designs, environments, concept art and prototypes, and generative AI more broadly for code, narrative, voices and placeholder content, valuing it for cost and for filling skill gaps. The most frequent risks were copyright and legal exposure from AI-made assets (12.5% of posts) and the inability to produce new content or keep a consistent style (10.1%), alongside fewer jobs for artists and voice actors (9.3%). Posters asked for models that reflect a team's own artistic style.
notes: Text extracted from the author-hosted PDF and searched by keyword; findings table and selected passages read, not the whole paper. Full text read 2026-10-15 from the author-hosted PDF (all 26 pages extracted; method, findings table, Sec. 4.1-4.2 and discussion read). Summary corrected: placeholder content is attributed to generative AI in general, not specifically to image generators. Metadata matches Crossref (PACM HCI 8, CHI PLAY, Article 317).

title: Production Essentials Summit: No Mavericks, No Martyrs: Sustainable, Collaborative Production
summary: Obsidian game director on two habits that pull teams into crunch: the 'maverick' who hacks content in outside the pipelines and the 'martyr' who adds work through unscheduled overtime. An extra quest one person squeezes in becomes work for design, narrative, combat, art, cinematics, lighting, audio and effects; overtime-inflated history corrupts later estimates. Remedies: aim at a minimum viable version at every stage to catch scope and direction problems early, cross-disciplinary strike teams, scope as a shared team responsibility, schedules that do not assume 100% efficiency, explained cuts, and leads who go home on time. Examples are hypothetical.
notes: Vault page offers the slide deck free; the session was read from the GDC YouTube upload. Audit 2026-09-26 (transcript): the extra-quest cost list names design, narrative, combat systems, environment art, cinematics, lighting, audio and VFX; QA is not mentioned, so it was removed from the summary. Alternate Vault pages for the same session (same title and conference in the Vault crawl) are listed in alt_urls.

title: Evaluating the Effectiveness of HUDs and Diegetic Ammo Displays in First-Person Shooter Games
summary: Controlled lab experiment with 20 regular FPS players (16 male) comparing five ammunition displays in a custom-built first-person shooter: three HUD designs (bar, icons, counter) and two diegetic displays beside the weapon (a number and bullets). The diegetic number beside the weapon performed best: compared with the worst display (icons on the HUD), players fired 35% fewer shots after running out of ammunition and reloaded 26% faster, and 70% of participants preferred it. The result covers one kind of information in one test game.
notes: Audit 08: read the full paper (author copy at cas.mcmaster.ca/~teather/pdfs/GEM2015_HUDs.pdf, listed as green open access by Semantic Scholar). Added sample size and the custom test game to the summary; title, authors, year and venue match Crossref.

title: Solving an Invisible Problem: Designing for Color-Blindness in Games
summary: A colour-blind producer at Creative Assembly on colour-vision deficiency and how games fail those players: team colours, UI states, health gradients and puzzles that rely on hue alone, including Halo Wars 2, where Pennant, who worked on it, couldn't see features, so they went unreported. Guidance: never convey information by colour alone; use colour-safe palettes and pairs such as blue and orange; define semantic colour presets (friend, enemy) so artists do not rebalance each use; check with simulators but test in context with colour-blind players; prefer letting players pick UI colours over full-screen filters; make options discoverable. Pennant cites about 1 in 12 men and 1 in 200 women.
notes: Alternate Vault pages for the same session (same title and conference in the Vault crawl) are listed in alt_urls.

title: The Video Game Theory Reader 2
summary: Edited collection, cited only for Jesper Juul's chapter 'Fear of Failing? The Many Meanings of Difficulty in Video Games' (pp. 237-252). Juul separates energy, life, game-termination and setback punishment and argues all failures end up as setbacks, so time is the underlying cost. In an online test of one Pac-Man-like prototype (85 mostly male, avid players), those who failed some and then finished rated it highest (p=0.06), and those who blamed their own mistake rated it higher than those who blamed the game. Juul suggests casual games spare players setback punishment.
notes: Entry is the edited volume (editors as authors) so the ISBN verifies; the cited content is Juul's chapter, DOI 10.4324/9780203887660-18, read in full on the author's site. The chapter also reports a small online test, summarised with its limits.

title: The perils of project-based work: attempting resistance to extreme work practices in video game development
summary: Analyses two blogs by spouses of game developers about extreme working hours, and the reader comments. Challenges the belief that long hours are necessary to make successful games, documents the toll on workers and families, and argues that project-based structures and the perceived race to deadlines both create extreme work and make it hard for workers to resist, or even to recognise it as extreme.

title: What went wrong? A survey of problems in game development
summary: Surveys problems in game development, collected mainly from published game postmortems, and compares them with well-known problems of traditional information-systems projects. An early peer-reviewed analysis of game postmortems; Politowski et al. (2021) based their initial list of problem types on it and on Washburn et al. (2016).
notes: Only the abstract was available. Its specific findings (for example which problems were most common) are cited in the text through Politowski et al. 2021, which summarises them. Audit 2026-09-26: re-read the Crossref abstract (the ResearchGate evidence file is a block page). Removed the claim that Washburn et al. 2016 built their categories on this paper: Washburn's categories start from Shirinian's, and it cites Petrillo only as related work. Politowski et al. 2021 list Callele et al. 2005 as an earlier postmortem analysis, so this paper is an early one, not the first.

title: Predatory Monetisation? A Categorisation of Unfair, Misleading and Aggressive Monetisation Techniques in Digital Games from the Player Perspective
summary: 1,104 players recruited on game subreddits and Twitter described transactions they found misleading, aggressive or unfair; content analysis (final inter-rater kappa 0.84) produced 35 techniques in eight domains: game dynamics designed to drive spending (pay or grind, pay or wait, a 'nerf cycle' for paid items, escalating dependency, unfair matchups), product not meeting expectations, monetisation of basic quality of life, predatory advertising, in-game currency (disguised prices, multiple currencies, fixed bundle sizes), pay to win, general presence of microtransactions, and other. Limits: self-report, perceived rather than verified mechanisms, no demographics.
notes: Published online 2021 (issue 2022). Open access (CC BY).

title: Phaser.Physics.Arcade.World
summary: API reference. The Arcade physics world's timeScale is a scaling factor on the physics frame rate with inverse meaning: 1.0 is normal speed, 2.0 half speed and 0.5 double speed. The world also exposes a fixed-step setting and a physics steps-per-second rate.

title: Phaser.Time.Clock
summary: API reference. A scene's Clock drives timer events using game time and respects scene pausing; its timeScale speeds up or slows down all timer events belonging to it independently of the rest of the game.

title: Scenes
summary: Concept page. A scene's callback methods are init(), preload(), create() and update(time, delta): configure the scene, queue asset loading, create objects with loaded assets, then update each game step.
notes: The concept page carries no version number and its text was written for Phaser 3; the lifecycle methods cited are unchanged in Phaser 4, but re-check against the installed version.

title: All Choice No Consequence: Efficiently Branching Narrative
summary: A creative manager at Episode, a mobile interactive-story platform, on branching at low cost. Recommends outlining the story before adding branches and finishing the script before adding choices; finding branches in outline disagreements, reorderable beats and the 'how' between fixed goals; reacting to every choice immediately; giving options equal weight and clear stakes; and avoiding false, misleading and vague options. Reports the platform's internal observations that a no-choice version retained players worse, that doubling the number of choices did not change retention, and that heavy branching did not raise replay rates.
notes: Alternate Vault pages for the same session (same title and conference in the Vault crawl) are listed in alt_urls.

title: Tools Tutorial Day: Tools to Reduce Open Bug Count at Media Molecule
summary: Media Molecule's small tools team joined off-the-shelf services with glue code so each stage of a bug's life took one click: automated smoke tests after every check-in that run each test twice to detect out-of-sync state, result emails naming the changes and owners, bug reports prefilled with build revision, location and a replay, and a one-click path from a bug to its replay in the debugger. No before-and-after bug counts are given. In the Q&A Phillips estimated that about half of out-of-sync failures came from uninitialized variables and that keeping the game deterministic takes sustained work.
notes: Alternate Vault pages for the same session (same title and conference in the Vault crawl) are listed in alt_urls.

title: Designing Game Feel: A Survey
summary: Surveys over 200 academic and practitioner sources on game feel and sorts techniques by design purpose into three domains: physicality, polished by tuning movement, gravity and collision for cohesion and predictability; amplification, polished by juicing (screen shake, particles, hit stop, flashes, audio and haptics) for empowerment and clear feedback; and support, polished by streamlining (coyote time, jump buffering, corner correction, invincibility frames, aim assist) so the game acts on the player's intent. Distinguishes hit stop, pausing particular objects on impact, from freeze frames that halt game time. Notes that much of this knowledge exists mainly in practitioner writing.
notes: First published online in 2021; the issue is dated 2022.

title: Math for Game Programmers: Dark Secrets of the RNG
summary: Applied RNG techniques from a Hearthstone-prototype and CCG programmer. Bagging (shuffling a set and drawing without replacement) stops long streaks, though the reshuffle boundary still allows doubled runs. Any possible random edge case will eventually reach a live player, so programmers should flag them. Players misjudge probability and complain about fair odds; a 'pity timer' guarantees a rare drop eventually. Nested weighted lookup tables with dynamic weights implement pity and can reweight loot, for example by class popularity, since drops are an input to the economy. Also covers seeding bugs and hash-based seeds for procedural hierarchies.
notes: Alternate Vault pages for the same session (same title and conference in the Vault crawl) are listed in alt_urls.

title: Heuristic evaluation for games: usability principles for video game design
venue: Proceedings of the SIGCHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI 2008)
summary: Derives ten usability heuristics for inspecting video games from an analysis of published reviews of 108 PC games (18 in each of six genres), which yielded twelve recurring classes of usability problems. The heuristics are meant for both early and functional prototypes. A preliminary evaluation suggests they help evaluators find game-specific usability problems that are otherwise easy to overlook. The heuristics address the usability of game interfaces.
notes: Audit 2026-09-26: only the abstract is reachable (Semantic Scholar/OpenAlex report closed access). The summary's last sentence ('not whether a game is fun') went beyond the abstract; reworded to what the abstract states. Metadata matches Crossref (the published title splits the subtitle).

title: Level Design in a Day: Procedural Level Design in Eldritch
summary: Solo developer of Eldritch on why levels were generated (the design wanted perennial discovery; scope; the developer's programming strengths; content reuse) and how: a 3D maze from a modified Prim's algorithm with tuning knobs and extra walls removed for loops; special rooms prescribed before maze growth so they always fit; modules with a guaranteed-open region on each connecting face; rotation and mirroring to cut module count; a tool that generated 10,000 mazes to count configuration frequency; rule-driven spawners with population limits and a minimum distance from the player start. Pittman argues generation is design, and that placement rules mattered most.
notes: Alternate Vault pages for the same session (same title and conference in the Vault crawl) are listed in alt_urls.

title: Math for Game Programmers: Building A Better Jump
summary: Pittman (Minor Key Games, formerly Gearbox) derives jump physics from designer targets instead of starting from gravity constants. Treating the avatar as a particle under constant gravity, the arc is a parabola; from apex height and time to apex, Pittman solves for gravity and launch velocity, or replaces the time with horizontal distance to apex divided by air speed. Horizontal and vertical velocity stay separate. Arcs can join partial parabolas: heavier gravity after the apex, heavier gravity on early button release for variable height (with a minimum height), a new parabola per extra jump. Prefers a simplified velocity Verlet step to Euler, whose results can shift when frame rate drops.
notes: The transcript states the equations f'(t) = gt + v0 and f(t) = 1/2 g t^2 + v0 t and the apex conditions; the closed forms v0 = 2h/t_h and g = -2h/t_h^2 (up positive) follow directly and were derived by hand, since the slide itself is not in the captions. Alternate Vault pages for the same session (same title and conference in the Vault crawl) are listed in alt_urls.

title: Animate with text (New)
summary: Tool page for PixelLab's newer text animation tool. It animates one reference image from an action description, with 4 to 16 frames (even counts), keeps the input image as frame 1, limits width x height x frames to 524,288 pixels, accepts references up to 256x256, and prices by image size and frame count.

title: Animate with text (Pro)
summary: Tool page for PixelLab's Pro text animation tool. The number of frames returned depends on the reference size: 16 frames for a 32x32 or 64x64 reference and 4 frames for references from 65 to 256 pixels, at a cost that rises with size. Options include view, direction, transparent background, seed and a beta colour palette that every frame is restricted to.

title: PixelLab API v2
summary: OpenAPI specification of PixelLab's pixel-art generation API. Documents fields and limits for skeleton animation v3 (one sprite plus 18-joint poses, 3 to 15 frames, billed so one long clip costs less than several short ones), text animation v3 (even frame counts, a colour de-flicker toward the first frame), PixMiniMax (4 to 40 frames, separate subject, pose, view and direction captions, describe movement rather than appearance), template animation strictness, character creation sizes, skeleton estimation, and shared-palette colour reduction and unzoom.
notes: Read the descriptions and request schemas of /animate-character, /characters/animations, /animate-with-skeleton-v3, /animate-with-text-v3, /animate-pixminimax, /estimate-skeleton, /create-character-v3, /reduce-colors and /unzoom on the checked date. The spec changes without version numbers; re-check limits before relying on them. Audit re-read 2026-10-15 of the same endpoints: target_palette is a property only of /generate-image-v2 and /animate-with-text-v2; 'Prompt complexity scales with size' is on the image_size field of /enhance-character-v3-prompt; /animate-character's description gives ai_freedom as 0=strict, 1000=creative while the MCP guide gives 0-900; spec info.version is 'dev'.

title: PixelLab MCP tools
summary: Reference for the tools of PixelLab's MCP server. Documents create_character (size default 48 px and per-mode limits, proportions presets, and that whatever a v3 reference sprite faces is taken as south, so it must face the viewer straight on), animate_character modes (template mode with ai_freedom from 0 to 900, default 0; skeleton-v3 mode, which poses a template onto the character and moves it instead of redrawing it each frame; v3 and pixminimax modes) with about 50 humanoid animation templates, animate_image for text-described motion, and animate_with_skeleton_v3 for user-posed skeletons.
notes: Read the create_character, animate_character and animate_image sections on the checked date. Audit re-read 2026-10-15: animate_character's mode list is template, skeleton-v3, v3, pixminimax; 'pro' is a mode of create_character and animate_object, not animate_character, so the summary was corrected. Also read animate_image and animate_with_skeleton_v3 sections.

title: Rotating a character
summary: Guide to PixelLab's Rotate tool. Describes two ways to produce a character's eight directions: generate every direction from one camera-facing reference, or update the reference after each generation so each rotation is 45 degrees from the previous one. Notes that the second way benefits from the model being better at small rotations, but that any errors accumulate after each generation.

title: Skill-Building Series: Pixel Art and Animation in the Hi-Bit Age
venue: GDC Summer 2020, Skill-Building Series (Student Program track)
summary: Plummer surveys modern pixel-art games (post-process shaders, normal-mapped or voxel-backed lighting, mixed resolutions, which the speaker says few games pull off) and demonstrates in GraphicsGale. On UFO 50 the team follows self-imposed colours-per-tile and sprite limits but bends them for readability. At small sizes one pixel can carry a detail. Rendering and animation are separate costs, so drop details such as zippers or laces that would need secondary motion. Outline quickly with a colour-replace brush. Lines on the four cardinal axes survive in-engine rotation far better than diagonals. Large sprites get a high-resolution concept first; small ones are drawn directly.
notes: Moderated by Joel Couture. Transcript is GDC YouTube captions.

title: Game industry problems: an extensive analysis of the gray literature
summary: Codes 927 problems from 200 postmortems (1997-2019) into 20 types. Management and production problems appear in similar proportion; game design and technical problems are most frequent (11% each); the most common root causes concern people, not technology (insufficient workforce, work environment, underestimation, unclear design vision, lack of fun, misaligned teams). Scope problems recur and feature creep persists though it declined. Advice: prototype and playtest in pre-production until the core fun is clear, keep scope realistic, small teams. Postmortems cover shipped games only.
notes: Read the authors' arXiv version (2009.02440v3, January 2021) of the journal article.

title: A Survey of Video Game Testing
venue: 2021 IEEE/ACM International Conference on Automation of Software Test (AST)
summary: Survey of academic and grey literature on how game developers test. The authors report that developers rely almost exclusively on manual play-testing and testers' own knowledge, conclude that current processes fall short for lack of automation, and caution that existing game-testing techniques may not generalize to different types of games.

title: DreamFusion: Text-to-3D using 2D Diffusion
summary: Introduces score distillation: a radiance field (NeRF) is optimised so that renders from random views look right to a frozen 2D text-to-image diffusion model, with no 3D training data. Stated limits: results are oversaturated and oversmoothed, vary little between seeds, are limited in detail by the 64x64 diffusion model, and take about 1.5 hours per asset on four TPUv4 chips. The ill-posed optimisation can paint content onto flat surfaces, give a subject several faces, or carve colour detail into the geometry. The authors add that CLIP-based scores miss geometry quality.
notes: ICLR 2023 (OpenReview-reviewed main conference): the ICLR virtual site lists it as an oral, top 5%, Outstanding Paper award. No DOI. OpenReview forum FjNys5c7VyY (linked from ML Anthology) blocked automated access. Full text read on ar5iv (Discussion, ablations, evaluation).

title: An empirical study of issues and barriers to mainstream video game accessibility
venue: Proceedings of the 15th International ACM SIGACCESS Conference on Computers and Accessibility (ASSETS 2013)
summary: Two studies: an online survey of 55 gamers with disabilities (69% reporting motor impairments, recruited partly via AbleGamers, a possible selection bias) and interviews with six industry practitioners. The most common barrier was incompatibility with the assistive technology players rely on; many asked others for help, reluctantly, and many avoided multiplayer. Developers said easy features such as colour-blind palettes and subtitles get done first, that motor needs vary too much for a single fix, and that colleagues with impairments catch problems early, as when a tester who could not use a key layout prompted remappable controls. Most saw middleware support as the best route.

title: Automated Testing and Instant Replays in Retro City Rampage
summary: A solo developer records only player input at the lowest input layer and relies on a deterministic engine to replay sessions, using replays for automated playthroughs on every platform, bug reproduction, leaderboard replays and attract mode. Provinciano lists threats to determinism: uninitialized variables, a shared random generator, engine callbacks, middleware, frame-dependent accumulation, asynchronous file operations and floating-point differences on PC. The developer used separate random streams per purpose, per-frame checksums of entity state, and diffed logs of recording versus playback to find divergence. Test mode stubs out online services and keeps saves in memory.
notes: Alternate Vault pages for the same session (same title and conference in the Vault crawl) are listed in alt_urls.

title: A Motivational Model of Video Game Engagement
summary: Review presenting the authors' self-determination-theory model of video game engagement: appeal and short-term well-being effects come from satisfying needs for competence, autonomy and relatedness. Drawing mainly on their own studies, it argues that mastery of controls is necessary but not sufficient and that a steep learning curve is felt as a price of admission; that presence depends more on need satisfaction than on audiovisual fidelity; that violent content added little appeal for most players; and that play thwarting competence (complex controls, too little practice) was linked to aggression after play. A theory-and-review article, not a new study.
notes: Read the authors' copy: abstract, the competence, autonomy and relatedness sections, mastery of controls, immersion and conclusion.

title: random — Generate pseudo-random numbers
summary: API documentation. Its reproducibility notes state that reusing a seed reproduces the sequence from run to run as long as multiple threads are not running, and that most of the module's algorithms and seeding functions may change across Python versions; only random() given a backward-compatible seeder is guaranteed to keep producing the same sequence.
notes: Living documentation (read as the Python 3.14 docs); year is the access year.

title: Fast Iteration for Far Cry 4 - Optimizing Key Parts of the Dunia Pipeline
summary: Ubisoft Montreal engine architect on shortening code, data-build and distribution loops between Far Cry 3 and 4. A distributed, cached build tool cut an editor rebuild from about 40 to about 4 minutes; profiling the nightly data build's subprocesses and caching official resources cut it from about 6 hours for three platforms to about 1.5 hours for five; packages streamed on demand; locally changed inputs were recompiled into a patch mounted over the build. Quenin says understanding the pipeline through profiling and avoiding redundant work mattered most, and notes caches need strong hardware and are invalidated by tool changes.
notes: Alternate Vault pages for the same session (same title and conference in the Vault crawl) are listed in alt_urls.

title: Game AI Pro: Collected Wisdom of Game AI Professionals
summary: Edited volume of practitioner chapters. Read: Dill, 'What Is Game AI?' (AI exists to deliver the intended player experience; avoid visibly wrong 'artificial stupidity'; balance authorial control against reactivity; cheat only when it improves the experience and is unlikely to be caught, with Kohan 2 examples); Dawe, Gargolinski, Dicken, Humphreys and Mark, 'Behavior Selection Algorithms: An Overview' (how FSMs, hierarchical FSMs, behavior trees, utility systems, GOAP and HTN planners work, where each fits and how each fails); Sturtevant, 'Choosing a Search Space Representation' (trade-offs of grids, waypoint graphs and navigation meshes).
notes: Editor listed as author. Chapters 1, 4 and 18 were read in full from the free official chapter PDFs at gameaipro.com; other chapters were not read.

title: Game AI Pro 2: Collected Wisdom of Game AI Professionals
summary: Edited volume of practitioner chapters. Read: Rabin, 'Agent Reaction Time' (from reaction-time research, about 0.2 s simple and 0.4 s go/no-go, longer for weak stimuli or inattention); Fray, 'Context Steering' (blended steering behaviors cancel or become coupled when players watch individuals; context maps used on F1 2011); Walsh, 'Modeling Perception and Awareness in Splinter Cell: Blacklist' (fairness, feedback and plausibility in stealth detection); Dyckhoff, 'Ellie: Buddy AI in The Last of Us' (keep the companion close, generate follow and cover positions, never teleport for convenience, ration help, reverse shooting logic, hide buddies from enemies during stealth).

title: Low Poly Modeling: Style Through Economy
venue: Game Developers Conference 2017, Game Career Seminar
summary: An independent developer making a Sega Saturn-style 3D game treats detail as a budget. Curves have a point of sufficiency: a 16-sided circle reads as round, and halving the rings of a sphere goes unnoticed until banding shows. Keep a consistent smallest-polygon size (the speaker calls it atomic size) so a scene reads at one scale; a global size gives a rough, sparse look, while per-object sizes spend the same triangles (two 800-triangle scenes) on denser elements. Model silhouette-defining and shadow-casting parts in geometry rather than alpha. A shared palette texture lets a whole game run on two or three materials, which batches well.
notes: Numbers from captions. Vault access tier not confirmed, so members is the cautious default; the full talk is on GDC's official YouTube channel. title: Keep it Together: Encouraging Cooperative Behavior During Co-op Play
summary: Ubisoft Toronto's game director (co-op director on Splinter Cell: Conviction) argues players cooperate when cooperation measurably improves outcomes and widens individual expression, and lists seven cooperative dynamics from coercive to voluntary: gating, exotic challenges, punitive states that need rescue, buffing, asymmetric abilities, combined actions and survival. From Conviction, Redding reports that shared target marks changed how players used abilities and that exotic challenges interrupt social flow. The director doubts developers can police bad behavior and advises against making co-op the hardcore mode.

title: Networking Scripted Weapons and Abilities in 'Overwatch'
summary: Blizzard engineer on Statescript, the visual scripting language behind Overwatch's hero weapons, abilities, game modes and some UI. Scripts are graphs of entries, conditions, actions and time-extended states; a state undoes everything it started when it deactivates, which the speaker credits for fewer lifetime and desync bugs. The same script runs on server and client: the server is authoritative, clients send only button input, and the local hero is predicted, rolled back and re-simulated on correction. Costs: a large up-front runtime, editor and debugger investment, judging what belongs in code versus script, and occasional workarounds because replication is state-based, not event-based.

title: Lessons Learned from 'Job Simulator' to 'Vacation Simulator': Advanced Interactions for Room-Scale VR
summary: Owlchemy Labs' CEO and CTO on moving from Job Simulator to Vacation Simulator; their first rule is avoiding sickness. Point-anywhere teleport made targets and bounds hard to judge and caused teleport fatigue; zone-based teleport guarantees that visible things are reachable but must be designed in from the start. Automatically rotating the world for front-facing tracking disoriented players in every test, so layouts put interactions in front of the player. Robot characters avoid the uncanny valley and need idle animation; constant staring was creepy. Players expect everyday objects to work, so food was rebuilt as general systems (stacking, slicing, bites) and books became openable.

title: Live Ops in 'Star Wars: Galaxy of Heroes'
summary: Capital Games' live producer ties live operations to the game's pillars (a durable character economy, incremental progress, respect for player investment), which bring power creep, roster bloat and pressure to avoid nerfs. The team released about every two weeks, used events (some needing engineering, others built by designers in data) to give neglected characters a purpose, chained reworks so new content made old characters useful, tracked which characters players actually used, and made necessary nerfs transparent. Reinhart presents this as one team's experience with a licensed property.
notes: Alternate Vault pages for the same session (same title and conference in the Vault crawl) are listed in alt_urls.

title: Interactive Story Without Challenge Mechanics: The Design of 'Firewatch'
summary: Firewatch's designer on a story game with no failure state, organized around believability, reactivity and flexibility. Dialogue choices are mutually exclusive, usually timed and all recorded as facts; implicit choices use existing verbs such as picking up objects; hard cuts between days manage pacing in a contiguous world but made some players hesitant to explore. A shared registry of what each character knew prevented duplicate facts that caused false negatives. Playtests surfaced actions worth supporting, and critical-path conversations were cut to fit measured travel times. Argues writers must be integrated with design and tools.

title: Flocks, herds and schools: A distributed behavioral model
venue: SIGGRAPH '87: Proceedings of the 14th Annual Conference on Computer Graphics and Interactive Techniques
summary: Introduces 'boids': each simulated bird steers from local, filtered perception using three urges (collision avoidance, velocity matching, flock centering), and flocking emerges from their interaction. Shows that plain weighted averaging of steering requests can cancel out and leave an agent flying into an obstacle, and instead allocates a fixed acceleration budget to behaviors in priority order. Notes that the naive algorithm scales with the square of flock size and that localized perception is essential to flock-like motion.
notes: Full text read from the author-hosted PDF at red3d.com. Access marked free on the strength of that copy; the ACM landing page refused scripted requests.

title: TEXTure: Text-Guided Texturing of 3D Shapes
summary: Paints a texture onto an existing mesh by generating views with a depth-guided diffusion model and projecting them into a 1024x1024 UV atlas, tracking which areas to keep, refine or newly generate so that views agree. It shows that naive view-by-view painting gives inconsistent patches, visible seams and blur on surfaces seen at a slant. Stated limits: details hidden in early views can clash when revealed (such as mismatched eyes), fixed viewpoints can miss unusual geometry and their order changes results, and the diffusion model sometimes ignores the mesh depth. It does not discuss baked lighting.
notes: Full text read on ar5iv; DOI and SIGGRAPH 2023 proceedings from Crossref. Access marked free for the arXiv version.

title: Level Design Case Studies: Trainyard and Cut the Rope
summary: Two mobile puzzle designers on level sequencing. Rix (Trainyard) teaches one element at a time and treats combinations as new elements (A, B, A+B, C, A+C, B+C...), spreads tutorials over the game (the last one more than 70 puzzles in), brings taught elements back, and dips difficulty every few levels. Voinov (Cut the Rope, ZeptoLab) tracks a failing rate and a skipping rate for every level: high failure means players understand but cannot execute, high skipping means they do not understand the puzzle. The hardest level in each 25-level box is the second to last.
notes: Captions garble 'failing rate' as 'trailing rate' at one point; the next sentence names it correctly. Alternate Vault pages for the same session (same title and conference in the Vault crawl) are listed in alt_urls.

title: Independent Games Summit: Crafting A Tiny Open World: 'A Short Hike' Postmortem
summary: A solo developer's postmortem of A Short Hike, a small open-world exploration game made in about three months after shelving a larger project. A low-resolution rendering style and palette-based shading were scope tools. Monthly milestones split core work from stretch goals, many added after release. Playtest-driven fixes: a cave leading back to the tutorial for players who swam around it; a frequently missed optional item placed in several spots with the extras removed once one was taken; a climbing tip only for players who had not climbed; NPCs visibly climbing to prime the idea; a late rebuild of the final area with a visible route and more upgrade items to protect pacing.

title: Super Powering Technical Artists Using Deep Learning
venue: Game Developers Conference 2019, Visual Arts track
summary: A Unity machine-learning engineer surveys research tools for artists: style transfer, image-to-image translation, and super-resolution (ESRGAN) that upscales textures better than bicubic stretching and that fans had already used to remaster old games. Judgement points: outputs show artifacts and are not production quality, so they serve exploration and the artist decides when work is ready; artists want more control than most techniques give; and check each code licence before shipping, since GPLv3 code would oblige open-sourcing the product, while MIT, Apache 2 and BSD code needs only credit.
notes: Pre-dates current diffusion tools. Vault also lists the session as 1026408. Vault access tier not confirmed, so members is the cautious default; the full talk is on GDC's official YouTube channel. Access set to free because the full talk is on the official GDC YouTube channel (alt_urls).

title: Predicting game difficulty and churn without players
venue: Proceedings of the Annual Symposium on Computer-Human Interaction in Play (CHI PLAY 2020)
summary: Deep reinforcement learning agents play 168 levels of the mobile puzzle game Angry Birds Dream Blast to estimate level difficulty, and a simple simulation of a player population (skill, persistence, boredom, learning) turns those estimates into per-level pass and churn predictions that beat a baseline using agent data alone, checked against real player data. Limits stated by the authors: not yet validated in actual design work, agent difficulty estimates are not human-like on the hardest levels, and training agents per level is slow.
notes: Read the arXiv version (2008.12937v1) of the CHI PLAY paper.

title: Twenty Years, Twenty Lessons
summary: Magic: The Gathering's head designer gives twenty lessons from two decades on one card game, each tied to a card or set. Balance-relevant ones: make the fun part also the correct strategy to win (Unhinged 'Gotcha' cards rewarded silent, joyless play); interesting is not the same as fun; design each component for the audience it is meant for (a coin-flip card satisfied neither thrill-seekers nor competitive players); be blunt when players miss a strong play; R&D prefers cards that split opinion strongly over cards everyone rates mildly; players are good at recognizing problems and poor at solving them.
notes: Alternate Vault pages for the same session (same title and conference in the Vault crawl) are listed in alt_urls.

title: 'Assassin's Creed Origins': Monitoring and Validation of World Design Data
summary: Ubisoft design technical director on nightly automated validation of Assassin's Creed Origins world data. Breakage came from everyone: content placement, a prop fix reused elsewhere, engine or gameplay code changes, procedural placement and build order. Editor scripts ran objective pass/fail checks on placed gameplay objects (such as zipline clearance and angle), AI network nodes on navmesh with reachable schedule stations, and each location's contents against a design-intent spreadsheet. Results went to spreadsheets with plain-language errors and editor links, a daily email with deltas per team, and a map view. The speaker says the game could not have shipped at its scope otherwise.

title: AI-driven Dynamic Dialog through Fuzzy Pattern Matching. Empower Your Writers!
summary: Valve's rule-based dialogue system, used from Half-Life 2 through Left 4 Dead and Dota 2. Each query gathers facts about speaker, world and memory into one flat dictionary; rules are lists of criteria that must all match, the matching rule with the most criteria wins and ties are broken at random, so specific lines override general fallbacks. Responses can write facts back into memory for running gags and follow-ups, and replies are looked up only when the previous line ends, so interrupted conversations stop by themselves. Argues writers should own the rules, tools should suit the actual writers, and debugging needs fact provenance and match-score output.
notes: Audit 2026-09-26: transcript states that all criteria in a rule must match; 'the rule with the most satisfied criteria wins' reworded to the matching rule with the most criteria. Metadata ok. title: Three Statistical Tests Every Game Developer Should Know
summary: Insomniac programmer's practical guide, deliberately simplified, to settling A/B questions with statistics in a spreadsheet. Small samples drawn from the same distribution can give very different averages; choose the significance threshold before testing; a significant difference may still be too small to matter, and a confidence interval spanning zero is no result; paired designs remove person-to-person variation; skewed data such as play time from a friends-and-family playtest calls for medians and a rank test (Mann-Whitney). Warns against running many tests and mining for a hit, and against reading correlation as cause.
notes: Programming track session.

title: The Motivational Pull of Video Games: A Self-Determination Theory Approach
summary: Four studies applying self-determination theory to play. Studies 1-3 used short lab sessions with mostly undergraduate participants (Study 1: 20 minutes of Super Mario 64): perceived in-game autonomy and competence predicted enjoyment, preference for future play and short-term well-being change, and intuitive controls related to competence and presence. Study 4 surveyed 730 mostly male members of an online community with MMO experience: autonomy, competence and relatedness each independently predicted enjoyment and intended future play, while Yee's achievement motive was negatively related to post-play mood. The authors flag new measures and short-term outcomes only.
notes: Read the authors' copy on selfdeterminationtheory.org: abstract, introduction, Study 1 and Study 4 methods, and the general discussion.

title: Rules of Play: Game Design Fundamentals
summary: Textbook presenting a unified model for looking at all kinds of games. The excerpt read, an essay of selections from the book, develops the magic circle: the boundary in space and time within which a game's rules and meanings apply and through which players enter play. Most games can be framed as closed systems bounded by that circle, but some (the A.I. alternate reality game, Assassin-style games played through daily life) deliberately blur it and behave as open systems mixed with everyday life, while some part of the game structure always remains.
notes: Read Salen and Zimmerman, 'This Is Not a Game: Play in Cultural Environments' (DiGRA 2003, doi 10.26503/dl.v2003i1.31), which the authors describe as selections from the book. MIT Press pages and previews were blocked to automated access.

title: Silhouette clipping
venue: Proceedings of the 27th annual conference on Computer graphics and interactive techniques - SIGGRAPH '00, pp. 327-334
summary: Sander and colleagues observe that a coarse mesh carrying texture and normal maps reproduces interior surface detail but still betrays itself through polygonal silhouettes. The method clips rendering of the coarse mesh to the exact silhouette of the original model, using progressive hulls and a precomputed search over silhouette edges, and reports quality similar to the high-resolution mesh at lower rendering cost. The paper also gives an improved method for building texture and normal maps over the coarse mesh.
notes: Peer-reviewed SIGGRAPH 2000 paper. Metadata from Crossref; abstract and page numbers from the project page. Full text read 2026-10-15 from the author PDF at https://hhoppe.com/silclip.pdf. Summary and metadata confirmed; no other change.

title: Texture mapping progressive meshes
venue: Proceedings of the 28th annual conference on Computer graphics and interactive techniques (SIGGRAPH 2001), pp. 409-416
summary: The authors build one texture atlas shared by every level of detail of a progressive mesh. The parametrization minimises texture stretch, where small texture distances map onto large surface distances, which balances sampling rate across the surface and across directions; it also minimises texture deviation between levels. The mesh is split into compact, near-planar charts that are sized by their stretch, simplified without crossing chart boundaries, and packed into an atlas used for colour and normal maps.
notes: Peer-reviewed SIGGRAPH 2001 paper. Metadata from Crossref; abstract from the project page. Full text read 2026-10-15 from the author PDF at https://hhoppe.com/tmpm.pdf. Summary and metadata confirmed; no other change.

title: Dark Patterns: How Good UX Can Be Bad UX
summary: UX Summit talk by a Frontier Developments UI designer distinguishing effective UX from ethically good UX. Recreated (unnamed) examples of dark patterns: an ad close button that opens the store, hidden cancel buttons, demoralizing wording, daily 'rewards' dangling very low-probability items, guilt-tripping notifications, social pressure, and store screens that highlight the most expensive bundle. Better practice: clear trade-offs such as optional rewarded ads or a one-time ad removal, balanced store layouts, clear language, and rewarding loyal players. Argues metrics that show a tactic works do not settle whether it should be used.

title: 10 Key Quest Design Lessons from 'The Witcher 3' and 'Cyberpunk 2077'
summary: CD Projekt Red's quest director on quest design: a pipeline from story outline to quest design document to playable draft in which any stage can be sent back; withholding information to create curiosity; building quests around emotional beats and quiet character moments; cutting repeated information; delivering key exposition when the player's freedom to act is low; offering a choice when the situation makes players expect one; and telegraphing consequences, since subtle ones such as changed radio and TV content went largely unnoticed. Includes a failure case where one of two rival candidates was far more appealing, and notes star casting skews player choices.

title: '09 to '19: A Decade of Approachability in Fighting Games
summary: An Iron Galaxy designer who worked on Killer Instinct surveys a decade of fighting-game approachability. Fighters are real-time, low in randomness and give perfect information, so skill gaps are not softened and losing hurts. Training modes help already-motivated players and can widen gaps; Killer Instinct's dojo sent players to real matches after a few lessons. Toggled assist modes carry stigma and wall players off from real play, while always-on simplified inputs built from real techniques can teach. Button count is a poor proxy for difficulty, input rules shared across characters help players move up, and removing fundamentals has costs. Argues for designing for appeal, not only ease.

title: Far Cry 4: Gameplay Team Workflow, Iteration and Philosophy
summary: Ubisoft Montreal's lead gameplay programmer on Far Cry 4's gameplay team: programmers, animators, designers and embedded testers seated together, with features moving from idea and gut check through a sign-off document, an in-game prototype, alpha, beta and final. Planning put de-risking first, to the point of prototyping risky minor features before polishing safe major ones; risks were realisation, design, technical and balance. Features were playtested from the prototype stage, cut on cost versus value, and brought to alpha together. Tools that shortened iteration included faster builds and per-change preflight builds. A large multi-studio AAA context.
notes: Production track session.

title: Lessons Learned Creating UI for 'The Division'
summary: Massive Entertainment's lead UI programmer on The Division's UI in the Snowdrop engine: a node-graph visual scripting system shared with other content types, immediate-mode vector UI, and iteration as a core pillar, with saved data updating the running game in the editor. Lessons include graph performance pitfalls, a debug feature showing which file draws any UI element, automatically choosing which prompt to display for a game action on console, on PC and on PC with a controller, right-to-left layout support, and a menu system built on global variables that worked but was hacky.

title: Do (Say) The Right Thing: Choice Architecture, Player Expression, and Narrative Design in Fallout: New Vegas
summary: Obsidian's project director on dialogue choice in Fallout: New Vegas. Choice conflict arises when the best mechanical option clashes with the character the player wants to play, as speech checks sometimes did. Recommends defining kinds of choice, range of expression and narrative goals before writing; option order is not neutral because players drift to the top. New Vegas let players kill almost anyone, and its first main quest used independent information steps that players could skip or take in any order. The game never defined character archetypes up front, giving wide but inconsistent responses. Small, tense endings landed harder than spectacle; many small branches beat a few big ones.
notes: Audit 2026-09-26: the transcript describes the first quest's steps as independent so they can be skipped or reordered; it does not say they were built to survive dead contacts, so that wording was removed. Metadata ok. Alternate Vault pages for the same session (same title and conference in the Vault crawl) are listed in alt_urls.

title: Gods and Dumps: Attribute Tuning in 'Pillars of Eternity'
summary: Obsidian's game director on Pillars of Eternity's six attributes. Goals: every attribute useful to every class, no build unviable, and dumping a stat should sting. Linear, narrow scaling kept unusual builds viable but made attributes matter less, a trade-off kept despite complaints. Re-centering attributes so 10 is neutral and lower values are penalties made players refuse to go below 10, which Sawyer attributes to loss aversion. Beta and patch changes cut an attribute that players maxed everywhere and raised one they always dumped. Percentages were hard for players to read, so the UI added breakdowns and class recommendations. The director calls the evidence anecdotal, not data.
