title: The Art of Game Design: A Book of Lenses
summary: Practitioner textbook that organizes design knowledge as lenses: short sets of questions for examining a game from one perspective. The 113 lens texts read in the official Deck of Lenses app include Emotion and Essential Experience (define the experience players should have and what is essential to it), Holographic Design (see game elements and player experience at once), Unification (reinforce the theme by every available means), Flow (clear goals, distractions, steadily rising challenge), Needs (competence, autonomy, relatedness), Meaningful Choices (including dominant strategies) and Triangularity (safe low reward versus risky high reward).
notes: Book text not read. Lens wording read in the official Deck of Lenses web app, whose numbering (Lens 1 Emotion, 2 Essential Experience, 113 in total) matches the third edition. Citing claims stay within those lens texts.

title: A Course About Game Balance
summary: GDC Education Summit summary of a college game-balance course. Defines balance as creating the appearance of fairness, so perception matters as much as the numbers. Lists four methods (designer intuition, playtesting, analytics, mathematical modelling) and covers numeric relationships, cost curves for transitive objects in a spreadsheet, situational value treated as a trigger probability, probability and the ways humans misjudge it, Monte Carlo checks, reward schedules and level curves, statistics and metric plans, and intransitive mechanics via payoff matrices. Raises ethics questions about fudging rolls and revenue-driven pain points without answering them.
notes: Alternate Vault pages for the same session (same title and conference in the Vault crawl) are listed in alt_urls.

title: Game Balance
summary: Textbook on game balance mixing mathematics, psychology and spreadsheet practice. Chapters cover what balance means in single-player (challenge at current ability, no sudden spikes) and competitive play (equal chances at the start given equal skill), anchors, progression curves and F2P 'ramping out' non-payers, fixed and player-driven economies, transitive cost curves and situational value, progression in PvE and PvP, analytics, luck versus skill, input and output randomness, human misjudgment of probability, pseudorandom numbers, statistics, and intransitive mechanics.
notes: Content check limited to the publisher description and the per-chapter abstracts registered with Crossref (DOIs 10.1201/9781315156422-1 to -26); claims citing this entry stay within those abstracts.

title: Physiological Effects of Crunch: A Look at the Science
summary: Game designer and educator's own review of occupational-health and sleep research on long hours (sources on the slides, not named aloud). Schreiber reports that output per hour falls with long hours, that knowledge and creative work suffer more than rote work, that fatigue raises the risk of costly errors, that long hours are linked to illness and poor sleep, and that a short crunch followed by recovery is still a net loss. The conclusion: crunch usually signals an unrealistic schedule, so cut scope, move the date or add staff early enough to ramp up; Schreiber sees no justification for crunch beyond about a month.
notes: Advocacy track. The studies are cited on Schreiber's slides, which were not read; citing claims are limited to the speaker's conclusions and recommendations as spoken. Alternate Vault pages for the same session (same title and conference in the Vault crawl) are listed in alt_urls.

title: Understanding and evaluating cooperative games
venue: Proceedings of the SIGCHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI 2010)
summary: The authors derive cooperative design patterns from an analysis of 14 cooperative games and propose Cooperative Performance Metrics for annotating play. In a study with 60 participants playing four commercial co-op games in groups of two or three, annotated behaviors were mapped back to the patterns that caused them, identifying effective cooperative patterns and lessons for co-op design.

title: Cutting Apart The Diegetic Interface of 'Hardspace: Shipbreaker'
summary: A Blackbird Interactive designer on redesigning Hardspace: Shipbreaker's UI in early access with a small team and no budget for cutscenes, so the UI carried much of the world-building (contracts and safety reports as in-world paperwork). A fully diegetic helmet HUD from the prototype cut off elements and burned text; the shipped HUD is mostly diegetic with deliberate exceptions. Core information was grouped near the bottom centre, notifications and hazards got fixed sides, and subtitles stopped overlapping other UI. Replacing a work-order checklist with a salvage bar shifted play toward exploration but required retuning the economy. Lack of formal user testing is named as a gap.
notes: Alternate Vault pages for the same session (same title and conference in the Vault crawl) are listed in alt_urls.

title: Procedural Content Generation in Games
summary: Textbook with author-hosted chapters. Ch. 1 defines PCG, lists desirable properties that trade off (speed, reliability, controllability, expressivity, believability) and a taxonomy (online/offline, necessary/optional, seed vs parameters, generic/adaptive, stochastic/deterministic, constructive/generate-and-test, automatic/mixed-initiative). Ch. 3 covers constructive dungeon methods (space partitioning, digging agents, grammars, cellular automata, multi-pass placement). Ch. 8 covers answer set programming, including recursive reachability constraints. Ch. 12 covers evaluation: expressive range, metric choice, controllability, and player-based studies.
notes: Read the author-hosted chapters 1 and 12 in full and chapters 3 and 8 in part (pcgbook.com).

title: How to Launch an Online Game and Still Attend the Launch Party
summary: Odyssey Interactive's CTO on launching Omega Strikers with a two-to-three-person services team: managed cloud services around one custom match finder, scripted deploys that can stand the stack up in a new region, a single production environment with feature flags and end-to-end tests, and tracing kept for 30 days so playtest reports can be investigated afterwards. In one beta incident an all-forward party blocked a queue that required a goalkeeper; tracing found it and a hot fix shipped in about 25 minutes. They over-provisioned for launch and scaled down.

title: Level Design Workshop: Invisible Intuition: Blockmesh and Lighting Tips to Guide Players and Set the Mood
venue: Game Developers Conference 2018, Level Design Workshop
summary: Naughty Dog's David Shaver gives blockmesh techniques for guiding players without HUD markers: block out a rough version of the whole level early, watch anyone play, and iterate until layout lock; give affordances a consistent shape and colour that follow the game's metrics; make denied affordances visibly explained; place a landmark first and build back from it; use openings, lines, light and motion; add breadcrumbs only after early playtests; treat scripted motion as a late bandage. Naughty Dog logs failed grab attempts to find misleading geometry. Robert Yang then covers lighting blockouts.
notes: YouTube upload is titled 'Level Design Workshop: Blockmesh and Lighting Tips'. Alternate Vault pages for the same session (same title and conference in the Vault crawl) are listed in alt_urls.

title: Level Design Summit: Level and Quest Design Collaboration from 'Skyrim' to 'Starfield'
summary: Former Bethesda leads on how quest and level design divided work from Skyrim to Starfield: level design owned locations, layout and combat; quest design owned story, dialogue and non-combat NPCs. Cases show quests layered into existing locations and level designers learning quest tools to build a shared language. Lessons: optional puzzle levels not marked as optional were treated as mandatory; multiplayer server iteration times reduced bespoke scripting; large teams silo and drift toward content that is easy to implement, so project-level goals need stating; decide early who makes final calls.
notes: Alternate Vault pages for the same session (same title and conference in the Vault crawl) are listed in alt_urls.

title: Evolving Combat in 'God of War' for a New Perspective
summary: Santa Monica Studio talk on adapting God of War combat to a close over-the-shoulder camera. Relevant to encounter control: enemies are periodically scored for aggression (whether they may attack, a designer priority applied within a range, whether the player is targeting them, on-screen position and distance) and granted tokens from a fixed pool, each enemy type claiming a different number; those left without tokens stay non-aggressive. Enemies interrupted by a hit keep their tokens briefly, rewarding sustained offense. Difficulty changes token claims and the attacks enemies may use.

title: MVDream: Multi-view Diffusion for 3D Generation
summary: A diffusion model that generates several mutually consistent views of an object from text, used to guide 3D generation. It describes the multi-face Janus problem, where the subject named in the prompt is regenerated on several sides, and content drift, where appearance changes between views, and traces both to a 2D model judging each view without knowing the others. Stated limits: 256x256 output, generalisation bounded by the base model, and lighting and texture styles biased toward the rendered synthetic training data.
notes: ICLR 2024 main conference (OpenReview-reviewed), confirmed on the ICLR proceedings page. No DOI. title: Connecting Players and Franchise: A Compelling Solution to the Cross-Platform Challenge
summary: BioWare producer on the Dragon Age Keep, a web service holding players' franchise choices. Importing local saves between games had produced errors such as dead characters reappearing and choices being overturned; plot interdependencies were hard to test, fixes required client patches, and new console generations would strand saves. The team selected key choices, encoded plot rules and preconditions, and built a solver that resolves conflicting selections to a nearby valid world state, so every stored state is valid. Each game reads only the facts it needs, and the logic can be corrected on the server.
notes: The official GDC YouTube upload is titled 'Connecting Players and Franchise Across Console Generations in the Dragon Age Keep'; same speaker, year and content as the Vault session. Alternate Vault pages for the same session (same title and conference in the Vault crawl) are listed in alt_urls.

title: Procedural Generation in Game Design
summary: Edited collection of 27 practitioner chapters. Per the publisher's chapter abstracts: Grey on when and why to use generation, noting that quilted premade blocks tend to pass quality assurance and that tuning continues after release; Backus on generation replacing content creation but not content design (Sky Rogue); Shepard on mixing handcrafted zones into generated play (Dungeonmans); Dormans on cyclic generation in Unexplored, with graph rules for patterns such as lock-and-key; Cheng on enemy-wave spawning schemes; G. Smith on expressive range.
notes: Editors listed as authors. Only the publisher's table of contents and chapter abstracts (taylorfrancis.com, doi 10.1201/9781315156378) were read; claims stay within them.

title: Finding Balance: Realizing Responsive High Fidelity Character Movement in Just Cause 3
summary: Avalanche Studios' lead character programmer and lead animator on responsive control versus animation fidelity. Their goal was that the player never waits for an animation to finish before the next maneuver. Game-driven movement (logic moves the character, animation follows) is flexible and responsive; animation-driven root motion looks best but feels less responsive and needs more animation. Their approach decouples the pose update from the animation's extracted motion, then per state or animation segment keeps, corrects or overrides facing, moving direction and speed, e.g. spreading a rotation correction across a start animation's turn so the character ends facing the stick direction.
notes: The official GDC YouTube upload drops the 'Finding Balance:' prefix. Captions garble Jeet Shroff's name.

title: Defining Game Mechanics
summary: Defines game mechanics as methods invoked by agents to interact with the game world, phrased after object-oriented programming, and separates mechanics (performative) from rules (normative). Criticizes earlier definitions, MDA's among them, as too loose to identify a mechanic: MDA's 'behaviors afforded to the player' mixes strategies a level merely suggests (taking cover in Gears of War) with calculations the system runs in the background. Discusses core, primary and secondary mechanics and applies the definition to Rez, Every Extend Extra and Shadow of the Colossus. Conceptual analysis.
notes: Game Studies is a peer-reviewed open-access journal that does not issue DOIs; the stable journal URL was checked by hand.

title: MeshGPT: Generating Triangle Meshes with Decoder-Only Transformers
venue: 2024 IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR), pp. 19615-19625
summary: Generates triangle meshes directly, one triangle token at a time, with a GPT-style model. It argues that methods built on neural fields need marching cubes, which yields dense, over-tessellated, oversmoothed and bumpy meshes that decimate poorly, whereas artist meshes are compact with sharp edges. Stated limits: 30 to 90 seconds per mesh, training meshes capped below 800 faces, only ShapeNet with four furniture-type categories, geometry without textures, and doubtful scaling to scenes. In a 49-person study people preferred its meshes to earlier generators.
notes: Full text read on ar5iv; venue on the CVF open-access page.

title: Darkest Dungeon: A Design Postmortem
summary: Red Hook's design director on Darkest Dungeon. Fifteen hero classes were deliberately left unevenly powered because strict balance mattered less in a single-player RPG; heroes are judged on their whole kit. Deliberate variance was kept without an AI director. A dominant strategy (focus-fire the front enemy so the formation collapses) was fixed in Early Access by leaving corpses in place, which caused a severe community backlash and negative reviews. Lessons: warn players, test big changes on a beta branch, offer toggles, invest in community management. Random loss of items and losing a full veteran party drove some players away.

title: Level Design in a Day: The Last of Us: Casting Shadows
venue: Game Developers Conference 2014, Level Design in a Day
summary: A Naughty Dog level designer describes building The Last of Us's combat tutorial across a sequence of spaces. A listen-mode popup was cut because the space could not support it; enemy placement and a companion demonstration invited stealth kills. In a dock area many playtesters died because an elevated covered position invited a firefight while most enemies were out of sight; the cheap fix was to have the characters drop down in the cutscene, remove the cover, and show every enemy on entry. That area served as the final test of the earlier lessons.
notes: YouTube upload is titled 'Designing the Tutorial for The Last of Us'. Alternate Vault pages for the same session (same title and conference in the Vault crawl) are listed in alt_urls.

title: Manifest Destiny: Localizing Bungie's Destiny for the World
summary: Bungie's localization manager on Destiny. Art assets were not localized, so no gameplay-critical information went into environment text, key information moved into localizable UI and icons, and English-derived acronyms caused a logo that fit few languages. Dialogue branched only where a language needed gendered forms; mission voice lines were freed from matching English length, except lip-synced cinematics; early throwaway translation exposed UI space problems, leading to auto-resizing, second lines and font scaling. Also covers web and mobile translation queues and in-house localization editors.
notes: Alternate Vault pages for the same session (same title and conference in the Vault crawl) are listed in alt_urls.

title: How to Present Game Difficulty Choices? Exploring the Impact on Player Experience
venue: Proceedings of the 2016 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems
summary: Two studies of how difficulty adjustment is offered. In the first, 40 participants played a casual game in motion-based or seated mode with menu-based, embedded or automatic difficulty adjustment; the second used an adapted version of fl0w for seated casual play. The type of adjustment affected perceived autonomy, and most players said they preferred choosing difficulty manually, but other player-experience measures were not notably affected by automatic adjustment. Casual games only.

title: Rhythm-based level generation for 2D platformers
venue: Proceedings of the 4th International Conference on Foundations of Digital Games (FDG 2009)
summary: Generates 2D platformer levels in two layers: first a rhythm of player actions (move, jump, wait, with length, density and beat type), then geometry fitted to that rhythm under a physics model of the avatar (size, top speed, jump height per button-hold time, air time), which keeps every level playable. Rhythm groups are joined by small rest platforms, and critics pick among 1000 candidates for fit to a designer-drawn path and component mix. Evaluated by argument and examples rather than player testing; targets dexterity platformers in the Mario and Sonic mould.

title: Analyzing the expressive range of a level generator
venue: Proceedings of the 2010 Workshop on Procedural Content Generation in Games (PCGames '10)
summary: Proposes expressive range analysis: pick metrics of emergent level properties rather than the generator's inputs, generate a large sample (10,000 levels here), plot 2D histograms, and compare them across parameter settings. Applied to Launchpad, a rhythm-based 2D platformer generator that ensures playability through a movement model. The analysis revealed a linearity bias caused by a small late change (raising the odds of repeating a component), showed how rhythm and component parameters shift the space, and found only about 100 of 10,000 levels met the critics' thresholds.
notes: PCGames 2010 was a peer-reviewed workshop held with FDG 2010; this is a 7-page full paper in the ACM proceedings. Evidence is a computational analysis of one generator, not a player study.

title: What Happened Here? Environmental Storytelling
summary: Presents the game environment as a narrative device that invites players to interpret, or pull, information instead of receiving exposition. Lists common environmental storytelling tools (props, scripted events, texturing, lighting, scene composition) and proposes using game systems whose reactions to player actions convey narrative, framing environmental storytelling as making the player an active participant. Summary based only on the Vault session abstract.
notes: No official GDC YouTube captions found; claims limited to the Vault abstract. Alternate Vault pages for the same session (same title and conference in the Vault crawl) are listed in alt_urls.

title: Advanced Environmental Storytelling in 'Spider: Rite of the Shrouded Moon'
summary: Tiger Style's designer on a nonlinear story without dialogue, told mainly through props in an abandoned mansion; the story is optional and pulled by the player. Methods: brainstorm visual anchor moments, count levels per character or theme, and list every inference a player must make, tying each to a specific prop. Reported difficulties: timelines, causality, motives and missing objects are hard to show; realistic props act as red herrings; inconsistent clue density misled players. Playtests exposed misreadings, and text was used sparingly where comprehension failed.
notes: Audit 2026-09-26: Smith calls the 'no words, text or dialogue' framing an exaggeration; the game uses text subtly throughout and as a crutch in a couple of places. Summary no longer calls the story wordless.

title: The Art of 'FAITH': Horror at 192x160 Pixels
summary: Smith (Airdorf Games) chose a 192x160 canvas loosely after the Atari 2600, capped the game at 15 fps and kept to roughly six to eight colours on screen, arguing that picking a constraint and keeping it matters more than hardware accuracy. Sprites are built additively: start from black, add just enough detail to be recognised, and remove pixels when a sprite is over-produced. Negative space implies paths and threat. Rotoscoped cutscenes were self-filmed, retimed, scaled to working resolution, converted to 15 fps and traced on separate Photoshop video layers; each took about 75-120 drawings, and the low frame rate kept that workload feasible.
notes: Numbers from captions. A separate design talk on the same game (smith2021-faith-horror) is already registered. Vault access tier not confirmed, so members is the cautious default; the full talk is on GDC's official YouTube channel. Access set to free because the full talk is on the official GDC YouTube channel (alt_urls). Transcript re-checked 2026-10-15: the 192x160 canvas is confirmed by the Vault session title and a repeated spoken mention; the 15 fps cap is stated three times in the talk. The six-to-eight colour count is a single hedged spoken mention ('probably no more than').

title: MORTIS 101: 'FAITH's' Horror Design Toolkit
summary: Solo developer of the horror series FAITH on their design toolkit. Every decision must serve the chosen narrative, mechanics and intended emotion (for FAITH, dread more than shock); a flashback that hurt pacing was cut. Techniques: disorienting spaces, safe areas whose safety is later broken, silence after music, and turning each mechanic against the player (notes, pause menu, examine view). One-hit deaths raise tension, but repeated retries turn the unknown into the known, so QA playthroughs located deaths and generous respawn and save points were added. Threats are telegraphed, verbs kept minimal, and detail often removed to keep the fear of the unknown. Evidence: observed playthroughs.

title: Usertesting without the user: opportunities and challenges of an AI-driven approach in games user research
summary: Position paper on replacing human participants with AI-driven 'user' agents for some stages of game user testing, motivated by the cost, time and sampling problems of human tests. It argues that imitating cognitive processes such as spatial reasoning, memory and goal-directed decisions makes such agents more useful, explores proxy agents that mimic human navigation to evaluate level designs, and proposes configurable agent populations as a data-rich supplement to, not a replacement for, current games user research.

title: 8 Frames in 16ms: Rollback Networking in 'Mortal Kombat' and 'Injustice 2'
summary: NetherRealm replaced delay-based lockstep, whose input delay varied with the connection, with peer-to-peer rollback: a constant three frames of input delay plus up to seven frames of rollback, covering about 333 ms round trip before pausing. It needed bit-for-bit determinism checked at many points, saving and restoring mutable state, and heavy optimization so seven resimulated frames plus a rendered frame fit the frame budget. A debug mode rolling back seven frames every frame was used from the start; replays with recorded network timing reproduced desyncs. Initial cost was about 7-8 engineer-years.
notes: Alternate Vault pages for the same session (same title and conference in the Vault crawl) are listed in alt_urls.

title: Game Accessibility: Practical Visual Fixes from EA's 'Madden NFL' Franchise
summary: An EA Madden engineer on low-cost visual accessibility built in about a month for Madden NFL 17. An enlarge option scaled on-field icons and moved the kick meter from world space to a fixed screen position. A colour-blind post-process adapted from Daltonize (the standard version pushed a game's bright colours together) was tuned by asking colour-blind testers, without leading, how many colours they saw; brightness and contrast controls were exposed. A faint watermark shows when accessibility settings are on. Stevens advises reviewing art mockups for accessibility before implementation, treating 30 px as a floor for text, and a 4.5:1 contrast ratio.
notes: Alternate Vault pages for the same session (same title and conference in the Vault crawl) are listed in alt_urls.

title: I Can't Hear You: Considering Deaf Gamers
summary: EA's accessibility lead, who is deaf, on designing for deaf and hard-of-hearing players. Offer separate volume channels. Subtitles should be large (Stevens suggests about 3% of screen height, roughly 32 px at 1080p, never below 28 px), sans-serif, resizable, on a configurable background box, placed consistently where they do not cover important UI, timed to speech, ideally two lines. Captions describe sounds rather than actions, in brackets. Important sounds also need visual or haptic equivalents and direction indicators; test with deaf players, or at least fresh testers who play muted; put settings at first launch and in the pause menu. Stevens recommends a 4.5:1 text contrast ratio.
notes: Alternate Vault pages for the same session (same title and conference in the Vault crawl) are listed in alt_urls.

title: Accessibility Best Practices: Mobility Considerations
summary: EA's director of accessibility, drawing on their own hand impairments, lists motor accessibility practices with examples: support many input devices including keyboard-only play; configurable dead zones and sensitivity per axis; one-stick play; stick swapping; toggles instead of holds and optional button mashing and quick-time events; automatic actions such as auto-aim, auto-jump and auto-grab; reduced-button modes such as FIFA's one-button mode; optional, levelled haptics; a friendly-fire toggle; chat wheels; flexible saving. On difficulty, citing Celeste's speed and invincibility assists as what let Stevens play, the talk argues for many options and against policing how others play.

title: Build Great Tools: Workflow Guidelines from Vicarious Visions
summary: Vicarious Visions' guidelines for in-house tools: design workflows for the people using them rather than for the engine's data layout, group tools by task, make tools easy to use correctly and hard to use incorrectly, present data in users' terms, offer undo and source-control integration as low-level services, validate with messages that say how to fix the problem, preview before committing, and look for the need behind a feature request. The speaker states the guidelines come from observation and user feedback, not quantitative research.
notes: Alternate Vault pages for the same session (same title and conference in the Vault crawl) are listed in alt_urls.

title: Motion Sickness and Postural Sway in Console Video Games
summary: Lab study in which 40 undergraduates played an off-the-shelf console game for up to 50 minutes, standing or sitting, at varied distances from the screen. Between 42% and 56% developed motion sickness, with no difference across conditions, and head and torso sway differed between players who became sick and those who did not before symptoms began. The authors conclude that console games carry a significant risk of motion sickness.

title: Balancing 'League of Legends' for Every Player, from Bronze to Bengi
summary: Riot's design lead on balancing one rule set across a huge skill range. Execution difficulty, interruptible channels, AI-controlled power, short power windows and early snowballing all change value by skill tier. Riot targets 50% champion win rates at every tier but reads them by tier, by games played on the champion and by sample size, and uses judgment: a champion near 55% was left alone because counterpicks and in-game counterplay existed. Popularity from theme is not a nerf reason; betas are poor for balance testing; disruptive changes are grouped into preseason; repeated nerfs to one champion feel bad; balanced can still be frustrating.
notes: Alternate Vault pages for the same session (same title and conference in the Vault crawl) are listed in alt_urls.

title: Beyond Framerate: Taming Your Timeslice Through Asynchrony
summary: Havok AI's lead programmer argues that expensive, infrequent, latency-tolerant work such as pathfinding and navmesh rebuilds can be spread across frames within a fixed per-frame time slice, trading response delay for a stable frame, while physics, rendering, audio and reactive AI cannot. Manual slicing and background threads both have problems (saved state, priority inversion, no guaranteed CPU time), so Havok used a foreground thread pool that checks a timer cooperatively. Costs: results arrive later, the world can change between slices, and retrofitting check points into existing code takes work.

title: Beat it. A Retrospective of 'Need for Speed: Hot Pursuit'
summary: Criterion's producer on Autolog, the asynchronous friend competition in Need for Speed: Hot Pursuit (2010). Telemetry from EA titles suggested many players had few friends online at the same time, so the team built asynchronous competition instead of pushing synchronous multiplayer. An in-game web version iterated fast but had poor console usability; auto-generated story feeds added noise that hid the racing. The fix was one recommendation feed framed as 'a friend beat you', with time records preferred over points because they need no explanation. Reports that many event starts came from recommendations; notes asynchronous play cannot be judged in one playtest session.
notes: Alternate Vault pages for the same session (same title and conference in the Vault crawl) are listed in alt_urls.

title: GameFlow: A Model for Evaluating Player Enjoyment in Games
summary: Integrates heuristics from the game literature into a model of enjoyment structured by flow. GameFlow has eight elements (concentration, challenge, player skills, control, clear goals, feedback, immersion, social interaction), each with criteria for achieving enjoyment. An initial validation used expert reviews of two real-time strategy games, one highly rated and one poorly rated: the criteria distinguished the two and explained why one succeeded, and the exercise also exposed weaknesses of the model as an evaluation tool. A heuristic model checked only by expert review in one genre.
notes: Full text is closed (no open copy found); summary and citing claims are limited to the Crossref abstract.

title: A PORTAL Post-Mortem: Integrating Writing and Design
summary: Portal's team lead and writer on keeping the story told by dialogue consistent with the story told by the player's actions. Frequent observed playtests drove cuts to exposition (testers were asked to retell the story), story embedded in environment scribbles, and dialogue written to serve gameplay needs, as with the companion cube and the incinerator that trains the final fight. Complex puzzles slowed pacing in boss prototypes; the shipped finale paired a simple puzzle with time pressure, strong visuals and a dramatic moment.
notes: Alternate Vault pages for the same session (same title and conference in the Vault crawl) are listed in alt_urls.

title: Game Feel: A Game Designer's Guide to Virtual Sensation
summary: Book-length theory of game feel built on three parts: real-time control of a virtual object, a simulated space that gives motion context, and polish that emphasizes interactions. Notes that designers lack a shared definition and use words like floaty or responsive. Grounds real-time control in the Model Human Processor and proposes describing feel through input, response, context, polish, metaphor and rules metrics. Defines polish as non-simulated cues about objects' physical properties: removing it leaves the game functional but changes how players read its physics. Closes with principles such as predictable results; case studies include Asteroids and Super Mario Bros.
notes: Content checked against the publisher's chapter abstracts for the CRC Press reissue (DOIs 10.1201/9781482267334-9 to -27, e.g. Defining Game Feel, Game Feel and Human Perception, Response Metrics, Polish Metrics, Principles of Game Feel) and the definition as quoted in peer-reviewed papers. The book's specific perceptual timing thresholds were not read and must not be cited from this entry.

title: 'RimWorld': Contrarian, Ridiculous, and Impossible Game Design Methods
summary: RimWorld's designer treats the game as a story generator rather than a contest that rewards skill in proportion. Failure was made elastic: raiders that once wiped out colonies now often loot or kidnap and leave, poor colonies get mood allowances, and players can flee. Minimal, symbolic art leaves emotion to the player's imagination and frees effort for content. Features are tested against whether they enrich characters' emotional stories, which ruled out popular requests such as deep crafting chains. Sylvester plans from a ranked idea list, not a fixed design, and asks if the game can ship without a feature. Players accepted outside threats as fair but resented colonists' own breakdowns.
notes: Alternate Vault pages for the same session (same title and conference in the Vault crawl) are listed in alt_urls.

title: Ten Principles for Good Level Design
summary: A Square Enix Montreal level designer (formerly on Medal of Honor and Hitman) offers ten opinion-based principles modelled on Dieter Rams: clear navigation except where confusion is deliberate, a consistent visual language on the critical path, levels that keep introducing or subverting mechanics, surprise instead of predictable rollercoaster pacing (Dead Space 2 holds back enemies for about 15 minutes after the return to the Ishimura), risk/reward routes so players choose difficulty in play, reuse of space, and the level as a delivery system for mechanics. Grey-box risky ideas early; a Medal of Honor puzzle type was cut late because it was never proven.
notes: Alternate Vault pages for the same session (same title and conference in the Vault crawl) are listed in alt_urls.

title: Puzzle Game Magic Secrets
summary: The designer of the puzzle game Limelight frames puzzle difficulty around working memory. 'Noise' is anything that takes attention without being part of the solution: state the solution in a sentence and remove what the sentence does not mention. Every level needs a purpose (teach, reinforce, a unique moment, a breather); knowing the answer but failing to execute it is not fun, so keep execution apart from reasoning; make actions obviously possible or impossible. Warning signs: a player asks 'was that right?' or keeps repeating an impossible action.
notes: Alternate Vault pages for the same session (same title and conference in the Vault crawl) are listed in alt_urls.

title: Reading the Rules of 'Baba Is You'
summary: The solo developer of Baba Is You on its rule parser. From the jam prototype on, objects have no built-in properties; only rules formed from word blocks give them meaning. Rules read in straight lines, and the parser works in passes: discard short word runs, check word-type order and allowed neighbours, then expand 'all', 'not' and 'and', with disabling rules winning. The rule data format was rebuilt several times as conditionals were added. Features kept for fit with the theme made parsing much harder and left known edge-case bugs, which level design hid by not giving players the tools to reach them; a level editor with sharing removes that protection. An 'if' word was cut.
notes: Alternate Vault pages for the same session (same title and conference in the Vault crawl) are listed in alt_urls.

title: Generative AI in Game Development: A Qualitative Research Synthesis
venue: Proceedings of the 2026 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems
summary: Meta-ethnography of ten qualitative studies (2020-2025) of generative AI in game development, synthesised into nine constructs. Output is provisional and needs expert curation and editing; value is clearest in ideation and prototyping and weakest at downstream asset inclusion, where slowdowns appear. Unedited 3D output was rarely usable (sparse evidence), and in image generation acceptable results came from curating many outputs. Risks include stylistic convergence and labour precarity. Recommends per-asset-class acceptance criteria, QA hand-offs, provenance capture, codified licensing and data ownership, and budgeted evaluation time.
notes: Read the arXiv v2 HTML in two passes. A synthesis of secondary studies, several with student or small samples. Re-checked 2026-10-15 against arXiv HTML v2 (C1-C9 synthesis and discussion). Summary narrowed: the curation finding is stated for image generation, 3D evidence is flagged as sparse, and labour precarity is general rather than specific to concept artists. title: Producer Bootcamp: The Bane of All Development Postmortems: Communication is Hard So Give Up Now
summary: Gearbox head of production surveys communication failures named in published postmortems and Gearbox's own practice: specs not kept current as plans changed, cross-team dependencies without a plan, cuts made too late because nobody owned them. Recommends listening before talking, retrospectives soon after milestones (start, stop, continue), knowing project status without polling people, clear ownership and a named customer for every feature, showing the whole dependency chain when proposing a cut, and making it acceptable to say 'I don't know'. Based on Thibault's reading and experience, not a study.
notes: Vault id 1022224 is the same session; 1022223 is used consistently. Alternate Vault pages for the same session (same title and conference in the Vault crawl) are listed in alt_urls.

title: Level Design Workshop: Designing 'Celeste'
venue: Game Developers Conference 2017, Level Design Workshop
summary: Celeste's designer on levels for a hard precision platformer: an impossible route must look impossible or players keep trying it; safety (solid ground, grip, crumbling blocks) is the main pacing tool; rooms are short and death returns the player to the room start, so extra length raises the stakes; the only teaching text is the controls; mechanics are primed before they are required, with cheap deaths as feedback; an optional two-room teaching branch was added where most testers stalled, invisible to players who solve the room alone; a post-climax cool-down improved once all hazards were removed.
notes: The Vault lists the speaker as Matt Thorson; Thorson now publishes as Maddy Thorson.

title: Search-Based Procedural Content Generation: A Taxonomy and Survey
venue: IEEE Transactions on Computational Intelligence and AI in Games 3(3)
summary: Survey that names search-based PCG. Its taxonomy separates online from offline generation (online needs speed and predictable runtime and quality), necessary from optional content (necessary content must always be correct), seeds from parameter vectors, stochastic from deterministic, and constructive from generate-and-test methods. It discusses representation (direct vs indirect encodings, locality; searching over raw seeds is no better than random search) and evaluation functions (direct, simulation-based with agents, interactive with players), and notes search has no guaranteed completion time or quality.
notes: The author-hosted PDF is served only over plain HTTP (the HTTPS host presents an unrelated certificate), so no alternate URL is listed.

title: An Architectural Approach to Level Design: Second Edition
summary: Applies architectural history and spatial theory to level design. The publisher's preview read here (front matter, table of contents, introduction, opening of chapter 1) defines level design as the execution of gameplay into a space for players to inhabit, argues that architectural vocabulary for sight lines, orientation and spatial sequence complements playtesting, notes that terms such as grayboxing mean different things to different designers, and lists chapters on workflows, pacing, spatial types, tutorial levels and procedural generation. Claims are limited to that preview.

title: The Game Outcomes Project: How Teamwork, Leadership and Culture Drive Results
summary: Reports a 2014 survey of 273 developers about their most recent non-cancelled project, relating 116 culture questions to a composite outcome score (return, timeliness, acclaim, internal goals). Development methodology showed no significant link to outcomes; a shared vision was the strongest correlate; teams with the least crunch had the best outcomes and, after controlling for culture, crunch added little. Tozour stresses the limits: not peer-reviewed, self-reported and retrospective, correlational, crunch not precisely defined, and questions not validated instruments.
notes: A practitioner survey presented at GDC, not peer-reviewed; cited only with its stated limits. Vault id 1023258 is the same session; the Vault page offers the slides free. Alternate Vault pages for the same session (same title and conference in the Vault crawl) are listed in alt_urls.

title: System-Centric Puzzle Design in 'Patrick's Parabox'
summary: The designer of Patrick's Parabox kept puzzles approachable to showcase one recursive system: Traynor removed unnecessary solution steps, trimmed options unrelated to the solution, moved harder variants to optional puzzles, treated puzzle ordering as a skill as important as making puzzles, always left several puzzles open so players could not get stuck, and ran about 15 full-game think-aloud video playtests with new players. Ideas came from forcing discovered interactions, pairing each mechanic with every other, and near-misses seen in playtests.
notes: Alternate Vault pages for the same session (same title and conference in the Vault crawl) are listed in alt_urls.

title: Shared World Shooter: Destiny's Networked Mission Architecture
summary: Bungie's engineering lead on Destiny's hybrid topology: combat, physics and AI run peer-to-peer on a console "physics host" for low latency, while mission scripts and a minimal, atomically reconciled activity state run on cloud activity hosts that never migrate and arbitrate host migration. Players in public areas saw a physics host migration about every 160 seconds; a new host reconciles every sensor against the activity state. Dedicated servers for everything were rejected on cost and latency. Costs: up-front engineering for every sensor, designer complexity, and an exploit where boss logic lived in client-side systems.

title: Belief in the law of small numbers
summary: Classic paper arguing that people hold strong but wrong intuitions about chance: they expect a random sample, even a small one, to be highly representative of its population. Illustrated with questionnaire responses from professional psychologists, who overestimated how likely a finding was to replicate. The paper concerns research practice, not games; it is cited here only for the general intuition that short random sequences are expected to mirror the underlying odds.

title: Twine Reference: Basic Concepts
summary: Official Twine reference page describing Twine as a tool for editing, not playing, interactive narratives. A story is made of one or more passages, one of which is the start passage shown first; four story formats ship with Twine (Harlowe, the default; Chapbook; Snowman; SugarCube), and a shared story is an HTML file that opens in any web browser without Twine.

summary: Manual page on the order of MonoBehaviour event functions. Its limitations section says you cannot rely on the order in which the same event function runs for different GameObjects unless that order is documented or set explicitly, and cannot set it between instances of the same script.

title: MonoBehaviour.FixedUpdate
summary: Script reference. FixedUpdate runs on the physics update interval set by Time.fixedDeltaTime, 0.02 seconds by default, and may run zero, one or several times per rendered frame, whereas Update runs once per rendered frame. Physics work such as applying forces belongs in FixedUpdate.

title: ScriptableObject
summary: Manual page. A ScriptableObject holds data shared by reference, so many objects use one copy in memory. In the Editor, data can be saved to ScriptableObjects in Edit and Play mode; a standalone player at run time can only read saved data. Changes made by script in Edit mode need to be marked dirty to be saved.

title: Run tests from the command line
summary: Unity Test Framework page showing how to run tests from the Editor command line with -runTests, -batchmode, -projectPath, -testResults and -testPlatform, and advising -batchmode so no manual input is needed.

title: Time.timeScale
summary: Script reference. timeScale scales game time; changes take effect on following frames. At zero, FixedUpdate and coroutines waiting with WaitForSeconds are not called. Changing timeScale does not change fixedDeltaTime, so the physics rate stays constant relative to game time rather than real time.

title: Copyright Registration Guidance: Works Containing Material Generated by Artificial Intelligence
summary: Policy statement of 16 March 2023. Material whose expressive elements an AI system determined from a prompt lacks human authorship and must be disclaimed. A work containing AI material can be registered for its human parts, such as creative selection, arrangement or sufficient modification. Applicants must disclose AI content that is more than de minimis, describe the human contribution, exclude the AI material in the claim, and correct earlier filings by supplementary registration.
notes: US registration practice only; read the govinfo copy.

title: Copyright and Artificial Intelligence, Part 2: Copyrightability
summary: Report released 29 January 2025. Generative-AI output is protected by US copyright only where a human author has determined sufficient expressive elements: a perceptible human-authored work within the output, or creative selection, arrangement or modification of the output. Given current generally available technology, prompts alone do not give enough control. Using AI as an assistive tool, or including AI material in a larger human-made work, does not bar protection; contributions are judged case by case. The Office found existing law adequate and no case for new protection of AI output; Part 3 covers training.
notes: Read the Office's news release and the Copyright Office blog summary, not the full report PDF. US law only. Full text read 2026-10-15 from the Office's report PDF at https://www.copyright.gov/ai/Copyright-and-Artificial-Intelligence-Part-2-Copyrightability-Report.pdf (52 PDF pages): executive summary, prompts analysis (p. 18) and conclusion (p. 41). Summary now keeps the report's 'current generally available technology' condition on prompts.

title: Coming Soon (Steamworks Documentation)
summary: Explains Steam's Coming Soon store page. For new products, a Coming Soon page must be up for at least two weeks before release; Valve recommends publishing it as soon as the developer is ready to talk publicly about the game, so players can follow and wishlist it.
notes: Platform requirement; page read on the checked date. Requirements change, so recheck before shipping.

title: Content Survey (Steamworks Documentation)
summary: Section 3 of the Steam content survey covers generative AI used to create content that ships with the game and that players consume (artwork, sound, narrative, localisation) or used inside the product. Two categories: Pre-Generated (made with AI tools during development) and Live-Generated (made while the game runs). Developers describe their use, promise the game has no illegal or infringing content and matches its marketing, and for live generation describe guardrails. AI content is reviewed like other content; efficiency gains from tools are not the section's focus.
notes: Policy as read on the checked date; the page gives no dates and does not say how disclosures appear on store pages. Recheck before shipping.

title: Review Process (Steamworks Documentation)
summary: Steam reviews a new product's store page and its build before release. Each review typically takes 3-5 business days; Valve asks developers to submit at least 7 business days before the page should go live and to plan at least 7 business days for build review. The build must launch on every supported OS and implement every feature listed on the store page. After approval, updates need no further review.
notes: Platform requirement; page read on the checked date. Requirements change, so recheck before shipping.

title: Between challenge and defeat: repeated player-death and game enjoyment
summary: Facial electromyography study in which players of a shooter died often and occasionally reached safe zones. Players smiled after dying even though they later rated deaths negatively; the smile response weakened as deaths repeated, and reaching safe zones did not produce a pleasure pattern. The authors propose that dying at first signals an enjoyable challenge, but stops being enjoyable when repeated deaths come without clear progress. Only the abstract was read.

title: Automated Testing and Profiling for 'Call of Duty'
summary: Activision's build and test system runs every check-in through compile, asset conversion, a game run and screenshots; records any statistic (frame time, memory, build time) per build as a graph linked to changelists; and nightly teleports the player to stored map locations for 30-second performance captures colored against budget. Failures are bucketed by error signature and retried automatically with retries kept visible. Scale was about 700 worker PCs and 300 devkits. Van Valburg recommends configuration as code in source control, automating only repetitive checks, and not writing your own build server.
notes: Alternate Vault pages for the same session (same title and conference in the Vault crawl) are listed in alt_urls.

title: Building a Mixing Sandbox for 'Just Cause 4'
summary: Avalanche's sound designer on rebuilding Just Cause 4's mix as a system begun at the design phase rather than a late pass. In the previous game's priority and sidechain mix, designers of low-priority sounds pushed assets hot and the mix pumped. JC4 routed the player's vehicle to higher-priority paths, cleared surround space layer by layer, used discrete subwoofer content, and replaced most compression with context snapshots: global states such as combat or storms, and local microstates such as an enemy targeting the player. Storms start overwhelming and fade over time before normal hierarchy returns; ambience drops as enemy count rises. The approach depended on playtest feedback.

title: "An Adapt-or-Die Type of Situation": Perception, Adoption, and Use of Text-to-Image-Generation AI by Game Industry Professionals
venue: Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction 7 (CHI PLAY)
summary: Interviews with 14 Finnish game professionals (Template Analysis, 12 themes). Almost all used text-to-image output for inspiration and to prototype ideas, leads especially to pitch; over half reported using it for production-ready art, yet most said it could not deliver production-ready content and almost all edited it (anatomy errors, details that missed intent). Weak points: style consistency across assets, project-specific styles, randomness and poor control. Concerns: jobs, devalued skills, copyright, use of other artists' work as training data without adequate compensation, expected pressure to adopt. Most described their role shifting from craftsperson toward director of the tool.
notes: Read arXiv HTML v5 up to section 5.3.3 (about 100k of 164k characters); ACM full text returned 403. Crossref gives pages 131-164; arXiv gives Article 379. Full text read 2026-10-15 from arXiv HTML v5 (all sections incl. discussion and limitations). Summary corrected: the interviewees' training-data concern is about lack of adequate compensation (and copyright); 'without consent' is a press quote in the paper's media review, not an interview finding. Role shift reported by most participants, not some. Metadata matches Crossref (PACM HCI 7, CHI PLAY; Crossref pages 131-164).

title: Less is More: Designing Awesome AI
summary: Frames game AI as a perception problem: players find patterns, anthropomorphize and invent stories for behavior, and higher fidelity raises expectations. Describes building the opponent for ROCKETSROCKETSROCKETS by watching people play, naming broad behaviors, starting with a deliberately simple follower and adding only what observed play needed, using raycast navigation plus a small state machine and non-uniform randomness. Advice: support the core experience, start simple, and remember that once an AI looks stupid that impression is hard to undo.
notes: Transcript from the official GDC YouTube upload (titled 'Less is More: Designing Awesome AI for Games'). The Vault also lists id 1022430. Alternate Vault pages for the same session (same title and conference in the Vault crawl) are listed in alt_urls.

title: Modeling AI Perception and Awareness in Splinter Cell: Blacklist
summary: Ubisoft Toronto's perception model for a stealth game, judged by whether detection feels fair, gives consistent feedback and looks plausible, goals that often conflict. Vision used nested cone and 'coffin' shapes, raycasts to several body points and lighting, and needed repeated playtest tuning; players wanted a less forgiving model than expected. A room-and-chokepoint graph gave environmental awareness and path-based sound distances; noticing changed objects such as opened doors was cheap and noticed by reviewers. Off-screen distant NPCs had hearing halved for some events, tiered barks explained reactions, and detection spread only through explicit communication.
notes: Transcript from the official GDC YouTube upload. The halved-hearing figure was cross-checked against Walsh's chapter in Game AI Pro 2. The Vault also lists ids 1020436 and 1021236. Audit 2026-09-26: content checks out against the transcript. Venue says '(AI Summit)', but lookup.py vault reports track 'Design' for ids 1020195, 1020436 and 1021236; the transcript's Q&A hints at an AI Summit context but the Vault does not confirm it, so consider 'Game Developers Conference 2014'. Alternate Vault pages for the same session (same title and conference in the Vault crawl) are listed in alt_urls.

title: Automated Level of Detail Generation for HALO: REACH
summary: Bungie's graphics engineer on why Halo: Reach generated LODs by default. Earlier games let artists attach hand-made low-res models, but artists mostly did not, so with a large asset count and constant iteration the system rebuilt simplified meshes and impostors on every update, carried animation data over, and moved distant shading to cheaper per-vertex lighting. Artists and QA kept a manual switch to disable broken cases. The speaker concludes that the automatic result covers most assets, but artists should be able to author their own LODs for the rest, and that an in-house simplifier could take artist hints.
notes: Captions are heavily garbled. The impostor switch distance (about 30 times the bounding radius) and the share of assets the tool handled (about 90-95%) are from captions, low confidence. Vault access tier not confirmed, so members is the cautious default; the full talk is on GDC's official YouTube channel. Access set to free because the full talk is on the official GDC YouTube channel (alt_urls).

title: Boosting 3D Object Generation through PBR Materials
summary: Adds PBR materials to image-to-3D output: a fine-tuned diffusion model estimates albedo, a bump map is optimised against a predicted normal map, and roughness and metalness are set per part by segmenting the mesh and asking a vision-language model for values that an artist can then adjust. It argues that colour-only textures block relighting and editing, and notes highlights or shadows left in the albedo of some baselines. Stated limits: albedo colours can drift from the input, single-colour objects fail, output is triangle meshes only, and segmentation is slow.
notes: Full text read as arXiv HTML v1; DOI from Crossref.

title: Agency Reconsidered
venue: DiGRA 2009: Breaking New Ground: Innovation in Games, Play, Practice and Theory
summary: Conceptual paper that treats agency as something occurring between player and game when the actions players want are among those the game supports through an underlying model. Reviews Murray, Church and Mateas: adventure games offer more available actions than dramatic reasons to take them; agency needs a playable model of the fiction's domain rather than surface illusions; stronger presence can raise expectations beyond what the model supports (citing Dow's study of Facade); and designs can let plans fail without ending play. Theoretical argument, not an experiment.
notes: DiGRA 2009 conference proceedings (peer-reviewed full paper); read in the authors' PDF.

title: "What went right and what went wrong": an analysis of 155 postmortems from game development
venue: Proceedings of the 38th International Conference on Software Engineering Companion (ICSE SEIP 2016)
summary: Two authors coded 155 Gamasutra postmortems (1998-2015; mostly teams of 20 or fewer, most projects under two years) into 22 categories of what went right and wrong. Game design (50%), development process (43%), team and art went right most often; obstacles (37%), schedule (25%), development process (24%) and game design (22%, often over-ambitious designs) went wrong most often. Successful processes combined up-front planning, prototypes as proofs of concept and iteration. Postmortems are self-reported and may omit failures.
notes: Full paper in the ICSE 2016 Software Engineering in Practice (SEIP) track, which ACM publishes in the ICSE Companion proceedings; SEIP papers are peer-reviewed full papers, so the companion-track warning is expected. Read the author-hosted PDF.

title: Saving the Galaxy: Managing State in 'Star Wars Jedi: Survivor'
summary: Session description only. Respawn on managing persistent global state in a series that mixes non-linear Metroidvania structure with a strong central story. Facts such as a shortcut being unlocked, a line of dialogue having played or a boss being beaten depend on one another, yet there is no single order in which they must occur. The talk reviews the failures of the unstructured approach used on Star Wars Jedi: Fallen Order and describes the centralized state system built for Star Wars Jedi: Survivor.
notes: No official GDC YouTube upload found; claims are limited to the Vault session description.

title: Game a Week: Teaching Students to Prototype
summary: Two educators describe classes (NYU from 2014, RMIT from 2016) where students make a small digital game every week. The motive: students over-commit to their first idea and engineer early code for large scope, and long projects make it hard to drop weak ideas. Each prototype should answer an open question about a mechanic, an aesthetic or an experience, need not be bug-free, and may reuse scripts and assets; grading only the best few rewards risk-taking. Many attempts raised the odds of one strong idea. Cautions: the pace is hard for students still learning their tools, and they added a skip week.
notes: Educators Summit session.

title: Feeding the Maw: Managing a Live Narrative Game in 'Fallen London'
summary: Failbetter's writer and editor on running Fallen London, a long-lived free-to-play browser narrative game. Its content is not a branching plot: thousands of variables called qualities gate content and are changed by choices, allowing callbacks across the game, and some content is dealt from a card deck. Covers adding a monthly narrative subscription, the writing load on a small content team, themed story runs to constrain writing, use of freelancers, and a stated policy of not selling mechanically optimal choices or escape from permanent failure. Content-volume figures given are the studio's own.
notes: Alternate Vault pages for the same session (same title and conference in the Vault crawl) are listed in alt_urls.

title: Balancing the Economy for 'Albion Online'
summary: Former EVE Online designer on Albion's player-driven economy. The economy is the extrinsic incentive structure, so the most efficient path is what the game tells players to do; the aim is to make the most enjoyable activities also the most rewarding. Process: goals, then relationships, then simple geometric math from one anchor. Power rises about 1.2x per tier while resource rarity triples; top-tier gear acts as a wealth sink. Salvage and transmutation set a price floor and ceiling. Automate spreadsheet exports, expect players to solve simple systems, and use metrics to refine causal models rather than optimize blindly.

title: GPT-4V(ision) is a Human-Aligned Evaluator for Text-to-3D Generation
venue: 2024 IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR), pp. 22227-22238
summary: Has GPT-4V compare pairs of text-to-3D assets from multi-view colour and normal renders on chosen criteria and turns the votes into Elo ratings. Single-purpose metrics such as CLIP similarity, an aesthetic score and PickScore each match human rankings on some criteria but poorly on others, worst on 3D plausibility (best baseline Kendall tau 0.484 against 0.641). Stated limits: small experiments, hallucination and position bias, possible gaming, miscounted objects, overreaction to geometric noise, and poor agreement among general users (kappa about 0.3), so experts supplied the reference labels.
notes: Read about 97% of the arXiv HTML v2 (the final 3.7k characters not read).

title: Structured 3D Latents for Scalable and Versatile 3D Generation
venue: 2025 IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR), pp. 21469-21480
summary: TRELLIS generates a sparse voxel structure carrying learned features, trained on 500K objects, and decodes it to 3D Gaussians, radiance fields or meshes. Meshes carry per-vertex colours and normals; the paper describes no UV layout or PBR materials. The authors state that image-to-3D does not separate lighting, so shading and highlights from the input image are baked into the asset, with PBR prediction left to future work. Its user study judged appearance on the Gaussian output and geometry on the mesh output.
notes: Project page labels it a CVPR 2025 Highlight. Read arXiv HTML v1 in full, including Appendix E (limitations).

title: ToonCrafter: Generative Cartoon Interpolation
summary: Method paper on generating in-between frames for cartoons. Argues that traditional correspondence-based interpolation, which implicitly assumes linear motion and no dis-occlusion, often struggles with the exaggerated, large, non-linear motion and occlusion common in cartoons. Adapts live-action video diffusion priors to the cartoon domain with a toon rectification learning strategy, adds a dual-reference 3D decoder to recover details lost in the compressed latent space, and supports sketch guidance.
notes: Journal paper in ACM TOG, presented at SIGGRAPH Asia 2024. Abstract read via arXiv. Full text read 2026-10-15 from arXiv 2405.17933v1 (the only arXiv version); the ACM DL copy returns 403 to the fetcher, and Crossref's abstract for the TOG version matches arXiv word for word. Crossref gives volume 43, issue 6 (published 19 Nov 2024), added to venue. Summary unchanged.

title: A systematic classification of cheating in online games
venue: Proceedings of the 4th ACM SIGCOMM Workshop on Network and System Support for Games (NetGames '05)
summary: Taxonomy of online-game cheating by the vulnerability exploited, the consequence and who cheats, built from known cases. One category is exploiting a bug or design loophole without modifying code or data, illustrated by Lucasfilm's Habitat: a pricing error let players buy items from a vending machine and sell them to a pawn shop for more, repeating the loop to become rich overnight. Other categories include compromised servers, insider misuse and social engineering. The authors argue that fairness, in addition to confidentiality, integrity, availability and authenticity, is needed to explain cheating.
notes: Full text read from the author-hosted PDF.

title: Artificial Intelligence and Games
summary: Academic textbook on AI in games. Sections read: 1.4 (why AI for games: NPC behavior, content generation, player modeling); 2.2 (FSMs, behavior trees and utility-based AI as hand-authored methods: FSMs simple but predictable and unwieldy at scale; behavior trees modular and widely adopted after Halo 2; utility AI scores every option from considerations such as range, inertia and noise); 3.1.4 (NPCs usually need an illusion of intelligence or deliberate predictability, such as learnable stealth patrols and boss patterns, rather than winning play); 4.6 (evaluating content generators: functional versus aesthetic properties, constraints, expressive-range visualization, AI and human playtesting).
notes: Read from the authors' free January 2018 draft at gameaibook.org; sections 1.4, 2.2, 3.1.4 and 4.6 only. Extend this entry if other sections are cited.

title: Yarn Spinner documentation: Saliency, Functions, Variable Storage, Line Tagging
summary: Official Yarn Spinner 3 documentation. Node groups and line groups choose content through saliency strategies (first, best by condition complexity, best least recently viewed, and a random variant that is the default). Built-in visited() and visited_count() test whether nodes have run. Variables are limited to strings, numbers, booleans and enums and live in a replaceable variable storage the game can supply. Every line has a line ID, unique across the project, that links it to voice-over and translations.
notes: Living documentation; year is the access year. Only the pages listed were read.

title: Motivations for Play in Online Games
summary: Factor analysis of 40 motivation items answered online by about 3,000 players of EverQuest, Dark Age of Camelot, Ultima Online and Star Wars Galaxies. Ten subcomponents grouped into three weakly correlated components: achievement (advancement, mechanics, competition), social (socializing, relationship, teamwork) and immersion (discovery, role-playing, customization, escapism). High scores on one component did not suppress others, contrary to the trade-off assumed by Bartle's player types. Age explained achievement scores better than gender; escapism best predicted self-reported problematic use. Self-selected MMORPG sample.
notes: Read the author's manuscript copy (its header gives 2007); the Crossref record gives the 2006 volume 9 issue.

title: The Reward for Luck: Understanding the Effect of Random Reward Mechanisms in Video Games on Player Experience
venue: CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI '22)
summary: Qualitative study: video analysis of 35 random reward mechanisms in 28 games plus semi-structured interviews with 14 players (snowball sample, mostly young men). Participants valued random rewards for freshness and replay, saw a luck-versus-skill trade-off that casual players welcomed and competitive settings resisted, and disliked progress gated by random drops; one preferred a deterministic grind. Paid pulls turned randomness into 'simulated determinism'. Pity systems, most common in paid mechanisms, were seen both as fair guarantees and as temptations to keep spending; near-miss presentations were noticed. Presentation expectations scaled with reward value and cost.
notes: CHI full paper (peer-reviewed). Read the author-hosted PDF.

title: The Full Spelunky on SPELUNKY XBLA
summary: Yu and Hull on turning freeware Spelunky into the Xbox Live Arcade version. Yu outlines the level generator: a 4x4 grid of rooms, a path drawn from an entrance at the top to an exit at the bottom, room templates chosen by whether a room lies on that path and by game area, randomized chunks inside templates, then monsters, treasure and traps. Yu says item and event rarities were set by feel and adjusted in testing, and describes choosing the simplest brute-force approach that produced working levels.
notes: The official GDC YouTube upload of this session is titled 'The Spelunky HD Postmortem'; speakers and content match the Vault session.

title: Independent Games Summit: One More Run: The Making of 'Spelunky 2'
summary: Derek Yu on making Spelunky 2 with a larger, remote team. The sequel built on what Yu saw as Spelunky's distinctive trait among roguelikes: high interactivity, with monsters following the player's rules, destructible terrain and chain reactions. Covers investing in debug tools (spawning, replays, slow motion) that Yu had avoided on the first game, limiting costly liquid simulation, a rollback online mode whose console launch was largely unplayable for many players, optional system-tied quests in a text-light game, room-grid level generation with a linked back layer, and adding comfort without losing the game's harshness. Early Access was skipped because the design vision was firm.

title: Game accessibility: a survey
venue: Universal Access in the Information Society 10(1)
summary: Survey of game accessibility research and practice. It models play as three steps (receive stimuli, determine a response, provide input) and maps impairments onto them: sensory impairments block the first, cognitive impairments the second, motor impairments the third. From accessible and modified games it distils high-level strategies (enhance or replace stimuli; reduce stimuli, time pressure or input; replace input) and low-level ones such as captions, high contrast, slowing the game or automating input. It notes trade-offs: converting feedback between senses loses information, and automating input can change the gameplay or give an unfair edge in multiplayer.
notes: Full text read from the authors' preprint hosted by the University of Nevada, Reno.

title: Animation Bootcamp: Tricks of the Trade
summary: Rapid-fire tips from six game animators. Lab Zero found that detail that worked in a close fighting-game camera became noise when the camera pulled back for a platformer, so animation had to be simplified and exaggerated; silhouettes also read differently from above. For first-person, Boss Key's animator advises not putting style ahead of readability: break an action into key beats, hold each long enough to register, then add style. Sparkypants' lead starts hit reactions from a bigger recovery pose for a quicker, clearer read and adds a recognition pose before an NPC's anticipation. Another speaker asks of each gameplay animation whether it reads, how it feels, and when control returns.

title: Dark Patterns in the Design of Games
venue: Proceedings of the 8th International Conference on the Foundations of Digital Games (FDG 2013)
summary: Defines a dark game design pattern as one used intentionally by a game's creator to cause negative experiences for players that are against their best interests and happen without their consent, distinguishing it from honest bad design and from player-accepted hardship or benevolent deception such as rubber-band AI. Describes temporal patterns (grinding, playing by appointment), monetary patterns (pay to skip, pre-delivered content, monetized rivalries or pay to win) and social-capital patterns (social pyramid schemes), and offers guiding questions, for example whether players can judge the time or money a goal will require.
notes: FDG 2013 full paper; FDG is a peer-reviewed conference and its 2013 proceedings (SASDG) have no DOI. The url is the DBLP record, which may serve a bot check, so verify_sources cannot find the title there; title and authors were confirmed by hand against the full text, read at http://www.fdg2013.org/program/papers/paper06_zagal_etal.pdf, which is http only.

title: Video game loot boxes are linked to problem gambling: Results of a large-scale survey
summary: Online survey of 7,422 self-selected adult gamers recruited through Reddit. Loot box spending was associated with problem gambling severity (PGSI), a small-to-medium effect (eta squared 0.054), much stronger than the link between problem gambling and other microtransaction spending (0.004). The design is correlational, so it cannot say whether loot boxes lead to problem gambling or problem gamblers spend more on them; the sample was unblinded and may not represent gamers. The authors argue this supports regulating loot boxes, for example restricting them to players of legal gambling age.

title: Paint3D: Paint Anything 3D with Lighting-Less Texture Diffusion Models
venue: 2024 IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR), pp. 4252-4262
summary: Generates 2K UV texture maps for an untextured mesh from text or an image: views from a depth-aware diffusion model form a coarse texture, then diffusion models working in UV space fill gaps and remove lighting artifacts. It argues that textures from earlier 2D-diffusion methods have lighting baked in, which clashes with new lighting in a normal game or render pipeline. Stated limits: the coarse stage still shows the multi-face problem, and it cannot make material (PBR) maps or change geometry. Evaluated with FID and KID on 20 views and a 30-person rating study.
notes: Full text read as arXiv HTML v2.

title: Adding Conditional Control to Text-to-Image Diffusion Models
venue: 2023 IEEE/CVF International Conference on Computer Vision (ICCV)
summary: Presents ControlNet, an architecture that adds spatial conditioning to large pretrained text-to-image diffusion models while keeping the pretrained model locked, connecting the new layers through zero-initialized convolutions. Tests conditions such as edges, depth, segmentation and human pose with Stable Diffusion, alone or combined, with or without text prompts, and reports robust training on both small and large datasets.
notes: ICCV 2023 main conference paper. Abstract read via arXiv. Full text read 2026-10-15 from the ICCV 2023 CVF open-access PDF (openaccess.thecvf.com/content/ICCV2023/papers/Zhang_Adding_Conditional_Control_to_Text-to-Image_Diffusion_Models_ICCV_2023_paper.pdf); arXiv v3 also downloaded. Summary, title and authors match. Summary unchanged.
